en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Aṭṭhaka-nipāta of the Aṅguttara Nikāya
1. The First Fifty-Section (Paṭhamapaṇṇāsaka) 1.
The Chapter on Loving-kindness (Mettāvagga) 1.
Commentary on the Discourse on Loving-kindness (Mettāsuttavaṇṇanā)
1. In the first [sutta] of the *Aṭṭhaka-nipāta*: "Cultivated" (*āsevitā*) means practiced with diligence. "Developed" (*bhāvitā*) means increased.
"Made much of" (*bahulīkatā*) means performed repeatedly. "Made a vehicle" (*yānikatā*) means made like a suitable vehicle.
"Made a basis" (*vatthukatā*) means made like a foundation in the sense of being a support. "Established" (*anuṭṭhitā*) means present before one. "Well-purified" (*paricitā*) means...
"From all sides" means from every direction; "heaped up" means accumulated. "Well undertaken" means well-initiated and well-performed.
"Blessings" refers to virtues. Regarding what should be said about the phrases "he sleeps happily," and so forth, we shall explain that in the Eleventh Chapter (Ekādasaka-nipāta).
"Immeasurable" means immeasurable by way of pervasion. "The fetters become thin for one who sees the destruction of acquisitions."

The meaning is that for one who has gradually attained arahantship—known as the exhaustion of acquisitions (*upadhikkhaya*)—through insight (*vipassanā*) based on the foundation of loving-kindness (*mettā*), the ten fetters (*saṃyojana*) are abandoned.
Alternatively, "the fetters become attenuated" means that both aversion (*paṭigha*) and the fetters associated with aversion become thin.
"Of one who sees the exhaustion of acquisitions" refers to the exhaustion of those very same defilement-acquisitions (*kilesūpadhi*).
For one who perceives [beings] by way of attaining loving-kindness (*mettā*). "He becomes skilled thereby" means that through that practice of loving-kindness, he becomes skilled.
"Possessing a multitude of beings" means endowed with a multitude designated as "beings"; the sense is "filled with beings.
"Having conquered" means having won by means of the Dhamma alone, without staff or sword. "Sovereign kings" refers to righteous kings who resemble seers (*isi*). "Performing sacrifices" means...
Giving gifts, they wandered about. Regarding the "horse-sacrifice" and so forth:

it is said that in ancient times during the era of kings, there were four bases of social integration—namely, the grain-sacrifice (*sassa-medha*), the human-sacrifice (*purisa-medha*), the *sammā-pāsa*, and the *vācā-peyya*—by means of which kings held the world together. Among those, from the grain that had been produced...
The taking of a tenth share [of the harvest] is called the *sassamedha*; the meaning is that one is wise (*medhāvī*) in the successful cultivation of crops.
The provision of food and wages for six months to great warriors is called the *purisamedha*; the meaning is that one is wise in winning over men.
Taking a written contract from the hands of poor people and providing them with wealth amounting to one or two thousand [coins] for three years without interest—
It is called *sammāpāsa*. For it truly causes people to look toward [the king], as if fixing them in their hearts; therefore, it is called *sammāpāsa*.
Furthermore, speaking with gentle words in the manner beginning with “Dear father,” “Uncle,” and so forth, is called *vācāpeyya*, which means pleasant speech.
Thus, a kingdom embraced by these four bases of sympathy (*saṅgahavatthu*) becomes prosperous.

It was prosperous, flourishing, abundant in food and drink, secure, and free from calamity. People lived in joy and delight, clutching their children to their breasts, dwelling with their houses open.
Because there were no door-bolts at the entrances of these houses, it is called "Niraggaḷa" (boltless). This is the ancient tradition.

Later, however, during the time of King Okkāka, the brahmins—having exchanged these four bases of social integration for this prosperity of the kingdom and having turned it upside down—performed the five sacrifices known as the horse-sacrifice (*assamedha*), the human-sacrifice (*purisamedha*), and so forth.
Among those, "horse-sacrifice" (*assamedha*) means they sacrifice (or kill) horses; it is that which is to be sacrificed by means of two preliminary rites (*pariyañña*).

This is a designation for a sacrifice that, on its very last day, involves the terrifying slaughter of ninety-seven hundred and five animals and humans, and where all remaining wealth is given as a sacrificial fee, with the exception of the ground and the men themselves. Because they "sacrifice" (medhanti) the men here, it is called a *purisamedha*.
It is that which is to be sacrificed by means of four types of sacrificial sessions (*pariyañña*), together with the ground.
This is a designation for the sacrifice in which the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consists of the wealth described in the *Assamedha*.

It is called *Sammāpāsa* because they throw the *samma* (a pin) there correctly. Day after day, having thrown the *samma*—which is a stick used for inserting [the horse] through the hole of the yoke—and having constructed an altar at the spot where it falls, [they proceed] with the portable sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) and so forth from the place submerged in the river Sarassatī.
This is a designation for the *sattra* sacrifice that is to be performed by one going in reverse order. It is called the *vājapeyya* because they drink the *vāja* (strength) therein.
This is a designation for the sacrifice of the Beluva-tree pillar, which is to be performed with a single *pariyañña* rite using seventeen animals and seventeen sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*).
It is called *niraggaḷa* because there are no bolts (*aggaḷa*) here. [It is a designation] for the sacrifice to be performed with nine *pariyañña* rites.

This is a designation for a variant of the *Aśvamedha* sacrifice— known by all the names of the "all-sacrifices" (*sabbamedha*)— which, along with the earth and its people, is described as having the splendor of a stated sacrificial fee.
All those great sacrifices do not equal even a sixteenth part of it, because of the greatness of the result of a single thought of loving-kindness (*mettācitta*).
"They are not worth a sixteenth part; they do not reach even a sixteenth portion"—this is the meaning.
"He does not conquer" means he does not cause loss to another by himself. "He does not cause to be conquered" means he does not cause another to cause loss to a third party.

"Being full of loving-kindness" means having a mental constituent that is practicing loving-kindness. "Toward all beings" means toward all sentient creatures. "No enmity exists for him toward anyone."
He has no unwholesome enmity toward anyone, nor any personal enmity toward any individual.
2. Commentary on the Discourse on Wisdom (Paññāsutta).
2. Regarding the second [discourse]: "The foundation of the holy life" means that which constitutes the beginning of the holy life of the Path. "By wisdom" means by insight (vipassanā).
*Garuṭṭhāniyaṃ* means that which is worthy of reverence, being the cause for the arising of respect. *Tibbaṃ* means intense or abundant.

*Paripucchati* means he asks about the meaning, the text, the connections, and the sequence of what precedes and follows. *Paripañhati* means he poses a question; he reflects, "I shall ask this and that. *Dvayena* means by way of two kinds.
*Anānākathiko* means one who does not engage in various [superfluous] discourses. *Atiracchānakathiko* means one who does not engage in irrelevant talk.
He does not engage in various kinds of frivolous talk. "Or the noble silence": the noble silence is the fourth jhāna;
however, attention to other meditation subjects is also permissible. "Knowing he knows" means he knows what ought to be known.
"Seeing he sees" means he sees what ought to be seen. "For the sake of endearment" means for the purpose of becoming beloved. "For the sake of respect" means...
"For the sake of respect": for the purpose of cultivation, or for the esteem of virtues. "For the sake of recluseship": for the purpose of the qualities of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*).
"For the sake of unity": for the purpose of uninterrupted continuity.
3–4. Commentary on the Two *Appiya* Suttas.
3–4. In the third [case], *appiyapasaṃsī* means one who praises or speaks in commendation of those who are disliked. *Piyagarahī* means one who censures or reviles those who are liked.
In the fourth, *anavaññattikāmo* means one who desires not to be despised, thinking, "O, may others not despise me.
*Akālaññū* means one who does not know the proper time for discourse; he speaks at an improper time. *Asucī* means by means of impurities.
One who is endowed with bodily action and so forth. 5.
Commentary on the First Discourse on Worldly Conditions (Lokadhamma).
5. Regarding the fifth [discourse]: "Worldly conditions" (*lokadhammā*) means the conditions of the world. There are none who are free from these; they occur even for the Buddhas.
Therefore it was said: "They revolve around the world" means they follow along and do not abandon it;
the meaning is that they do not turn away from the world. And "the world revolves around the eight worldly conditions" means this world follows after these and does not abandon them;
the meaning is that it does not turn away from those conditions.
"Gain and non-gain": when gain has come, it should be understood that non-gain has likewise come.
The same method applies to ill-repute and the rest. "He contemplates what is subject to change": he contemplates thus, "These things are subject to change.
"Completely shaken off" means dispelled, destroyed. "And having known the state": having known the state of Nibbāna. He understands rightly the nature of existence.

"Pāragū" means one who has gone to the further shore of existence (*bhava*), having reached the pinnacle of accomplishment; it is by knowing the state of Nibbāna that one rightly understands (*sammappajānāti*) the fact of having gone to that further shore.
In this sutta, the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and its cessation (*vivaṭṭa*) are explained.
6. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Worldly Conditions (*Lokadhamma Sutta*).

6. In the sixth [discourse], "What is the distinction? means what is the cause of distinction. "What is the underlying intention? means what is the superior application. "Having exhausted" means having grasped and brought to completion. Here too, only the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and its cessation (*vivaṭṭa*) are discussed.
7. Commentary on the Devadatta-vipatti-sutta:
In the seventh, "not long after he had departed" means not long after he had departed following the schism of the Saṅgha. "On account of" means by coming to, or depending upon.
"Having intended. "One's own failure" (*attavipatti*) means one's own misfortune or state of ruin. The same method applies to the remaining terms as well.
"Having overcome" (*abhibhuyya*) means having conquered or crushed.
8. Commentary on the *Uttaravipatti-sutta* (The Discourse on Higher Failure)
8. "In Vaṭajālikā" means in the monastery of that name. It is said that because it was situated in a grove of *vaṭa* trees, it became known as Vaṭajālikā.
"Appeared" means that having gone there with the intention of reporting this matter to the King of Devas, he became visible.
"The beginning of the holy life" means the beginning of the entire holy life of the Dispensation, which comprises the three trainings.

9. Commentary on the Nanda Sutta In the ninth [sutta], “a clansman” (*kulaputta*) means one born into a noble family. “Strong” (*balava*) means endowed with physical vigor. “Gracious” (*pāsādika*) means inspiring confidence through the perfection of his physical form.
“Intensely lustful” (*tibbarāga*) means possessed of thick, dense passion. Regarding the phrase “what else besides,” etc., the meaning is this: what other cause could there be?

"By this statement [it is shown]: 'This Nanda guards the doors of his sense faculties, is moderate in eating, is devoted to wakefulness, and is endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension—by means of these, Nanda is able to live the complete and pure holy life.
If he were not endowed with these causes, he would not be able. Thus, "therein" means in this way therein.
In this sutta, only the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) is discussed.
10. Commentary on the Kāraṇḍava Sutta:
In the tenth [sutta], "he evades one thing with another" means that by means of another reason or statement, he evades another reason or statement.
Or he conceals it. "He diverts the conversation to something external" means he introduces some other, irrelevant talk from outside.
"One who should be removed" (*apaneyyo*) means one who is to be taken out or expelled. "A defiler of recluses" (*samaṇadūsī*) means a corrupter of recluses. "Chaff among recluses" (*samaṇapalāpo*):
just as there is chaff among grains of rice, so too, because of his lack of essence, he is chaff among recluses. "Rushweed among recluses" (*samaṇakāraṇḍavo*) means refuse or dross among recluses.
“They throw it outside” means they carry it out. “In the barley-field” means in a field of barley.
“Of one winnowing” means of one who is winnowing in a great wind while standing on a high place.
“They sweep away” means they repeatedly sweep away so as to separate the strong grain from one side and the weak grain from the other; or [it refers to] the wind-catcher known as sweeping away.
They carry it out with soup or with cloth. *Daddara* means the sound of a *daddara*.
*Saṃvāsāyaṃ* means by way of living together. *Vijānātha* means you should know. *Santavāco* means one of gentle speech.
*Janavati* means in the midst of people. "He performs a deed in secret": a "deed" (*karaṇa*) refers to an evil action; that is performed in secret, concealed.
"Having sacrificed, he acts. "A crawler and a liar" means one who crawls after having lied; the meaning is that while speaking falsehood, he crawls or quivers.
In this sutta, only the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) is discussed, whereas in the verses, both the cycle of existence and its cessation (*vivaṭṭa*) are discussed.
The first chapter, the Chapter on Loving-kindness (*Mettāvagga*).
2. Mahāvagga 1.
Verañjasuttavaṇṇanā 11.

In the first [case] of the second [sutta], regarding the phrases "he pays homage" and so forth, it is according to the manner described here [in the phrase] "the ascetic Gotama is not [as he claims]."

Having thus applied [the words], the meaning here should be understood as follows: "He neither salutes nor rises from his seat, nor does he invite them to a seat by saying, 'May the venerable ones sit here.

For in this context, the word *vā* (or) has the sense of exclusion (*vibhāvana*), as in such examples as "Is form permanent or impermanent? Having spoken thus, [he does not perform] his own acts of salutation and so forth toward him who does not do so.
Having seen the Blessed One, he said: "This is indeed so, Master Gotama. What I have heard is exactly as it is;
my hearing and my seeing coincide and agree with one another, and in meaning they come to a single unity.
For Master Gotama does not... [as before] ...invite him to a seat. Thus, having reconciled what he himself had heard with what he had seen, he censured him.
He said: "Master Gotama, this is not right; that failure to perform salutations and so forth is indeed improper.

Then the Blessed One, without falling into the fault of self-exaltation and disparaging others, and having dispelled that ignorance with a heart cooled by compassion, spoke the words beginning with "I am not a brahmin," desiring to demonstrate the correctness of his position. In this regard, the following is [the explanation]:

The summary of the meaning: O Brahmin, even when surveying with my unimpeded eye of omniscience, I do not see such a person in this world—comprising the realms of devas and so forth—to whom I might pay homage, rise for, or invite to a seat.
Nor is this surprising, since it was only today that I attained omniscience; yet such a one...
I do not see any person worthy of such humble service.
Moreover, when I had just been born, I walked seven steps facing north and surveyed the entire ten-thousandfold world system;
even then, in this world consisting of devas and other realms, I did not see any person to whom I might perform such humble service.
Then, even the Great Brahmā Khīṇāsava, whose lifespan was sixteen thousand eons, raised his joined palms and, filled with joy, honored me, saying:
"You are a Great Man in the world; you are the foremost, the eldest, and the best in the world including its devas;
there is none superior to you. Even then, seeing no one superior to myself—
I uttered this lion’s roar: “I am the foremost in the world; I am the eldest in the world; I am the best in the world.
Even when I was just born, there was no person worthy of my salutation or other marks of respect.
Now that I have attained omniscience, whom should I salute? Therefore, O Brahmin, do not speak thus regarding the Tathāgata.
He made a supreme vow of renunciation. For, Brahmin, if the Tathāgata were to bow down to such a person...

or even if he were to invite him to a seat, at the end of that night, the head of that individual would break from the neck and fall suddenly to the ground, like a palm fruit released from its stalk when its bond has become loose through ripening.
Even when this was said, because of his lack of wisdom, the brahmin failed to perceive the Tathāgata’s status as the Eldest in the World;
unable to endure those words, he simply said: "Master Gotama is tasteless. His intention, it is said, was this:
"That which in the world is called the 'taste of concord'—namely, salutation, rising from one's seat, joining of palms, and respectful homage—is absent in Master [Gotama]."
“Gotama has none. Therefore, Master Gotama is one who lacks flavor, is of a nature lacking flavor, and is of a character lacking flavor.

Then, in order to produce a state of pliancy in his mind and avoiding a state of direct opposition, the Blessed One showed him that the meaning of those words applied to himself in another way, saying: “There is, however, O Brahmin, a way of speaking...,” and so forth.
In this context, *atthi khvesā* means "there indeed is this. *Pariyāyo* means "reason" or "ground. This is what is meant:

"There is indeed, O Brahmin, this reason by which a person speaking of me as 'the venerable Gotama is devoid of flavor' would be speaking rightly and would be reckoned as one who speaks truthfully. But what is that [reason]?"—namely, those...
“Brahmin, the flavors of forms... [and so on] ...the flavors of tangibles have been abandoned by the Tathāgata. What is meant by this?

Those flavors of form, reckoned as the gratification of sensual pleasure, which arise for even those ordinary persons who are esteemed as superior by birth or by rebirth—when they relish, delight in, and become attached to the objects of form and so forth.

There are tastes of sounds, tastes of smells, tastes of flavors, and tastes of tangibles—those which, as it were, pull this world toward them by binding it to their necks—and because they arise from the combination of bases, objects, and so forth, they are called "tastes of harmony.
All of these have been abandoned by the Tathāgata. Even when saying, "They have been abandoned by me," he does not exalt himself with the notion of "mine-ness" (*mamāyita*).
He teaches the Dhamma; or rather, this is the Tathāgata’s skill in teaching.

In this context, "abandoned" (*pahīnā*) means departed from the continuum of consciousness, or having been relinquished. Furthermore, in this sense, the genitive case should be understood as expressing the instrument.
They are "those whose roots are cut" (*ucchinnamūlā*), meaning those whose root consisting of craving and ignorance has been severed by the sword of the Noble Path.
Their basis has been made like the site of a palmyra tree; thus they are called "made into a palmyra-tree-site" (*tālāvatthukatā*).

For just as when a palmyra tree is uprooted along with its roots and only its site remains in that place, no further arising of that palmyra tree is perceived, so too, when the flavors of form and so forth have been uprooted along with their roots by the sword of the Noble Path, because of their having previously arisen... [they are said to be made into a palmyra-tree-site].
When the mental continuum has been reduced to its mere basis, all those [defilements] are said to be "rendered like palm-tree stumps.
Alternatively, they are "rendered like palm-tree stumps" because, being of a nature that does not grow further, they have been made like a palm tree cut at the top.
Furthermore, since they are thus rendered like palm-tree stumps, they are rendered such that they do not come into existence again, so that there is no future state for them; therefore, he said:
—“Made non-existent. “Subject to non-arising in the future” means having the nature of not arising again in the future.
“But it is not that which you have in mind when you say this”—that is to say, the method of explanation you employ does not apply.
For when this is said, is it not evident that the flavor of concord spoken of by the brahmin exists within oneself?

"Is she authorized? "She is not. For one who, being capable of creating the flavor of harmony, does not do so, deserves to be called "flavorless" due to that absence. But the Blessed One is simply incapable of doing this;
therefore, demonstrating his incapacity for such a purpose, he said: "But it is not as you say with reference to that. [This refers to] the method...
“Intending [something else], you said to me, ‘He is one who has no taste’; that cannot be said of us.
Thus, the brahmin, being unable to establish the state of having no taste as he intended, then said, “They are without enjoyment,” and so forth.
In all these modes of expression, one should understand the sequence of application according to the method already stated, and the meaning spoken with intentional reference (*sandhāya-bhāsita*).

It should be understood thus: the brahmin, perceiving that very act of salutation and so forth toward those advanced in age as "the enjoyment of social concord" in the world, and seeing its absence in the Blessed One, said to him, "You are one who enjoys solitude," and so forth.
And the Blessed One, perceiving within himself the absence of that enjoyment of desire and lust which beings have for form and the other sense objects, consented to another way of speaking.
Furthermore, the brahmin, perceiving the non-performance of those worldly customs such as saluting elders and the like—

which worldly people perform— declared the Blessed One to be a proponent of non-action (*akiriyavāda*). However, because the Blessed One speaks of the non-performance of bodily misconduct and so forth,
the brahmin, seeing that quality of non-action within the Blessed One himself, granted him another way of speaking.
In this context, with the exception of bodily misconduct and so forth, all remaining unwholesome states should be understood as "various kinds of evil, unwholesome states.

Furthermore, not seeing that very act of salutation and so on being performed toward the Blessed One, the brahmin thought, "Because of his coming here, this lineage of the world, this tradition of the world, will be cut off," and thus he called the Blessed One a proponent of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*). But as for the Blessed One, since—
He declares the eradication of lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure and of hatred associated with the two types of unwholesome consciousness by means of the non-returner path;
he declares the eradication of delusion—the source of all unwholesome states—by means of the arahant path;
and for the remaining evil, unwholesome phenomena, [he declares their eradication] by means of the four paths as appropriate.
He speaks of annihilation; therefore, perceiving that annihilationist view within himself, he allowed another explanation.

Again, the brahmin, thinking, "I suppose the ascetic Gotama feels disgust for this customary conduct of families—such as saluting those who are older in years—and that is why he does not perform it," said to the Blessed One, "He is one who feels disgust. But the Blessed One [spoke thus] because he truly feels disgust.
Regarding bodily misconduct and the rest— that is, all those instances of misconduct of body, speech, and mind, up to and including the attainment of and possession of unwholesome, base states—
a person whose nature is to adorn himself feels disgust for them and feels shame,
just as one would toward excrement. Therefore, perceiving that which is loathsome within himself, he allows another method [of practice].
In this context, the instrumental expressions beginning with "by bodily misconduct" (*kāyaduccaritena*) should be understood in the sense of the accusative.
Furthermore, not seeing that very act of salutation and so forth performed toward the Blessed One, the brahmin thought:
"This man leads away—that is, destroys—this deed which is the foremost in the world; or else, because he does not perform this duty of respectful service, he is one who ought to be led away."
Thinking, “He should be restrained,” he addressed the Blessed One as a “Venayika. Herein, this is the word-meaning: it disciplines (*vineti*), thus it is *vinaya*;
what is meant is that it destroys. *Vinaya* itself is *venayika*. Or, it deserves discipline (*vinaya*), thus it is *venayika*;
what is meant is that it deserves restraint. For the Blessed One, because of the disciplining and the pacifying of passion and the other defilements—

He teaches the Dhamma; therefore, he is a "Venayika" (one who subdues). And this is precisely the meaning of the word here: he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of discipline (*vinaya*), thus he is a "Venayika.
For the formation of derivative words (*taddhita*) is indeed manifold. Perceiving within himself that state of being a subduer, he allows another method of explanation.
Furthermore, because the brahmin— who, by performing respectful services such as salutations toward those advanced in age,
pleases and gladdens them, whereas by failing to do so, he torments and harasses them, causing them mental distress— and because the Blessed One does not perform those services,
the brahmin thinks, "This man torments those advanced in age. Or, because he is devoid of the conduct of a true noble person, [the brahmin thinks], "This is a wretched man."
Thinking, “He is one,” he said to the Blessed One, “You are an ascetic (*tapassī*). Herein, this is the meaning of the words: it scorches, thus it is *tapa*;
the meaning is that it irritates or harasses. This is a designation for the failure to perform proper duties. One who possesses such *tapa* is an *tapassī*.
According to the second interpretation of the meaning, without considering the literal etymology, a wretched person in the world is called an *tapassī*. [The Blessed One...]
However, because he has abandoned those unwholesome states which are called "torments" (*tapanīyāni*) since they torment the world, he has come to be designated as an "ascetic" (*tapassī*).
Therefore, perceiving that state of asceticism within himself, he allows another explanation. Herein, this is the etymology: they "torment," thus they are "torments" (*tapā*);

this is a designation for unwholesome states. He "possesses" (*assi*) those torments... [he does not]. Thus he is an "ascetic. (Note: The final portion of the sentence is elliptical, implying the absence of such torments.)
He is an ascetic (*tapassin*) because he has cast out,

abandoned, and destroyed [defilements]. Furthermore, the brahmin, thinking that such acts as salutation lead to birth in the womb of the deva-world— that is, to the attainment of rebirth in the deva-world—
and seeing that this was absent in the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as "one beyond the womb" (*apagabbha*).
Or, out of anger, even one who would point out a fault in the Blessed One’s taking of rebirth in his mother’s womb speaks thus.
Herein, this is the meaning of the words: “one gone away from the womb” (*apagabbho*); the intention is that he is incapable of reaching rebirth in the world of the gods.
Or, he is “one whose womb is inferior” (*apagabbho*). Because he is excluded from the womb of the world of the gods, he is destined in the future to obtain an inferior womb.

The intention is that his dwelling in the womb was inferior. However, because the Blessed One has for the future abandoned lying in a womb, he, perceiving within himself that state of being "one who has escaped the womb" (*apagabbha*), allows another way of explaining it.
And therein, regarding the passage: "Brahmin, for one who has abandoned lying in a womb for the future and the production of renewed existence," these...

The meaning of these terms should be understood as follows: "O Brahmin, for that person whose rebirth in a womb and production in a future existence have been abandoned because they have been destroyed by the unsurpassed Path—here, by the mention of 'womb-birth' (gabbhaseyyā), the moisture-born mode of birth is included;
and by the mention of 'production in a future existence' (punabbhavābhinibbatti), the other three modes of birth are also included."
Furthermore, "lying in a womb" means lying within a womb (*gabbhaseyyā*). "Rebirth" means the very process of arising into a new existence;
thus, "the arising of rebirth" (*punabbhavābhinibbatti*) is how the meaning should be understood here.

And just as when "stations of consciousness" (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*) are mentioned, there is no station of consciousness other than consciousness itself, so too here one should understand that there is no "lying" other than the womb. Moreover, what is called "arising" (*abhinibbatti*) is indeed of the nature of rebirth.
There is that which has become non-renewal of existence, but here it is the renewal of existence that is intended; therefore it is said:
"The very renewal of existence is rebirth, hence 'rebirth-renewal' (*punabbhavābhinibbatti*).
Thus, even when a brahmin reviles [the Buddha] with the eight grounds of abuse, such as being tasteless and so forth, starting from the time he arrived...
The Blessed One— the Lord of Dhamma, the King of Dhamma, the Master of Dhamma, the Tathāgata— out of compassion,
gazing upon the brahmin with his cool eye, and having thoroughly penetrated that element of Dhamma (*dhammadhātu*) by which a teaching becomes truly skillful in its exposition,
shone like the full moon in a cloudless sky during the autumn season.
Like the sun dispelling the darkness from the heart of a brahmin,
he demonstrated those very grounds for abuse in various ways and through different methods;

furthermore, he displayed his own expansion of compassion, his mental equanimity toward the earth— characterized by the qualities attained through being unshakable by the eight worldly conditions— and his state of imperturbability.
Explaining this, [the Blessed One said]: "This brahmin perceives his own state of old age merely through such things as grey hair, broken teeth, and wrinkled skin;

yet he does not know that he is followed by birth, pursued by aging, overcome by sickness, and struck down by death—that having died today, he must once again tomorrow return to the state of a child lying on its back. With great...

Thinking, "He has come to me with great effort; let his coming be fruitful," the Blessed One, demonstrating his own peerless pre-existence in this world, extended his teaching of the Dharma to the brahmin by way of the passage beginning, "Just as, O Brahmin... and so forth.
In this context, the meaning of the phrase "Just as... and so forth should be understood in the same manner as explained previously. However, this is the distinction:
according to the method stated before, those chicks emerge flapping their wings and crying out in a manner appropriate to that moment.
And among those emerging in this way, whichever one emerges first is the eldest.
Thus it is said. Therefore, desiring to establish his own seniority by means of that simile, the Blessed One asks the brahmin:
"Now, regarding those chicks of the hen... [etc. ...how should he be addressed? In this context, "kukkuṭacchāpakānaṃ" means "of the chicks of the hen.
"Kinti svāssa vacanīyo" means: how should he be addressed; what should he be called? What should be said of him?
“Whether he be the eldest or the youngest.
“He should be called ‘the eldest,’ Master Gotama; he should indeed be called ‘the eldest. Why is that?
Because he is their eldest,” meaning that he is the most senior among them. Then the Blessed One gave him a simile:
"Practicing in this very way," he said, "just as that chick, so am I. Regarding the phrase "for beings who have entered into ignorance":
"ignorance" (avijjā) refers to lack of knowledge; "who have entered into it" means having gone therein. "Beings" (pajā) is a designation for sentient beings;
it is said even with reference to those beings who have entered within the womb of ignorance. "Born from an egg" (aṇḍabhūtāya) means born, produced, or arisen from within an egg.
Just as certain beings born from an egg are called "egg-born," so too this entire generation is called "egg-born" because it is produced within the shell of the egg of ignorance (*avijjā*).
"Enveloped" means completely covered, bound, and wrapped by that shell of the egg of ignorance.
"Having burst open the shell of the egg of ignorance" means having shattered that shell consisting of ignorance.

Having broken through [the barriers]. "In this world, I alone": even throughout the entire habitation of the world, I am indeed the one, without a second. "I have fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment" (*anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhim abhisambuddho*):
this refers to the perfectly self-attained awakening that is supreme among all things and free from anything superior; or alternatively, it refers to the praised and beautiful awakening.
This is the name for the knowledge of the path of arahantship, and it is also the name for omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
Both are acceptable. Is the path to arahantship for others the unsurpassed enlightenment (anuttarā bodhi)?
It is not. Why? Because it does not bestow all qualities. For in their case, the path to arahantship bestows only the fruit of arahantship for some;

for some, the three knowledges (tisso vijjā); for some, the six direct knowledges (cha abhiññā); for some, the four analytical insights (catasso paṭisambhidā); and for some, the knowledge of the disciple’s perfection (sāvakapāramiñāṇa).

It bestows the very knowledge of paccekabodhi upon the paccekabuddhas, but for the Buddhas, it bestows the perfection of all qualities, just as an anointing confers upon a king the status of sovereign over the entire world. Therefore, no one else can possess unsurpassed enlightenment.
"Abhisambuddho" means "I have fully known," "I have penetrated"; what is meant is that "I have reached" or "I have attained."
Now, this application of the simile which was spoken by the Blessed One in the manner beginning with "In the same way," should be understood by correlating it with the meaning as follows:

just as that hen performed the threefold action of sitting upon her eggs and so forth, even so [did the Bodhisatta] while seated on the seat of enlightenment (bodhipallaṅka) in his state as a Bodhisatta.

The Blessed One’s practice of the threefold contemplation—impermanence, suffering, and non-self—within his own continuum is like the preservation of eggs from rotting through a hen’s performance of the threefold action.
Through the Blessed One’s practice as a Bodhisatta of these threefold contemplations, there was no decline in his insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*).
By the hen’s performance of the threefold action, the moisture and grease within the eggs are completely absorbed.

Just as the thinning of the eggshells occurs through the hen’s performance of the threefold action, so too, through the Blessed One’s— while he was a Bodhisatta— accomplishment of the threefold contemplation,
there occurred the exhaustion of the craving and affection associated with the three states of existence. Through the Blessed One’s— while he was a Bodhisatta—
accomplishment of the threefold contemplation, the shell of the egg of ignorance was thinned, just as the thinning of the eggshells occurs through the hen’s performance of the threefold action.

Just as the claws and beak of a chick possess a state of hardness and sharpness, so too does the knowledge of insight (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) of the Blessed One while he was a Bodhisatta possess a state of sharpness, hardness, clarity, and courage through the accomplishment of the threefold contemplation.
Just as the time for the transformation of a chick occurs through the hen performing her threefold activity, so it was for the Blessed One while he was a Bodhisatta...
The time for the transformation, growth, and conception of insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) through the accomplishment of the threefold contemplation is like the time when a hen,
by performing her threefold action, breaks open the shell of the egg with the tip of her claw or her beak,
spreads out her wings, and emerges safely. This is the case with the Blessed One.

It should be understood that by accomplishing the threefold contemplation, having caused the embryo of insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) to be conceived, and then— by means of the path to Arhatship attained through successive stages—

having shattered the eggshell of ignorance and burst open the wings of direct higher knowledge (*abhiññā*), the time of safely realizing all the qualities of a Buddha was reached. For it was said, "Brahmin, I am the eldest,
the most excellent in the world," just as in the case of those chicks, Brahmin.
Just as a chick that hatches first by breaking through the eggshell is considered the eldest, so too,
because I was the first among those in the world shrouded in ignorance to break through the eggshell of ignorance and be born into the noble birth,
I have come to be reckoned as the eldest and most senior; yet, because I am peerless in all virtues, I am the best.
Having thus declared to the brahmin his own state of being unsurpassed and supreme, the Blessed One now spoke the words beginning with "But, brahmin,
energy was aroused by me" in order to show the path by which that state was attained, starting from its preliminary stage.
In this context, "But, brahmin, energy was aroused by me" means:
"Brahmin, this unsurpassed state of being the eldest and most excellent was not attained by me while lazy, muddle-minded, with body agitated and mind distracted;
rather, for its attainment, I applied energy.
While seated at the seat of enlightenment, I applied and exerted energy consisting of the four right strivings."
It was set in motion without slackness. And because it was exerted, it was unwearied for me.
And not only was my energy thus, but mindfulness too was established through its being directed toward the object;
and because it was established, it was unconfused. "The body is tranquil and unagitated": by way of the tranquility of both body and mind, my body also became tranquil. In that regard—

Since the material body (*rūpakāya*) becomes tranquil precisely when the mental body (*nāmakāya*) is tranquil, it is therefore said, "the body is tranquil," without making a distinction between "mental body" and "material body.
"Unagitated" means that it is unagitated precisely because of its tranquility; what is meant is that it is free from distress.
"The mind is concentrated, one-pointed" means that my mind, too, has been rightly established.
It was well-established as if fixed; and because of its being concentrated, it was one-pointed, immovable, and unwavering.
Up to this point, the preliminary practice for jhāna has been explained.
Now, beginning with the first jhāna attained by means of this practice, [the path] culminating in the threefold clear-knowledge (vijjāttaya) [is described].
Showing a distinction, he said, "As for me... and so forth. Regarding that, whatever needs to be stated by way of the method of exposition has already been explained in the *Visuddhimagga*.
However, in such passages as "This, O Brahmin, is my true knowledge" (*vijjā*), "true knowledge" (*vijjā*) is so called in the sense of making something known. What does it make known?
Regarding "past lives": ignorance (*avijjā*) is the delusion that conceals those very past lives in the sense of making them unknown.
Darkness (*tama*) is that same delusion called "darkness" in the sense of concealing them. Light (*āloka*) is that same clear knowledge (*vijjā*) called "light" in the sense of illuminating them.
Here, the meaning is "clear knowledge has been attained"; the rest is words of praise. As for the construction here:
"Indeed, this knowledge (vijjā) has been attained by me; for me, having attained that knowledge, ignorance (avijjā) has been destroyed"—this is the meaning.
Why? Because knowledge has arisen. This same method applies to the other two phrases as well. Regarding the word *tanti*: here, *tanti* is merely a particle.
Through non-negligence (*appamattassa*) by means of not being separated from mindfulness, and through ardor (*ātāpino*) by means of the exertion of energy, [he dwells] regarding both body and life...
And "of one who is intent" means of one who has sent himself forth, who is free from longing. This is what is meant:
"Just as for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and intent, ignorance would be destroyed and true knowledge would arise;
darkness would be destroyed and light would arise—even so has ignorance been destroyed by me, true knowledge has arisen; darkness has been destroyed, and light has arisen."
"I have obtained a fruit exactly corresponding to this application of my striving.
"This, brahmin, was my first breaking out, like that of a chick from its eggshell.
"This, brahmin, was [the first time] I used the beak of the knowledge of recollecting past lives to [break through] the covering of the aggregates in which I had previously dwelt."
Having split the eggshell of ignorance, there was the first breaking forth, the first emergence, the first noble birth; just as a chick,
having split the eggshell with its beak or the tip of its claw, breaks out from that eggshell, emerges,
and is reborn into the flock of chickens— this, for now, is the method regarding the discourse on past lives.
In the discourse on the passing away and rebirth of beings (*cutūpapātakathā*), however, "knowledge" (*vijjā*) refers to the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhuñāṇavijjā*).
"Ignorance" (*avijjā*) refers to the ignorance that conceals the passing away and rebirth of beings.

Just as it was stated in the discourse on past lives (*pubbenivāsakathā*)—“having split open the eggshell of ignorance that conceals the aggregates in which one previously dwelt by means of the beak of the knowledge of recollecting past lives”—so too here [it is said]: “by means of the beak of the knowledge of passing away and rebirth...”
It should be said: “having split the eggshell of ignorance that conceals birth and rebirth.

Furthermore, when demonstrating to the brahmin the attainment of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsava-khaya-ñāṇa) as embraced by the knowledge of review (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa), he said:
“This, brahmin, is my third true knowledge,” and so forth. In this context, “true knowledge” (vijjā) refers to the true knowledge of the path of Arahantship.
"Ignorance" refers to the ignorance that conceals the Four Noble Truths. "This, O Brahmin, was my third breaking forth" means here:

"O Brahmin, this was my third breaking forth, my third emergence, my third noble birth, having split open the eggshell of ignorance that conceals the Four Noble Truths with the beak and tip of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints."
"Just as a chick, having split the eggshell with its beak or the tip of its claws,
emerges from that eggshell and is reborn into the class of chickens—
what does this demonstrate? "It demonstrates, brahmin, that after the chick has split the eggshell, it [emerges] from there..."

One who departs [from the womb] is born all at once; I, however, having first broken through the eggshell of ignorance that conceals the aggregates of my previous existence, was born by means of the knowledge and vision of the recollection of past lives (*pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇavijjā*).

Then, having split open the eggshell of ignorance that conceals the death and rebirth-linking of beings, I was born secondly by means of the knowledge and vision of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhuñāṇavijjā*). Furthermore, [having broken through] that which conceals the Four Noble Truths...
Having burst open the eggshell of ignorance, he was born through the third kind of knowledge, the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsava*).
Thus, "I am born thrice by means of the three knowledges (*vijjā*)," he shows that this birth of his is noble and perfectly pure.

And in showing this, [he demonstrates] the knowledge of the past through the knowledge of previous births (*pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa*), the knowledge of the present and future through the divine eye (*dibba-cakkhu*), and [the knowledge of the future] through the destruction of the taints.
"Having thus revealed all the qualities of an omniscient one through these three knowledges— namely, all mundane and supramundane qualities—
the Blessed One demonstrated to the brahmin his status as the eldest and most excellent within his own noble birth.
When this had been said, the brahmin of Verañjā [listened] as the Blessed One, out of compassion for the world and feeling compassion for the brahmin...
Although his noble birth and preeminent excellence were to be concealed, when the Blessed One spoke the teaching of the Dhamma that illuminates the threefold knowledge,
the brahmin of Verañjā— his body filled with the expansion of rapture upon hearing it— realized the Blessed One’s noble birth and preeminent excellence,
thinking: "Such as this is he, the eldest in all the world, endowed with every virtue..."
Having reproached himself, saying, "Alas, how foolish was my ignorance to say that the All-Knowing One does not perform such acts as salutation toward others," and having reached the conclusion,
"This one is now the eldest in the world by virtue of being born first into the noble birth,
and the most excellent by virtue of being peerless in all qualities," he said this to the Blessed One: "Master Gotama is the eldest."
"Venerable Gotama is the best. Having spoken thus, and further rejoicing in the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma, he said, "Excellent, O Gotama," and so forth.
The meaning of that has already been explained.
2. Commentary on the Sīha Sutta.

12. In the second [case], "renowned" means known, celebrated, and well-known. "In the assembly hall" (*santhāgāra*) refers to a building constructed for the purpose of providing rest for the great multitude.
It is said that this assembly hall was located in the center of the city and was visible from four locations;
people arriving from the four directions would first rest there and afterwards proceed to their own respective comfortable dwellings.
They go. They also say that a "house" was built for the purpose of carrying out the affairs of state for royal families;
for it is there that the Licchavi kings sit down to carry out, perform, and deliberate upon their state affairs.
"Seated" means they are seated upon costly and excellent rugs spread out specifically for them to sit on, with white parasols raised above.
Seated upon their seats, they spoke in many ways in praise of the Buddha;
that is, having deliberated on both the affairs of the royal court and the welfare of the world, they spoke, discussed, and illuminated the Buddha’s praises for many reasons.
For those kings were wise, endowed with faith and confidence, and were noble disciples who had attained the stages of stream-entry, once-returning, or non-returning.
Having severed all worldly entanglements, they all spoke the praises of the Three Jewels, beginning with the Buddha. In this regard, the praise of the Buddha is threefold:
the praise of his conduct (*cariyavaṇṇa*), the praise of his physical form (*sarīravaṇṇa*), and the praise of his qualities (*guṇavaṇṇa*). Among these, the kings began by praising his conduct:
"Indeed, a difficult task was performed by the Perfectly Enlightened One throughout more than one hundred thousand eons..."

"By fulfilling the thirty perfections— namely, the four incalculable eons of the ten perfections (*pāramī*), the ten near-perfections (*upapāramī*), and the ten ultimate perfections (*paramatthapāramī*)—
and by bringing to their culmination the conduct for the benefit of relatives, the conduct for the benefit of the world, and the conduct of a Buddha,
while making the five great renunciations," they spoke thus, praising the Buddha through one hundred and fifty Jātaka tales.
Having brought him to the Tusita heaven, they established him there.
Yet, while extolling the praise of the Dhamma, they said: "The Dhamma was taught by that Blessed One; according to its divisions, it consists of five Nikāyas;
according to the Piṭakas, three Piṭakas; according to the Aṅgas, nine Aṅgas; and according to the Khandhas, eighty-four thousand dhamma-khandhas."
They spoke of the qualities of the Dhamma by way of its divisions.

While praising the Saṅgha, they said: "Having heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma, sons of noble family who have gained faith renounce their masses of wealth as well as their circle of kinsmen, and [take up] the white parasol, the position of viceroy, the rank of commander-in-chief, treasurer, storekeeper, and so forth."
Disregarding [their worldly status], they went forth and received the going-forth in the sublime teaching of the Teacher.
Among those who went forth having abandoned the white parasol, there were eighty thousand royal renunciants during the Buddha’s time, such as King Bhaddiya, Mahākappina, Pukkusāti, and others.

Furthermore, there were hundreds of millions who went forth having abandoned wealth amounting to many hundreds of crores, such as the noble son Yasa, the merchant’s son Soṇa, the noble son Raṭṭhapāla, and others.
“There is no limit [to their number]. Such and such sons of noble family go forth in the Teacher’s dispensation”—thus they spoke of the qualities of the Saṅgha by way of a summary of the going-forth.
“Sīha the General” means a commander-in-chief of an army with that name. For in Vesālī there were seven thousand seven hundred...

And there were seven kings. They all assembled together and, having ascertained the will of everyone, said, "Search for one who is capable of governing the kingdom. While searching, they saw Prince Sīha;
concluding that "he will be able to do it," they made their decision and gave him the commander-in-chief’s parasol, which was the color of a red gem and covered with a woolen cloth.
With reference to him it was said: “Sīha the general. A disciple of the Nigaṇṭhas means one who provides requisites and attends upon the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta.
For there were three people in the land of Jambudīpa who were the foremost attendants of the Nigaṇṭhas:
at Nālandā, the householder Upāli; at Kapilavatthu, Vappa the Sakyan; and at Vesālī, this Sīha the general.
"He was seated" means that they prepared seats for the entourages of the other kings here and there, but for Sīha, they prepared one in the center;
he was seated upon that costly royal throne thus prepared. "Without doubt" means free from uncertainty;
"certainly" (addhā) means with absolute certainty, for they do not praise anyone of insignificant status in such a manner with hundreds of reasons.
"He approached the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta" means that the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta, having thought,
"If this Sīha hears anyone praising the ascetic Gotama and approaches the ascetic Gotama to see him,
there will be a loss for me," spoke thus to the general Sīha even earlier.
“General, many wander about in this world saying, ‘I am a Buddha, I am a Buddha.

If you wish to approach anyone for an audience, ask me; I will send you to the appropriate person and keep you away from the inappropriate one. Remembering those words, he thought, “If he sends me, I shall go.”
Thinking, "If not now, I shall not go," he approached where the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta was.

Then, upon hearing his words, the Nigaṇṭha was overwhelmed by a powerful sorrow as if by a great mountain, thinking, "I have become one who wishes to go to that very place where I did not wish her to go; I am ruined. Being displeased, [he thought: "What means of dissuasion can there be for him?"
Thinking, "I shall do so," he said, "But what [is it]? and so forth.

Speaking thus, he destroyed the joy that had arisen in the lion, like one striking a wandering ox with a staff, like one extinguishing a burning lamp, and like one overturning an alms-bowl filled with food.
The "volitional formation of going" (*gamiyābhisaṅkhāra*) refers to the act of preparing elephant-vehicles and the like, and the taking of perfumes, garlands, and so on.
The application was set in motion. "It subsided" means it was pacified.

"And for a second time" means for a second turn. And in this turn, while speaking the praises of the Buddha, [they defined] the limits of the Ten-Powered One from the Tuṣita abode down to the Great Seat of Enlightenment (Mahābodhipallaṅka), delimiting him from below by the soles of his feet and above by the tips of his hair.
They described the beauty of the body by way of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpurisalakkhaṇa*), the eighty minor characteristics (*anubyañjana*), and the fathom-wide aura of radiance.
When speaking in praise of the Dhamma, they described its qualities by way of its being well-spoken, saying: "There is not even a single word or a single syllable that is flawed.
When speaking in praise of the Saṅgha, they said: "Having abandoned such fame, glory, and wealth..."

"Those who have gone forth in the Teacher’s dispensation are not of a lazy nature; rather, having fulfilled the thirteen qualities of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), they apply themselves to the seven contemplations and employ the thirty-eight analytical objects of meditation.
Thus they spoke of the virtues of the Saṅgha by way of the practice.

On the third occasion, however, while speaking in praise of the Buddha, they described the qualities of the Buddha according to the method of the discourses (suttanta), saying, "Such indeed is the Blessed One";
the qualities of the Dhamma, saying, "The Dhamma has been well-expounded by the Blessed One," and so forth, according to the method of the discourses;
and the qualities of the Saṅgha, saying, "The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way," and so forth, according to the method of the discourses.
Then Sīha thought: “The mouths of these Licchavi princes will not suffice for speaking of the virtues of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha starting from the third day;
surely that Blessed One is endowed with extraordinary qualities.
Without abandoning this present rapture, I shall see the Perfectly Enlightened One today. Then he [asked]: “What—”
The thought arose in him: "What indeed will the Nigaṇṭhas do for me? In this context, "What indeed will the Nigaṇṭhas do for me?
means: what indeed will the Nigaṇṭhas do for me? "Whether they have been looked upon or not looked upon" means whether they have been asked for permission or not asked for permission.
For they would not, having been asked, grant him the excellence of vehicles and conveyances, nor would they grant him any distinction of sovereignty. Nor...
"They will take it without asking; their asking is fruitless"—this is the intended meaning.

"He departed from Vesālī" means that just as, during the summer season when it has rained, water flowing down enters a river and, after going only a short distance, stops and does not continue on, so too, on the first day [of his journey], Sīha thought, "I shall see the One of Ten Powers."
It was the time when the Nigaṇṭha had warded off the rapture that had arisen.
Just as on the second day after it has rained, when water flows down and enters a river, one might go a short distance, strike a heap of sand, and cause the flow to cease;
even so, on the second day, the Nigaṇṭha warded off the rapture that had arisen in Sīha at the thought, "I shall see the One of Ten Powers."

Just as on the third day, when it has rained, the flowing water enters a river, sweeps away old leaves, dry stalks, wood, rubbish, and the like, breaks through the mound of sand, and flows down toward the ocean;
even so, on the third day, having heard the discourse on the virtues of the three subjects, Sīha, filled with joy and gladness, thought: "The Nigaṇṭhas are fruitless; the Nigaṇṭhas are barren."
"What will these people do for me? I shall go into the presence of the Teacher," he resolved, and set out from Vesālī.
As he was departing, he thought, "It has been a long time since I have desired to go into the presence of the One of Ten Powers;
yet it is not fitting for me to go in an unknown guise. Thus, [he thought], "Whoever desires to go into the presence of the One of Ten Powers, let all..."
Having caused the proclamation “Let them come forth! to be made, he had five hundred chariots prepared;
standing upon his preeminent chariot, surrounded by those five hundred chariots and a great assembly, and having had perfumes, flowers, powders, incense, and other offerings taken up, he set out.
“In the middle of the day” means during the day, as soon as midday had passed.

He approached the place where the Blessed One was. As he entered the monastery, even from afar, he saw the eighty minor marks, the fathom-wide aura of radiance, the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, and the six-colored dense rays of the Buddha’s light.
Seeing this, he thought: "I have lived so near to such a man as this, yet for all this time I did not see him;
alas, I have been deceived! Alas, what a loss it has been for me!"—just like one who has discovered a great treasure.
Like a poor man who has become filled with joy and gladness, he approached the Blessed One.
"They explain in accordance with the Dhamma" means they speak of a reason that conforms to the reason stated by Master Gotama.

Here, the word *dhamma* has the sense of "reason," as in such passages as "the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma is knowledge regarding the cause. And here, "reason" refers to that which proceeds in such a manner.
The meaning of the word is intended [here], because it is the cause for the occurrence of that [word].
For the application of a word is connected with its meaning. "An imitation" (anukāraṇa) means that very thing being spoken thus by others.

"A reasoned discussion and rejoinder" (sahadhammiko vādānuvādo) means that your argument, being supported by reasons, or the subsequent rejoinder to it, is something that even the wise would not overlook.
A ground for censure does not arise as a reason [for your position]. This is what is meant:
Is there no ground for censure in your doctrine in every respect? "Not wishing to misrepresent" means not wishing to speak with what is untrue.
The meaning of the passages beginning with "There is the Simile of the Lion" should be understood according to the method already set forth in the Verañjakaṇḍa. "With the highest consolation."

"By means of the supreme [teaching] known as the four paths and four fruits. "I teach the Dhamma for consolation" means: I teach the Dhamma for the purpose of consoling and for the purpose of providing support.
Thus the Blessed One taught the Dhamma to the general Sīha by way of eight factors.
"Having investigated" means: having understood, having reflected, and having weighed; it is said that you should do what ought to be done. "Excellent!"

"He is handsome" means he is beautiful. For when people like you see me and go for refuge to me, while seeing a Nigaṇṭha and going for refuge to a Nigaṇṭha, the censure arises: "Why does this Siha go for refuge to whoever he sees?
Therefore, he shows that careful investigation is beneficial for people like you. "They would carry a banner."

It is said that having obtained such a disciple, they raise a banner and wander through the city proclaiming, "Such-and-such a king, or royal minister, or merchant, has gone for refuge to us and become our disciple. Why?
Because they think, "In this way, our greatness will be made manifest. But if he were to ask, "Why have I gone for refuge to them?"...
He might feel remorse, thinking, "I have gone [to them]," but having dispelled that by reflecting, "Many know my state of having gone for refuge;
it would now be painful to turn back," he will not retreat. Therefore it is said: "They would carry a banner.
"A well" means standing like a prepared reservoir of water. "Family" means your own residence.
"You should think, 'It must be given,'" he said. "In the past, when you saw ten, twenty, or even sixty people arrive, you did not say there was nothing and you gave;
now, for the mere reason that I have gone to you for refuge, do not cut off these people's means of giving. For indeed, what has been brought forward must be given.
"I have heard this, Bhante. "From whom did you hear it? "From the Nigaṇṭhas. "They..."
It seems that in the households they proclaim thus: “We say that a gift should be given to whoever has arrived;
but the ascetic Gotama says, ‘A gift should be given to me alone and not to others; a gift should be given to my disciples alone and not to the disciples of others;
a gift given to me alone is of great fruit, and not to others; [a gift] to me alone...”
"Gifts given to disciples bear great fruit, but not so for others"—it was with reference to this that he said, "I have heard this.
"Graduated discourse" means a discourse following a sequential order: after giving comes virtue, after virtue comes heaven, and after heaven comes the Path.
In that context, "discourse on giving" means: "This gift is the source of happiness, the source of prosperity..."
It is the root of all enjoyments, the foundation, the protection, the shelter, the resort, and the ultimate refuge for one who has fallen into adversity.
In this world and the next, there is no support, foundation, object, protection, shelter, resort, or ultimate refuge equal to giving.
For in the sense of being a support, it is like a lion-throne made of jewels; in the sense of being a foundation, it is like the great earth; and in the sense of being an object—
It is like a rope for an object of focus. For this [Dhamma] is a ship in the sense of crossing over suffering; a hero in battle in the sense of providing consolation;
a well-constructed city in the sense of protection from fear; a lotus in the sense of being unsullied by the stains of stinginess and so forth;
fire in the sense of burning them away; a venomous snake in the sense of being difficult to approach; a lion in the sense of being fearless; and powerful in the sense of...
The elephant is so called in the sense of being considered auspicious; the white bull in the sense of reaching the land of safety;
and the king of horses, Valāhaka, in the sense of bringing one to the realm of security. This giving is indeed the path I have traveled;

this is my lineage: while fulfilling the ten perfections, I performed the Velāma Great Sacrifice, the Mahāgovinda Great Sacrifice, the Mahāsudassana Great Sacrifice, and the Vessantara Great Sacrifice.
Many great sacrifices were performed; by one who was a companion of the sages, offering himself as a blazing mass of fire, the hearts of the beggars who had assembled were won.

For giving in this world bestows the attainment of Sakka, the attainment of Māra, the attainment of Brahmā, the attainment of a wheel-turning monarch, the knowledge of the perfections of a disciple, the knowledge of the enlightenment of a paccekabuddha, and the knowledge of supreme enlightenment—such is the discourse connected with the virtues of giving.

However, because one who gives a gift is able to undertake moral discipline (*sīla*), he spoke on the discourse of moral discipline immediately thereafter. Regarding the discourse on moral discipline:
this moral discipline is a support, a foundation, an object of focus, a refuge, a shelter, a resort, and a final goal.
This moral discipline is my lineage; it was [my lineage] during the time of the Naga King Saṅkhapāla, during the time of the Naga King Bhūridatta, and during the time of the Naga King Campeyya.
In infinite successive existences—such as during the time of Sīlavara the king, the time of Mātuposaka the elephant king, and the time of Chaddanta the elephant king—I fulfilled my virtue (sīla).
Indeed, there is no support, foundation, object, refuge, shelter, destination, or ultimate resort equal to virtue for the attainment of success in this world and the next;
there is no ornament equal to the ornament of virtue; there is no flower equal to the flower of virtue...
There is no flower; there is no fragrance equal to the fragrance of virtue (*sīlagandha*).

Indeed, even the world with its devas never tires of beholding one adorned with the ornament of virtue and anointed with the fragrance of virtue—such is the discourse connected with the qualities of virtue.
Then, in order to show that "by relying on this virtue, this heaven is obtained," the discourse on heaven follows immediately after the discourse on virtue.
He spoke. Regarding the "discourse on heaven": it is connected with the qualities of heaven, such as, "This is called heaven—desirable, lovely, and pleasing;
here there is constant play and constant attainment of prosperity. The gods of the Four Great Kings enjoy divine pleasure and divine prosperity for nine million years;
the Tāvatiṃsa gods [enjoy it] for thirty-six million years," and so forth.
How so? For the mouths of the Buddhas are never exhausted when speaking of the excellence of heaven. As it has been said:
"In many ways, monks, I might speak a discourse on heaven," and so forth.
Having thus enticed him with a discourse on heaven, he then adorned the elephant, as if cutting off its trunk.
In order to show that "this heaven too is impermanent and unstable;

no desire or lust should be directed toward it," he spoke of the danger, the degradation, and the defilement of sensual pleasures by way of such passages as: "Sensual pleasures provide little gratification, much suffering, and much despair;
herein the danger is greater. In this context, "danger" (ādīnava) means fault. "Degradation" (okāra) means a low state or base condition. "Defilement" (saṃkilesa) means...
By these [defilements], beings are defiled in *saṃsāra*. As it is said: "Alas, beings are indeed becoming defiled!
Having thus intimidated them by means of the danger of sensual desires (*kāma*), he proclaimed the benefit of renunciation (*nekkhamma*). "With a ready mind" means with a healthy mind.
"Self-proclaimed" (*sāmukkaṃsikā*) means self-exalted; it was taken up by being raised up by oneself, seen through the knowledge of the Self-Awakened One (*sayambhuñāṇa*).
"Unshared by others" means it is not common to others. What, then, is that? It is the teaching of the Noble Truths. For this very reason, he said: "Suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
"Dustless and stainless" means dustless due to the absence of the dust of passion and so forth, and stainless because of the removal of the stains of passion and so forth.
"The eye of Dhamma": here, the path of stream-entry is intended. This is stated for the purpose of showing the manner in which it arises.
"Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease," he said.

For it arises by making cessation its object, thus penetrating all conditioned things by way of its function. That which has seen the Dhamma of the Noble Truths is "one who has seen the Dhamma" (*diṭṭhadhammo*).
The same method applies to the others as well. One by whom doubt has been crossed over is "one who has crossed over doubt" (*tiṇṇavicikiccho*).
One whose doubt has departed is "one who has transcended doubt" (*vigata-kathaṃkatho*). One who has attained fearlessness is "one who has attained self-confidence" (*vesārajjappatto*).

Wherein? In the Teacher’s dispensation. One for whom there is no other condition, and who does not proceed here by means of faith in another, is "one who is not dependent on others" (*aparappaccayo*).
"Meat that is already circulating" means: having taken the price for meat that is naturally available and permissible, go and seek it at the marketplace.
The intention [is as follows]: "A number of Nigaṇṭhas" means about five hundred Nigaṇṭhas. "A fat animal" means a large-bodied animal, such as a cow-eared buffalo, a wild ox, or a pig.
"Specially prepared for him" means prepared by designating oneself; the meaning is that it was killed for one's sake.
"Dependent on that action" means that this act of killing living beings touches the person because of that meat. For that...
Their doctrine is that unwholesome [kamma] belongs half to the giver and half to the recipient. Another way:
*paṭiccakamma* means kamma performed in dependence upon oneself. Alternatively, *paṭiccakamma* is a designation for "indicative kamma" (*nimittakamma*);
because that indicative kamma exists therein, it is called *maṃsampi paṭiccakamma*. *Upakaṇṇake*: [near the ear].
"At the root of the ear. *Alaṃ* is a word of rejection; the meaning is "what is the use of this?

"But these [do not grow old]" means that even though these venerable ones have long desired disrepute and have spoken disrepute, they do not "grow old"—that is, they do not reach the end of their false accusations.
Alternatively, this word *jiridanti* should be understood in the sense of shame.
The meaning is "they do not feel shame.
3. Commentary on the *Assājānīyasutta*. 13.

In the third [sutta], "by means of the factors" (*aṅgaihīti*) means by means of the qualities as factors. "He is born in that direction" means he is born in that direction on the bank of the Sindhu river.
He is born [there]. Other noble thoroughbred horses are also born right there. "Whether wet or dry" means either green grass or dried grass.
"He does not frighten other horses" means he does not terrify, strike, bite, or provoke quarrels with other horses.
"Deceitfulness" (*sāṭheyya*) means the state of being deceitful. "Fraudulence" (*kūṭeyya*) means the state of being fraudulent. "Crookedness" (*jimheyya*) means the state of being crooked.

"Vaṅkeyyāni" means crooked states. Thus, by all four terms, his state of not having trained is described. "Vāhī" means one whose nature is to carry out; it refers to one who acts upon the advice given.
"Yāva jīvitamaraṇapariyādānā" means until the end of life through death.
"Sakkaccaṃ paribhuñjati" means he partakes [of the food] after reflecting upon it as if it were the Deathless (Amata). Regarding the phrases beginning with "purisathāmena":
The powers of knowledge (*ñāṇathāma*) and so forth have been explained. "Configuration" (*saṇṭhāna*) means subsiding or calming.
4. Commentary on the *Assakhaḷuṅkasutta* 14.
In the fourth [verse], where it is said "he is told 'go!'," it means he is told "depart! He drives the chariot from behind by means of the backbone.
Having compressed the yoke, it retreats by causing the rear of the chariot to roll back.
"It leaps backward and strikes the pole" means that it lifts its two hind legs and, striking with them, breaks the chariot pole (*kubbara*).
"It breaks the triple-bar" means there are three bars in front of the chariot, and it breaks them. "Having cast its hip against the chariot shaft" means—
Having bent its head, having lowered its yoke to the ground, and having struck the charioteer with its shoulder-blade.

“It tramples down” means it stands while treading upon the pole with its two forefeet. “It makes the chariot turn back” means it causes the chariot to ascend onto dry land or a place covered in thorns.
“Without taking heed” means without paying attention or without reckoning [the danger]. “Placing at the mouth” means for the purpose of putting it into the mouth.
The iron chain was given. "Standing like a stake" means that he stands in a position like a fixed post, having placed his four feet as immovable as pillars.
In this sutta, only the roundabout (the cycle of existence) is discussed.
5. Commentary on the Malasutta (The Sutta on Impurities).
15. In the fifth [verse], "the stain of non-recitation" means that the failure to recite the mantras one has learned is called a stain.
"Houses have the stain of inactivity" means that the absence of exertion and effort is the stain of houses. "Of beauty" refers to the beauty of the body.
"Protecting" refers to protecting whatever belongs to oneself. "Ignorance is the supreme stain" is said because it is the stain among all other unwholesome states.
Ignorance (*avijjā*), which consists of non-knowledge regarding eight points and is termed the root of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa-mūla*), is a dense darkness and the supreme defilement.
Indeed, there is nothing more defiled than this. In this sutta as well, it is precisely the round of existence that is discussed.
6. Commentary on the *Dūteyyasutta* (The Messenger Sutta)
16. In the sixth [verse], *dūteyya* means the work of a messenger. *Gantumarahati* means he is worthy of carrying that message known as *dūteyya*, having memorized it.
*Sotā* means he is a listener to the one who gives him that message.
*Sāvetā* means, having learned it, he is a repeater, saying, "This is exactly what you said. *Uggahetā* means he is one who has grasped it well, having mastered it. *Dhāretā* means...
"Having well-considered it, he should uphold it. "One who understands" means one who knows the meaning and the non-meaning. "One who makes understood" means one who causes another to understand.
"Skilled in what is appropriate and what is inappropriate" means one who is expert regarding what is suitable and what is unsuitable, thinking, "This is appropriate; this is inappropriate.
Being proficient in both what has been accepted and what has not been accepted, when announcing the teaching, he announces it after having observed what is appropriate. Not...
"It trembles" (*byathati*) means it quivers and does not falter. "Without doubt" (*asaṃsiddhaṃ*) means free from uncertainty, with suspicion gone.
"Questioned" (*pucchito*) means questioned for the sake of an inquiry.
7–8. Commentary on the Two Discourses on Bondage.

17–18. In the seventh [verse], "by weeping" means by crying. "By seizing" means by means of methods such as pulling at the lower garment or the upper robe. "By a forest-gathering" means by a gift of flowers, fruits, and so forth, brought back after being gathered from the forest.
The same method applies to the eighth [verse] as well. 9. Commentary on the *Pahārāda Sutta* 19.
In the ninth [verse], *Pahārāda* is one who has that name. *Asurinda* is the chief of the asuras; for among the asuras, there is Vepacitti.
“Rāhu, Pahārāda, and [Vepacitti]—these three are the eldest. “He approached where the Blessed One was”:

from the day the Blessed One attained full enlightenment, after eleven years had passed while he thought, “I will go today,” or “I will go tomorrow,” in the twelfth year, during the Teacher’s stay at Verañjā, he conceived the thought, “I shall go into the presence of the Perfectly Enlightened One.”
"It has been twelve years since I thought, 'Today or tomorrow,' so let me go right now.
At that very moment, surrounded by a host of asuras, he departed from the asura realm and approached the Blessed One during the day;
standing to one side, he reportedly thought, "I shall listen to the Dhamma only after asking the Tathāgata a question."
Having arrived, he was unable to ask [his question] out of reverence for the Buddha from the moment he had seen the Tathāgata;
nevertheless, after paying homage to the Teacher, he stood to one side. Then the Teacher thought:
"This Pahārāda will not be able to speak first unless I speak to him; therefore, I shall initiate the conversation with him by means of a question regarding his own past conduct."
“I shall ask one question,” he thought.
Then, asking him, he said, “But did you not strike [him],” and so forth. In that context, *abhiramanti* means they find delight;
the sense is that they dwell without longing for anything else. He was pleased, thinking, “The Blessed One is questioning me regarding a matter already well-mastered.”
"Having offered, they delight," he said. "Sloping gradually" (*anupubbaninna*) and all the following terms are synonyms for the state of being sloped in successive order.
"Not a precipice right from the start" means it is not a steep drop like a cliff or a great waterfall from the very beginning.

For that [slope] begins from the bank and proceeds by increments of one finger-breadth, two finger-breadths, a span, a cubit, a fathom, a *usabha*, half a *gāvuta*, a *gāvuta*, half a *yojana*, and so forth.
It shows that while moving along as something deep, it remains at the foot of Sineru being eighty-four thousand *yojanas* deep.

"Of stable nature" (*ṭhitadhammo*) means having a stable inherent character. "With a corpse" (*kuṇapena*) means with any carcass whatsoever, such as that of an elephant or a horse. "Throws up onto dry land" (*thalaṃ ussāreti*) means it hurls it onto dry land by the very force of its waves, as if grasping it with a hand.
Regarding the Ganges and Yamunā: it is appropriate here to explain the origin of these rivers starting from this point. This, first of all—
Jambudīpa measures ten thousand yojanas; of that, a region measuring four thousand yojanas is submerged by water and is reckoned as the Great Ocean.

Humans dwell within a space measuring three thousand yojanas, while the Himavat mountain stands within a space measuring three thousand yojanas, five hundred yojanas in height and adorned with eighty-four thousand peaks on all sides.
Variegated with five hundred flowing rivers, there stand seven great lakes—
Anotatta, Kaṇṇamuṇḍa, Rathakāra, Chaddanta, Kuṇāla, Mandākinī, and Sīhapapāta— each measuring fifty by fifty yojanas in length and breadth,
and one hundred and fifty yojanas in circumference, where they are established.
Among them, Anotatta is surrounded by these five mountains: Sudassana Peak, Citta Peak, Kāḷaka Peak, Gandhamādana Peak, and Kelāsa Peak. Therein, Sudassana Peak is made of gold;
two hundred yojanas in height, inwardly curved, and shaped like a crow’s beak, it stands covering that very lake. Citta Peak is composed entirely of all kinds of gems.
The Kālakūṭa mountain consists of collyrium; the peak of Gandhamādana consists of earth and is the color of green mung beans within;

it is abundant with these ten kinds of fragrance—the fragrance of the root, the fragrance of the heartwood, the fragrance of the softwood, the fragrance of the bark, the fragrance of the inner bark, the fragrance of the sap, the fragrance of the leaf, the fragrance of the flower, the fragrance of the fruit, and the fragrance of the scent itself—and it is covered with various kinds of medicinal herbs.
On the Uposatha day of the dark fortnight, it stands blazing like a glowing ember; Kelāsakūṭa is made of silver.
All [the peaks] are equal in height and shape to Sudassana, standing so as to cover that very lake.
All of them rain by the power of the gods and the power of the nāgas, and rivers flow within them. All of this—
