The water enters only the Anotatta lake. When the moon and sun pass to the south or north, they create a reflection there due to the intervening mountain range;
when they pass directly overhead, they do not. For this very reason, the name "Anotatta" (Unheated) arose for it.
Therein are delightful stone slabs, free from fish and turtles, with bathing pools of water as pure as crystal.
They were well-prepared, in which Buddhas whose taints were exhausted, Paccekabuddhas, and powerful seers bathed,
while gods, yakkhas, and others played in the water.
On its four sides were four [fountains] with the faces of a lion, an elephant, a horse, and a bull.
There are openings from which four rivers flow. On the banks of the river issuing from the lion’s mouth, lions are most numerous;
from the elephant’s mouth and the others, elephants, horses, and bulls emerge.
The river issuing from the eastern direction circles Lake Anotatta three times clockwise and, without joining the other three rivers, follows the path of non-humans toward the eastern Himavat.

Having gone, it enters the great ocean. The rivers emerging from the western direction and the northern direction likewise turn clockwise and, having traveled through the uninhabited regions of the western Himalayas and the northern Himalayas respectively, enter the great ocean.
However, the river emerging from the southern face [turns] three times...
Having performed a circumambulation to the right, it traveled sixty *yojanas* straight north along the surface of the rock;
then, striking the mountain, it rose up and became a stream of water sixty *gāvutas* in circumference.
Traveling sixty *yojanas* through the air, it fell upon the rock named Tiyaggaḷa, which was shattered by the force of the water’s impact. There, [the stream] measured fifty *yojanas* in width.
A great lotus pond named Tiyaggaḷā came into being; having broken through the bank of the pond and entered the rock, it traveled sixty yojanas.

Then, having broken through the solid earth and gone sixty yojanas underground by way of a tunnel, it struck the mountain Tiracchānapabbata known as Giñjha, whereupon five streams emerged like the five fingers on the palm of a hand.
Having been offered, it flows forth. Having circumambulated Anotatta three times to the right, the place where it has gone is called the Āvatta-Gaṅgā.
The place where it has gone straight along the surface of the rocks for sixty yojanas is the Kaṇha-Gaṅgā; the place where it has gone through the air for sixty yojanas is the Ākāsa-Gaṅgā;
and the fifty-yojana area situated upon the Tiyaṅgaḷa rock is the Tiyaṅgaḷa-Pokkharaṇī.
Where it has broken through the bank and entered the rock, having traveled sixty *yojanas*, it is called the "Thick Gaṅgā" (*Bahalagaṅgā*).
Where it has traveled sixty *yojanas* by way of a subterranean passage (*umaṅga*), it is called the "Subterranean Gaṅgā" (*Umaṅgagaṅgā*).
Furthermore, where it strikes the transverse mountain named Viñjha and flows forth as five streams, those places are known as the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Aciravatī, Sarabhū, [Mahī, and Sindhu].
“Mahī” refers to the five [rivers] collectively. Thus, it should be understood that these five great rivers flow forth from the Himālaya.
“Flowing” (*savantī*) means whatever great rivers or small streams go along flowing. “Enter” (*appenti*) means they adhere to and descend into [the ocean].
“Streams” (*dhārā*) refers to rain-showers. “Fullness” (*pūratta*) is the state of being filled; for this is the natural law (*dhammatā*) of the great ocean.
"It is not possible to say, 'At this time the rain has become light; we shall take our nets and catch fish and turtles,' nor can one say, 'At this time there is heavy rain;
shall we find a place to stretch out our backs? For since the time of the first aeon, the water has remained touching the base of Mount Sineru."
Then, not even a single finger’s breadth of water sinks below or rises above [the surface]. "Of one taste" means having an undifferentiated flavor.

"Pearls" are of many kinds, distinguished as small or large, round or long, and so forth. "Jewels" are of many kinds, distinguished as red, blue, and so forth. "Cat's-eye gems" (veḷuriya) are of many kinds, distinguished by colors such as bamboo or the sirīsapuppha flower.
"Conch shells" are of many kinds, distinguished as right-spiraling, copper-colored bellies, or trumpet-shaped, and so forth.

"Of many kinds": *sila* (stone) is of many kinds, distinguished by the colors of white, black, mung-bean, and so forth. *Pavāḷa* (coral) is of many kinds, distinguished by being small, large, red, deep red, and so forth.
*Masāragalla* is the *kabara* gem. "The *nāgas*" refers to both the *nāgas* who dwell on the backs of waves and the *nāgas* who reside in celestial palaces (*vimāna*).
"Eight strokes" means that the Teacher is able to speak eight, sixteen, thirty-two, or even sixty-four *dhammas*.
Although there are a thousand [ways], Pahārāda spoke of eight; thinking, "I too shall speak by making them similar to those," he said this.
Regarding the phrases beginning with "gradual training" (*anupubbasikkhā*): by "gradual training" the three trainings are included;

by "gradual practice" (*anupubbakiriyā*) the thirteen ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) are included; and by "gradual path" (*anupubbapaṭipadā*) the seven contemplations, the eighteen great insights (*mahāvipassanā*), and the thirty-eight [insights] are included.
The thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment are the classifications of objects.

"Full penetration of final knowledge does not come by leaping over" means that there is no such thing as attaining the state of an Arahant from the very beginning without first fulfilling morality and so forth—just as a frog cannot travel by leaping;
rather, the meaning is that one must attain Arahantship only after fulfilling morality, concentration, and wisdom in their proper sequence.
"Far away" means at a great distance. There is neither a deficiency nor a fullness in the element of Nibbāna by that;
even if Buddhas do not arise for incalculable eons, such that not a single being is able to attain final Nibbāna, even then it cannot be said that "the element of Nibbāna is empty.
And yet, during the time of a Buddha, in each single assembly, incalculable beings [attain] the Deathless.
Even then, it cannot be said that "the element of Nibbāna is full.
10. Commentary on the Uposatha Sutta: 20.
Regarding the phrase "was seated," he was seated in the Jewel Palace for the purpose of performing the Uposatha with the female lay follower. Having sat down...

However, while surveying the minds of the bhikkhus, he saw one person of immoral conduct and thought, "If I recite the Pātimokkha while this person is still sitting here, his head will split into seven pieces. Out of compassion for him, he remained silent.
*Abhikkantā* means passed by, exhausted, or come to an end. *Uddhaste aruṇe* means when the tip of the dawn has risen.

“With a joyful face” means with a contented face. Ānanda, when he said, “The assembly is impure,” he did not say, “Such-and-such a person is impure,” but rather, “Ānanda, the assembly is impure. The rest is clear everywhere.
This is the second chapter, the Mahāvagga.
3. The Chapter on Householders (Gahapativagga) 1. Commentary on the First Ugga Sutta (Paṭhamauggasuttavaṇṇanā) 21.
Regarding the phrase "he sat down on the seat prepared": it is said that in his house there was [room] for five hundred bhikkhus.
Five hundred seats were always prepared; he sat down on one of them. "Listen to that" means:
listen to that, or listen to those eight kinds of wonderful qualities. "The mind became serene" means:
not even a mere thought such as "Is he a Buddha or is he not a Buddha? arose; rather, the mental state arose: "He is indeed the Buddha."
It became clear and undisturbed. "To one's own kinsmen" means: let her go to the houses of her relatives, taking only as much wealth as is necessary for her own maintenance.
"To whom among you shall I give? means: tell me your intention—whom among you do I give to?
"Not divided" means: "I will give this much, I will not give that much; I will give this..."
For one who gives rise to the thought, "I will not give this," it is said that [the gift] has been partitioned; but for me, it is not so.
Rather, like what belongs to the Saṅgha or what belongs to a group, it is shared in common with those of virtuous conduct.
"I attend upon him with care" means that I serve him with my own hands and approach him with reverence.
"But it is not surprising for me, venerable sir," [he said], "that deities should approach me and announce this;
that is not surprising. But that I do not experience any inflation of mind on that account—that indeed I call surprising.
"Excellent, excellent, monk!"—here, although he addresses the monk, it is actually the lay follower who is being praised.
Furthermore, this "well done" (sādhukāra) is to be understood as an expression of approval for the explanation.
2. Commentary on the Second Ugga Sutta:
22. Regarding "in Nāgavana": it is said that the merchant had a park named Nāgavana; there, before the meal, he...
Having taken perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, and desiring to go for a pleasure excursion to a park, he went there and was being entertained; then he saw the Blessed One.
At the mere sight of him, his mind became serene in the same manner as before, and the intoxication arising from drinking liquor was abandoned at that very moment.
It was with reference to this that he said: "I offered it," meaning that having poured water into his hand, I gave it to him.

"Such-and-such a person is so-and-so. By saying, "I give with an even mind," he shows that he does not create a diversity of thought such as, "I will give a little to this one and much to that one," but rather treats the gift to be given as identical for all.
"They announce" means they announce while standing in the air. With the words, "There is no fetter for me," the lay follower declares his own attainment of the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala).
3. Commentary on the First Hatthaka Sutta. 23.
In the third [sutta], Hatthaka Āḷavaka is a prince who received the name "Hatthaka" because he was received from the hands of the yakkha Āḷavaka by the hands of the Blessed One.
"Virtuous" means possessed of virtue through the five precepts and the ten precepts. "Generous" means endowed with generosity.

"Is it so, venerable sir? means: "Venerable sir, is it so in this matter of the Blessed One’s explanation? "One of few desires" means one who is of few desires through the state of having attained fewness of wishes.
Commentary on the Second Hatthaka Sutta:
In the fourth [sutta], "with about five hundred lay followers" refers specifically to those noble disciple lay followers who are stream-enterers and once-returners.
Surrounded by five hundred [attendants], having finished his morning meal and taken perfumes, garlands, ointments, and powders, he approached the Blessed One.

"Bases of conciliation" (*saṅgahavatthūni*) means the causes for gathering [people]. "By these, indeed" (*tehi āhaṃ*) means: "I gather them by means of those. "I gather them through giving" (*taṃ dānena saṅgaṇhāmi*) means:
I gather them by giving such things as food for oxen and ploughs, seed-grain, and so forth, as well as perfumes, garlands, roots, and the like.
"By kindly speech" means: I win them over with soft, pleasant words that are agreeable to the ear, such as "Mother," "Father," "Brother," "Sister," and so forth.
"By beneficial conduct" means: having recognized, "This person has no need for gifts or kind words;
he is one who should be won over by beneficial conduct," one wins them over through beneficial conduct, which consists in the accomplishment of whatever need has arisen.
I favor him. By "equality" (samānattatā): thinking, "This person has no need for gifts and such services;
he should be favored through equality," I favor him by making myself equal to him in eating, drinking, sitting, and so forth.
"They do not think one should listen to a poor man in that way": [this refers to] one who is unable to give anything or do anything for a poor man.
They do not think they should listen to a pauper as they do to me;
rather, they think they should listen to me, they abide by the instruction given, and they do not think my admonition should be transgressed. "This is your source" means this is your means.
It should be understood that in both of these suttas, the Teacher has spoken of a combination of virtue, generosity, and wisdom.
5–6. Commentary on the Mahānāma Sutta, etc. (25–26).

In the fifth [sutta], "investigated the meaning" means that one investigates what is beneficial and what is harmful, as well as what is the cause and what is not the cause. In the sixth, faith, virtue, and generosity are spoken of in combination.
7. Commentary on the First Bala Sutta.
27. "The power of reproaching" (*ujjhānabala*) means the power of censuring. For fools, the very act of censuring—thinking, "That such-and-such person said this and that;
he said it to me, not to anyone else"—is their strength. "The power of convincing" (*nijjhānabala*) means the power of demonstrating what is right and what is wrong, thinking, "This is not so;
it is actually like this. "The power of reflection" (*paṭisaṅkhānabala*) means the power of reviewing. "The power of patience" (*khantibala*) means the power of endurance.
8. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Powers (Dutiyabalasutta) 28.
"Powers" (balāni) refers to the powers of knowledge (ñāṇabala). "He claims the destruction of the taints" (āsavānaṃ khayaṃ paṭijānāti) means he claims the state of Arahatship.

"As impermanent" (aniccato) means by way of the mode of non-existence after having been. "As it really is" (yathābhūtaṃ) means according to its true nature. "With right wisdom" (sammappaññāya) means together with insight (vipassanā).
"By means of path-wisdom (*maggapaññā*). "Compared to a pit of glowing embers": these sensual pleasures (*kāmā*) are compared to a pit of glowing embers in the sense of being burning.

"Inclined toward seclusion" (*vivekaninna*): inclined toward *nibbāna* by way of the attainment of the fruit (*phalasamāpatti*). "Set apart from seclusion" (*vivekaṭṭha*): free from defilements (*kilesa*), or having become distant from them.
"Delighting in renunciation" (*nekkhammābhirata*): delighting in the life of going forth (*pabbajjā*). "Brought to an end" (*byantibhūta*): having reached the limit of its cessation, even in part.
It is unattached, dissociated, and detached. "From things that are the basis for the taints" means from those defiled phenomena that serve as the causes for the taints by way of association;
this is the meaning. Alternatively, "become exhausted" (byantibhūta) means "gone away" (vigatavāya).
From what? From all things that are the basis for the taints; the meaning is, from all phenomena belonging to the three planes. In this sutta, it is the Noble Path.
The mundane and supramundane have been explained.
9. Commentary on the Akkhaṇa Sutta: 29.
In the ninth [verse], "one who performs duties at the proper time" (khaṇakicco) means one who performs duties only after having obtained the opportunity.

Meaning: "Dhamma" refers to the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. "Peaceful" (*opasamiko*) means that which brings about the pacification of the defilements (*kilesa*). "Leading to final Nibbāna" (*parinibbāyiko*) means that which effects the final extinction of the defilements.
"Leading to enlightenment" (*sambodhagāmī*) means that it goes to, or attains, enlightenment (*sambodhi*), which is defined as the knowledge of the four paths.

"The long-lived host of devas" is said with reference to the host of non-percipient devas (*asañña-devanikāya*). "Among those who do not understand" (*aviññātāresu*) means among those who are exceedingly ignorant.
"Suppavedite" means well-expounded. "Antarāyikā" means obstructive. "Khaṇo ve mā upaccagā" means let not this opportunity that has been obtained pass by.

"Idha ceva naṃ virādheti" means that if anyone who lives heedlessly, having obtained this opportunity here, violates the fixed course of the True Dhamma—the Noble Path—and does not accomplish it. "Atītattho" means the meaning of what has passed.
“Having lost his opportunity”: he will grieve for a long time (*cirarattaṃ*).
For example, if a merchant hears that goods have appeared in a certain place but does not go there, while others go and take them, they might obtain eight or ten times as much profit;
then the former merchant would regret it, thinking, "My opportunity has passed. In the same way, whoever here—
Having gained the opportunity, one who does not practice it violates the fixed course of the True Dhamma;
like that merchant whose wealth has passed away, he will long repent and grieve. Furthermore, "shrouded by ignorance" is likewise [the case].

"They penetrated" means they realized. "Restraints" refers to the restraints of virtue (*sīla-saṃvara*). "Followers of the realm of Māra" refers to *saṃsāra*, which is designated as the realm of Māra.
"Anugate": "Pāraṅgatā" means those who have gone to Nibbāna. "Ye pattā āsavakkhayaṃ" means those who have attained Arahantship.
Thus, in these verses, the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) and its cessation (vivaṭṭa) are explained.
10. Commentary on the Anuruddha-Mahāvitakka Sutta.
30. *Dasame Cetīsūti*: in the kingdom so named because it was the dwelling place of kings called Cetis. *Pācīnavaṃsadāyeti*:
in the bamboo grove situated to the east of the place where the One of Ten Powers (the Buddha) resided, a forest covered with bamboo that shone with a blue luster.
Thus a reflection arose in his mind; for it is said that after the Elder had gone forth...
Having attained meditative absorption even during his very first rains-retreat, he developed the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*), capable of seeing a thousandfold world-system.
He went to the presence of the Elder Sāriputta and said:
"Here, friend Sāriputta, with the purified divine eye, which surpasses that of humans, I survey a thousandfold world-system. Indeed, it has been undertaken..."
“Yet my energy is unflagging, my mindfulness is established and unconfused, my body is tranquil and not agitated, and my mind is concentrated and one-pointed.
And yet, my mind is not liberated from the taints through non-clinging.
Then the Elder said to him: “Friend Anuruddha, as for what you think: ‘With the divine eye... I survey...’”
This is in your mind. Furthermore, friend Anuruddha, when you think, “My energy is indeed aroused...

[and] my mind is one-pointed,” this is in your restlessness. Furthermore, friend Anuruddha, when you think, “And yet my mind is not liberated from the taints through non-clinging,” this is in your remorse. It would be well indeed if the Venerable...
"Anuruddha, having abandoned these three things and not attending to these three things, let him apply his mind to the deathless element.
Thus the Elder taught him the meditation subject.

Having taken up that meditation subject and received leave from the Teacher, he went to the Ceti country and spent eight months practicing the duties of a recluse while walking back and forth on a meditation path.
Thus, his body exhausted from being churned by the force of his exertion, he sat down beneath a bamboo thicket.
Then this reflection arose in his mind—the meaning is that this "thought of a Great Man" (mahāpurisa-vitakka) arose. Regarding the term *appiccha* (one of few desires):

here it refers to one who has few desires for requisites (*paccaya-appiccha*), one who has few desires for attainments (*adhigama-appiccha*), one who has few desires for the scriptures (*pariyatti-appiccha*), and one who has few desires for the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga-appiccha*).

There are four types of those with few desires (*appiccha*). Among them, one who has few desires regarding requisites (*paccayappiccha*) takes little when much is given, and takes even less when little is given;
he does not take everything. One who has few desires regarding attainment (*adhigamappiccha*) does not allow others to know of his own attainments, like the Elder Majjhantika.
One who has few desires regarding the scriptures (*pariyattiappiccha*), though he may be a master of the Three Pitakas, does not wish to make known his great learning.

It is like the Elder Sāketatissa. One who desires the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) does not allow others to know his state of maintaining those practices, as was the case with the elder brother among the two brothers, the Elders. The story is told in the *Visuddhimagga*.
This is the Dhamma: thus, by concealing one's existing virtues and by moderation in receiving gifts, such is the person of few desires (*appiccha*).
This ninefold supramundane Dhamma comes to fruition for one who is contented, not for one of great desire. Thus it should be applied in all cases.
"For one who is contented" means for one who is contented by the three kinds of contentment regarding the four requisites.

"For one who is secluded" means for one who is secluded through physical seclusion, mental seclusion, and seclusion from acquisitions (*upadhi*). Therein, physical seclusion is the state of being alone by dispelling the company of crowds, by way of applying oneself to the foundation of exertion.
The work is not accomplished by mere unification alone; therefore, having performed the preliminary exercise (*parikamma*) on the kasiṇas, one brings forth the eight attainments (*samāpatti*).
This is called seclusion of mind (*cittaviveka*). The work is not accomplished by the mere attainment alone;

therefore, making jhāna the basis, one contemplates conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) and attains Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*). This is [seclusion of phenomena] in every respect.
This is called seclusion from acquisitions. Therefore the Blessed One said: “There is seclusion of body for those who dwell secluded in body and delight in renunciation;

there is seclusion of mind for those whose minds are purified and have attained supreme clarity; and there is seclusion from acquisitions for persons who are without acquisitions and have reached the cessation of formations.”
"Delighting in company" means one who delights both in the company of crowds and in the company of defilements.
"One who has aroused energy" means one who has aroused energy by way of both bodily and mental effort.

"One whose mindfulness is established" means one whose mindfulness is established by way of the four foundations of mindfulness. "One who is concentrated" means one whose mind is one-pointed. "One who possesses wisdom" means one who possesses wisdom regarding the fact that one's own actions are one's own property (*kammassakata*).
"Excellent, excellent! he said, thus encouraging the Elder's thought.

Having reflected upon the seven thoughts of a Great Man, as if bestowing an eighth upon a man who had already obtained the seven treasures—just as one might give an eighth treasure to a man who has acquired the seven kinds of wealth—or as if giving an eighth jewel to a man who has already obtained the seven precious gems, the seven elephant-treasures, and the seven horse-treasures.
Explaining the eighth [quality] for one who stands firm, he said thus:

"To one who delights in the non-proliferated" means to one who takes delight in the state of Nibbāna, which is designated as "non-proliferated" because it is free from the proliferations of craving, conceit, and views. The other term is a synonym for that same quality.
"To one who delights in proliferation" means to one who takes delight in the aforementioned proliferations. The other term is a synonym for that same quality.
*Yato* means "whence" (when). *Tato* means "thence" (then). *Nānārattānaṃ* means "of those dyed with various colors," that is, dyed with various dyes such as blue, yellow, red, and white.
*Paṃsukūlaṃ* refers to the rag-robe situated in the twenty-three [types of] fields.
*Khāyissati* means that, just as for him at the time of the morning session or other times, whenever he wishes to put on whatever [robe] he desires, that chest of cloth—
“Appearing pleasing, it will appear and present itself to you as well, while you dwell content through the great noble lineage of contentment with robes. ‘For delight’ means for the sake of delight.
‘For non-distress’ means for the sake of being free from the distress of craving and views. ‘For a comfortable dwelling’ means for the sake of living in ease. For entering...”
"Of Nibbāna" means for the purpose of entering the deathless Nibbāna.

"A meal of alms-food scraps" refers to the food obtained as alms-food scraps by one who, relying on the strength of his legs, wanders from house to house in order through villages, market towns, and royal capitals.
"It will be eaten" means that it will be [eaten] like the meal of various exquisite flavors belonging to that householder.
"He will attend upon him": for one who dwells contented, that is, for one dwelling contented by means of the Great Noble Lineage of contentment with almsfood (*piṇḍapāta-santosamahāariyavaṃsa*).

"The foot of a tree as a lodging will appear to him": to that householder, the foot of a tree will appear like a gabled chamber (*kūṭāgāra*) fragrant with the scent of perfumed flowers, as if it were his own three-storied palace. "Contented": by means of the Great Noble Lineage of contentment with lodgings (*senāsana-santosamahāariyavaṃsa*).
"For one who is content. "A grass mat" means that which is spread out on the ground with grass, leaves, wooden planks, stone slabs, or any such thing.
"Putrid urine" refers to any kind of urine; even that collected at that very moment is called "putrid urine" because of its foul odor.
"Dwelling for one who is content" means by way of contentment with the requisite of medicine as a support for the sick.
“For one who dwells contented.
Thus the Blessed One, having taught the meditation subject while inserting the state of Arahantship in four places, reflected:
“In which kind of lodging will the meditation subject be suitable for one dwelling? And he perceived: “It will be suitable for one dwelling in that very place.”
Having understood this, he said, "Therefore, Anuruddha," and so forth. "Dwelling secluded" means dwelling secluded by means of the three kinds of seclusion.
"Connected with exhortation" means connected with words of exhortation; the meaning is that it is intended solely for their coming to attend upon him.
"In the cessation of proliferation" refers to the state of Nibbāna. "Enters into" means [to enter] by way of making it the object of cognition.
"It leaps forward. In such expressions as "it becomes serene," it should be understood that serenity, stability, and loftiness occur by way of the object itself.

Thus, after the Venerable Anuruddha had spoken of the eight thoughts of a great man in the Eastern Bamboo Grove at Ceti, the Blessed One sat down again at the Great Monastery in the Bhesakaḷā Grove and explained them in detail to the community of monks.
"Mind-made" (*manomaya*) refers both to a body produced by the mind and to a body gone [there] by means of the mind; here, he speaks thus with reference to a body gone by means of the mind.
"Just as my intention was" (*yathā me ahu saṅkappo*) means just as my thought (*vitakka*) was;
showing the eighth great person’s thought beyond that, he taught what was further than that. The rest is clear everywhere.
The Third Chapter on Householders.
4. The Chapter on Giving. 1.
Commentary on the First Discourse on Giving.
31. Regarding the first [of the four types of givers]: "He gives by approaching" means he gives after having reached [the recipient].
Having seen that someone has arrived, he seats them for just a moment, pays them honor, and then gives the gift; he does not weary himself with the thought, "I will give later.

"Out of fear" means out of fear of censure, thinking, "This person is stingy and ungenerous," or out of fear of the states of misery (apāya). "He gave to me" means, "In the past, this person gave such-and-such a thing to me."
He gives. Thinking, "He will give to me," he gives, thinking, "In the future, he will give this to me. Thinking, "Giving is good," he gives, thinking, "Giving is indeed good and beautiful;

it is praised by the wise, such as the Buddhas and others. He gives for the sake of adorning the mind and equipping the mind, meaning he gives for the purpose of adorning and equipping the mind of serenity and insight. For giving—
It makes the mind supple. He who receives it becomes supple-minded, thinking, "I have received it.
He who gives it also becomes supple-minded, thinking, "I have given it. Thus it makes the minds of both supple. For this very reason, it is called "the taming of the untamed.
As it is said: "Giving is the taming of the untamed; non-giving corrupts the tamed."
“By giving and by pleasant speech, they rise up and bow down.
Among these eight kinds of giving, however, the gift that is an adornment of the mind is the supreme.
2. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Giving.

32. In the second [verse], "through faith" (*saddhā*) refers to that faith by which one gives a gift. "Through shame" (*hirī*) refers to that very shame by which one gives a gift; this is what is intended. "Wholesome giving" (*kusalaṃ dānaṃ*) means blameless giving. "Leading to heaven" (*diviyaṃ*) means going to heaven (*divaṅgama*). 3. Commentary on the Discourse on the Bases of Giving (Dānavatthusutta) 33.

In the third [verse], "bases of giving" (*dānavatthūni*) means causes for giving. "One gives a gift out of desire" (*chandā dānaṃ deti*) means one gives a gift out of affection. "Out of hatred" (*dosā*)...
Being angry with hatred, one seizes whatever is available and gives it with haste. "Out of delusion" means that, being bewildered by delusion (*moha*), one gives.

"Out of fear" means that one gives out of fear of censure, or fear of the states of misery (*apāya*), or out of fear of this or that particular thing. "Family lineage" means the ancestral succession of the family.
4. Commentary on the Sutta on Fields (*Khettasutta*)
34. "In the fourth [case], it is not of great fruit" means that it is not of great fruit in terms of its grain-yield.
"It is not of great enjoyment" means that whatever yield it has, its enjoyment is not great; it is of slight enjoyment and not sweet.
"It is not of great excellence" means there is no increase in its value; the meaning is that it does not have a large arrangement of rice-stalks.
"Rising and falling" refers to uneven ground by way of its sloping toward the lowlands.
There, water does not remain on the high ground, yet it remains in great abundance in the lowlands. "Stony and gravelly" means possessed of flat stones spread out, small pebbles, and gravel.
"Saline" means where salt has welled up. "And not deep-seated" is due to the hardness of the soil.
It has followed a deep course; having made a furrow, it is not possible to plow further, for it remains merely a shallow furrow.
"Not endowed with an inlet" means it is not endowed with a path for the water to enter.
"Not endowed with an outlet" means it is not endowed with a path for the water to exit at the rear. "Not endowed with channels" means it is not endowed with small or large water-channels.

"It is well-endowed" means it is not lacking in field boundaries. All such terms as "not of great fruit" and so forth are to be understood solely in terms of the fruit of karmic result (*vipākaphala*).
"Well-endowed" means complete and possessed of excellence. "Sown with a good seed" means a well-endowed seed has been planted.
"Deve sampādayantamhīti" means when the gods rain properly.

"Anītisampadā hotīti" means that the absence of calamities such as insects, worms, and other harmful creatures constitutes the first accomplishment (*sampadā*). "Virūḷhīti" means growth; this is the second accomplishment.
"Vepullanti" means abundance; this is the third accomplishment. "Phalanti" means a full fruit; this is the fourth accomplishment. "Sampannasīlesūti" [means those whose virtue is accomplished].

Regarding those whose virtue is fulfilled (*paripuṇṇasīlesu*). "Perfection of food" (*bhojanasampadā*) means well-prepared, diverse food. "Perfection" (*sampadā*) is threefold, being the perfection of the wholesome (*kusala*).
"Brings near" (*upaneti*): that perfection of food brings [the result] near. Why?

Because that which has been done by him is perfected; the meaning is that the deed performed by him is accomplished and complete. "In the sense of being perfected" (*sampannatthūdha*) means perfected.
Let it be so here. "Endowed with true knowledge and conduct" means being possessed of the three types of true knowledge (*vijjā*) and the fifteen factors of conduct (*caraṇadhamma*).
"Having obtained" means that such a person, having attained the perfection of mind—the state of being complete and lacking nothing—performs the perfection of action;
that is, he performs complete action. He obtains the perfection of purpose; that is, he obtains a complete purpose.
He attains. "Perfection of view" means the view of insight (*vipassanā*). "Perfection of the path" means the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*).

"He goes with a perfected mind" means that, having become one whose mind is fulfilled, he goes to *arahantship*. "That is the perfection of all" means that liberation from all suffering is indeed called the perfection of all.
5. Commentary on the Discourse on Rebirth through Giving (Dānūpapatti-sutta) 35.
In the fifth [discourse], "rebirths through giving" (*dānūpapattiyo*) refers to rebirths conditioned by giving. "He establishes" (*dahati*) means he places [the mind].

"He resolves" (*adhiṭṭhāti*) is a synonym for that same term. "He develops" (*bhāveti*) means he increases it. "Liberated from the inferior" (*hīne vimuttaṃ*) refers to being liberated from the five inferior strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*).
"Liberated" means it is liberated from the defilements. "Not further developed" means it has not been cultivated beyond that for the sake of the higher paths and fruits.
"It leads to rebirth in that place" means it leads to being born in whatever state was aspired to when the wholesome deed was performed.
"Of one who is free from lust" refers to one whose lust has been eradicated by the path or suppressed by meditative attainment (*samāpatti*). By the mere act of giving...
For it is not possible to be reborn in the Brahma-world [without this], yet generosity is an ornament and an accessory to the mind of concentration and insight.
Therefore, with a mind made pliant by generosity, one develops the divine abodes (brahmavihāra) and is reborn in the Brahma-world. Hence it is said:
“of one free from lust, not of one possessed by lust.”
6. Commentary on the *Puññakiriyavatthusutta* 36.

In the sixth [discourse], they are called "bases for the performance of merit" (*puññakiriyavatthu*) because they are both acts of merit (*puññakiriya*) and the bases (*vatthu*) for their respective benefits.
For, having fixed the mind upon the characteristics of giving and so forth, one thinks: "Such a kind of gift should be given by us; such a kind of virtue..."
“Guarding must be practiced, and development must be cultivated”—thinking thus, beings perform meritorious deeds. Giving itself is "consisting of giving" (*dānamaya*);

or rather, it is the concluding volition produced from among the preceding volitions that constitutes what consists of giving, just as those consisting of virtue and so forth are distinguished by virtue and so on.
The same principle applies to the other two [categories]. "A small amount has been performed" means it has been done slightly or weakly. "It does not suffice" means...
It does not succeed. "It is unmade" means that the application of cultivation has simply not been undertaken; this is the meaning.
"Human misfortune" refers to the five kinds of low-born families among humans that lack prosperity. "Is reborn" means one approaches by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*);
the meaning is that one is produced there. "Done only in part" means done with measure; it is little, not much. "Human good fortune" [refers to the opposite].
Among humans, [they attain] the state of being fortunate and the threefold excellence of birth. "Excessive" (*adhimatta*) means exceeding the measure or powerful.
"They surpass" (*adhigaṇhanti*) means they take hold by overcoming; the meaning is that they become more distinguished and superior.
7. Commentary on the Discourse on the Gift of a True Person (*Sappurisadānasutta*).
37. "Pure" means he gives what is clean and pure. "Possessing beauty" means it is endowed with color. "Exquisite" means it is endowed with flavor.
"At the right time" means at the appropriate and fitting time. "Suitable" means he gives what is allowable (*kappiya*).
"Having discerned" means by way of seeking out a recipient, thinking: "What is given to this one will be of great fruit; what is given to that one will not be of great fruit."
Either giving with a specific aspiration, or giving after having carefully selected [the recipient].
8. Commentary on the Sappurisa-sutta (The Good Person). 38.

In the eighth [sutta], "for the sake of" (*atthāya*) means for the sake of welfare (*attha*). "For the benefit and happiness" (*hitāya sukhāya*) means for the sake of benefit (*hita*) and for the sake of happiness (*sukha*). "To those who have passed away before" (*pubbapetānaṃ*)...
For the sake of kinsmen who have passed to the other world. In this sutta, during the time when no Buddha has arisen, wheel-turning monarchs, bodhisattvas, and paccekabuddhas are found;
during the time of a Buddha, there are both Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddha.
Indeed, these lead to the welfare, benefit, and happiness of those aforementioned persons. "Truly, for the welfare of many, the wise one dwells at home."
A wise person living in the household truly becomes a source of benefit for many. "In the past" means first of all.
"Recalling what was done before" means recollecting the virtues of former services rendered by one's mother and father. "With the Dhamma" means he honors them with reasoned offerings of requisites.
"He honors those who live the holy life" means he pays respect to those practicing celibacy, adopting a humble manner toward them. "Amiable" means one of a pleasant character.
9. Commentary on the Abhisanda Sutta (39).
In the ninth discourse, "giving" (*dānāni*) refers to acts of volitional giving (*cetanādānāni*). The meaning of "foremost" (*aggaññāni*) and so forth has already been explained above.
10. Commentary on the Duccarita-vipāka Sutta.
40. "In the tenth [case], 'killing living beings' means the volition of killing living beings. 'The lightest of all' means the very least.
'Conducive to a short life-span' means that by means of that slight ripening of karma one becomes short-lived;

or else, one dissolves at the mere giving of the rebirth-linking, or at the mere moment of emerging from the mother's womb. For such a result belongs to no one else; it is the result of killing living beings alone."
"This is a path already traveled. "Leading to the ruin of wealth" means that it brings about the loss of wealth such that not even a single *kākaṇika* coin remains in one's hand.
"It leads to enmity with rivals" means that it brings about enmity together with rivals;
for his rivals become numerous, and whoever sees him perceives only enmity toward him.
It causes [suffering] to arise and does not lead to extinction. For such is the outcome of an offense against another’s property that has been protected and guarded.
It leads to false accusation: it brings about a false accusation by which whatever was done by someone else falls upon that very person.
It leads to estrangement from friends: it brings about a rift with friends.
Whomever one makes a friend, that very person breaks away. "Leading to unpleasant sounds" means it brings about unpleasant sounds.
That speech which is thorny, harsh, bitter, abusive, and piercing to the vitals—one hears only that wherever one goes;
one does not obtain the hearing of pleasant sounds. Such is the path traveled by harsh speech.
"Anādeyyavācāsaṃvattanikā" means it leads to having speech that is not to be accepted;
one falls into being subject to such remarks as, "Why do you speak? For who will accept your word? This is the path leading to idle chatter (*samphappalāpa*).
"It leads to madness" (*ummattakasaṃvattaniko*) means it leads to the state of madness; for by that, a person becomes mad.
Or he becomes deranged in mind, or he becomes a mute idiot. This is the outcome of drinking fermented liquor. In this sutta, only the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) is discussed.
The fourth chapter, the Chapter on Giving, is finished.
5. The Chapter on the Uposatha.
4. Commentary on the Vāseṭṭha Sutta 44.
In the fourth section of the fifth chapter, the Buddha speaks a simile by way of supposition, pointing to two *sāla* trees standing before him, saying:
"Vāseṭṭha, even these great *sāla* trees. This is what is meant: first, these great *sāla* trees are insentient. Even if they...

If they were to become conscious and observe the Uposatha complete with its eight factors, that observance of the Uposatha would lead to their welfare and happiness for a long time. But as for non-sentient beings, there is simply nothing to be said.
6. Commentary on the Anuruddha Sutta.

46. Regarding the sixth [verse], "By whom the venerable Anuruddha": it is said that those deities, having reflected upon their own prosperity and considering, "By what means was this prosperity obtained by us?", perceived the Elder.
Seeing him, they thought, "We were formerly handmaidens to our noble lord while he was exercising the sovereignty of a Wheel-turning Monarch; we remained steadfast in the instruction given by him..."
"We have obtained this prosperity; let us go, bring the Elder, and enjoy this prosperity together.
Thus they went during the day to where the Venerable Anuruddha was. "In three instances" means in three causes. "We obtain it instantly" means we obtain it at that very moment.
They remember either the sound of speech, the sound of song, or the sound of ornaments. Intoxicated...
He reflects by way of such thoughts as, "The tears and so forth have become blue; they will not be able to become yellow," and so on.
Yet those [tears] likewise became exactly like that, thinking, "Now the noble one desires our yellow state; now our red state.
"Clapped his hands" means he struck his palms together. "Of the fivefold [instrument]" refers to the *ātata*, the *vitata*, the *ātatavitata*, and so forth.

It is for one endowed with these five factors: solid (*ghana*), hollow (*susira*), and so forth. In this context, "stretched" (*ātata*) refers to single-sided musical instruments such as drums covered with leather;
"stretched-taut" (*vitata*) refers to those with both sides [covered]; "stretched-and-taut" (*ātatavitata*) refers to those completely covered;

"hollow" (*susira*) refers to flutes and the like; and "solid" (*ghana*) refers to the *sammādi* drum. "Well-trained" (*suvinīta*) means having been thoroughly refined through processes such as being pulled and loosened.
"Suppaṭipatāḷitassa" means well-tapped for the purpose of knowing whether it remains within the proper measure.
"Kusalehi susamannāhatassa" means played by those who are skilled and expert in playing it. "Vaggu" means clever and beautiful.
"Rajanīyo" means capable of delighting. "Kamanīyo" means worthy of being desired. Alternatively, "khamanīyo" is the reading, meaning [pleasant] even for a whole day.
"Even while being watched, he remains patient"—the meaning is that he does not feel revulsion. "Intoxicating" means that which produces the intoxication of pride and the intoxication of manhood.
"He cast down his faculties" means that thinking, "These deities are acting inappropriately," he cast his faculties downward;
he did not look by opening his eyes. "Venerable Anuruddha does not consent" means: "We are dancing and singing, yet the Venerable One..."
Anuruddha did not consent; he did not even look up with his eyes open, thinking, "What shall we do by dancing or singing?
and there they vanished right then and there. He approached the Blessed One, and having seen the power of those deities, [he wondered]:
"With how many qualities, indeed, must a woman be endowed to reach the delightful world of the gods?"
He approached in order to ask about this matter:
“...is reborn. 9–10. Commentary on the Two Discourses Concerning This World. 49–50.
Regarding the ninth discourse: “This world has been undertaken”—this world of his is so called because it is undertaken merely by means of activity within this world.
Because it is fulfilled, what was undertaken becomes fulfilled.

"Endowed with sixteen aspects" means being possessed of the eight aspects mentioned in the Sutta and the eight in the verses—thus, endowed with sixteen aspects; or alternatively, some say she is "endowed with sixteen aspects" because she not only possesses the eight factors herself but also encourages others in them.
Here, however, faith, virtue, and wisdom are spoken of in combination. Tenth.
This was told to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Furthermore, whatever has not been stated in all the suttas is of plain meaning because it follows the method already explained below.
