The first fifty [chapters] are completed.
2. The Second Fifty (6) 1.
The Chapter on Gotamī 1.
Commentary on the Gotamī Sutta
51. Regarding the first [section] of the sixth [chapter]: "He dwelt among the Sakyans" means that having gone by the first journey, he dwelt there.
"Mahāpajāpatī" is a name acquired because of her greatness through both her lineage of sons and her lineage of daughters.
"She approached the Blessed One" refers to the time when the Blessed One, having gone to Kapilavatthu, first ordained Nanda and on the seventh day, Rāhula Kumāra.
During the Cumbaṭaka conflict, when the inhabitants of both cities had set out for battle, the Teacher went there, persuaded those kings, and preached the Attadaṇḍa Sutta.
The kings, having gained faith, gave three hundred and fifty princes each;
these five hundred princes went forth into homelessness in the presence of the Teacher. Then their wives—
Having sent a message, they caused them to become dissatisfied.
The Teacher, knowing that dissatisfaction had arisen in them, led those five hundred young bhikkhus to the Kuṇāla Lake.

Sitting upon the stone slab where he himself had previously sat during his time as Kuṇāla, he dispelled their dissatisfaction by recounting the Kuṇāla Jātaka, and all of them attained the fruit of stream-entry.
He established [them], and having brought them back again to the Great Forest, they attained the fruit of *arahantship*.
To ascertain their state of mind, the wives sent word again to the Saṅgha. They sent back a reply, saying, "We are incapable of living the household life.
Those women thought, "It is no longer fitting for us to go to our own homes; we shall go to Mahāpajāpatī and receive the going-forth (*pabbajjā*)."
“Having obtained permission, we shall go forth,” they said; and so the five hundred women approached Mahāpajāpatī and said, “Noble lady, please grant us permission to go forth.
Taking those women with her, Mahāpajāpatī went to where the Blessed One was.
Some even say that she approached him while he was beneath the white parasol at the time of the King’s parinibbāna.
"Why did he refuse, saying, 'Enough, Gotamī, let it not please you'? Is it not the case that all Buddhas have four assemblies? [The answer is: Certainly they do;
however, she had entreated him many times, causing him weariness. He refused because, wishing to grant her ordination with due respect, he thought:
"Thinking, 'It was obtained with difficulty,' she will properly preserve the ordination that has now been granted. "She departed" means: again...

He entered Kapilavatthu itself. Having dwelt there as long as he desired means: having dwelt according to his inclination while observing the underlying conditions (*upanissaya*) of those beings who were to be awakened.

He set out on a wandering tour means: performing a gathering of the great multitude, he set out on a tour that was unhurried, with the supreme splendor of a Buddha and the incomparable grace of a Buddha.
"Along with many Sakyan women": within the very palace, five hundred Sakyan women had taken the robes of those who have gone forth dedicated to the One of Ten Powers;
having caused them all to take the robes of those who have gone forth, [the Blessed One] set out on a journey together with all those many Sakyan women.
"Set out on a journey" means he undertook the act of going. At the time of undertaking that journey, however—
Thinking, "Those delicate royal women will not be able to go on foot," the Sākiyan and Koliyan kings prepared golden palanquins.
However, thinking, "If they travel mounted in vehicles, it would show a lack of respect for the Teacher," they proceeded on foot for the entire fifty-one leagues.
The kings, having arranged for protection both in front and behind, [provided] rice, ghee, oil, and other provisions...
They filled carts and sent men with the instruction, "Prepare food wherever you go.
Regarding the phrase "with swollen feet": because they were so delicate, one blister would arise on their feet while another burst;
both feet became bloated as if covered with a lattice of bone fragments. Therefore it is said: "with swollen feet."
“Outside the gate-tower” means outside of the gate-tower. But why did she stand there? It is said that this thought occurred to her:

“I took the robes of one gone forth on my own initiative without being permitted by the Tathāgata, and the fact that I have done so has become well known throughout the whole of Jambudīpa. If the Teacher grants permission for my going forth, then this would be...”
"It would be well. But if he does not grant permission, there will be great reproach. Unable to enter the monastery, she stood there weeping.
"What is it, Gotamī? [The King asked: "Has some misfortune befallen the royal family?
For what reason have you come to such a state of disfigurement, standing here with such swollen feet...? "By another means" means by another cause.
Having described her virtues with the words, "She is very helpful, venerable sir," and so forth, she spoke thus while again requesting ordination. The Teacher, thinking, "Women are of limited wisdom;
if ordination were permitted by a mere single request, they would not take up my teaching with reverence," refused three times. Now, however, desiring to have them take it up with reverence, he said:
"If, Ānanda, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī accepts the eight *garudhammas*, let that itself be her full admission (*upasampadā*)," he said, beginning with these words.
In this context, "let that itself be hers" means: let that very thing be both her going forth (*pabbajjā*) and her full admission.

"Of one who has been fully admitted on that same day" refers to one who has received full admission on that very day. [Regarding] "salutation, rising from one's seat, and the gesture of joining the palms":
"Proper conduct (*sāmīcikamma*) should be performed" means that one should perform salutation by prostrating with the five limbs while refraining from both self-deprecation and arrogance;
rising from one's seat to meet [the guest] as they approach; joining the ten fingernails together in the gesture of reverential salutation (*añjali*);
and performing appropriate services such as preparing a seat and fanning, which are collectively termed "proper conduct. [This applies] when there are no other monks present.
“Residence” means: a place where, for one who dwells there, there is no teacher to give exhortation when she approaches for the purpose of receiving it without hindrance;
this is called a residence “without monks. One should not enter the rains retreat in such a residence.
“Every half-month” means: every Uposatha day. “Approaching for exhortation” means: approaching for the purpose of receiving exhortation. “By what is seen” means: ...
"By what has been seen with the eye. "By what has been heard" means by what has been heard with the ear. "By suspicion" means by that which is suspected on account of what has been seen or heard.
"A grave matter" (*garudhamma*) means a heavy offense of *saṅghādisesa*. "Probation for a fortnight" (*pakkhamānatta*) means a probation lasting no fewer than fifteen days.
"In the six rules" means in the training precepts, with the rule against eating at improper times as the sixth. "Having trained in the training" means...
"Having fulfilled the training by keeping even a single precept unbroken":
one should not revile another using any of the ten grounds for reviling; nor should one revile them with any kind of disparaging speech intended to instill fear.

"The path of speech for bhikkhunīs toward bhikkhus is restricted" means that the path of speech—consisting of exhortation, instruction, and Dhamma-talk—is barred and closed for bhikkhunīs toward bhikkhus;
no bhikkhu whatsoever may be exhorted or instructed by a bhikkhunī, [even] by way of tradition, such as saying:
"Venerable sir, the ancient elders fulfilled this robe-observance. Thus, by way of lineage...
It is appropriate to speak. "The path of speech for monks toward nuns is not barred" means that the path of speech for monks toward nuns is unrestricted;
they may exhort, instruct, and deliver Dhamma-talks according to their inclination. This is the summary here;
however, the detailed exposition of this discourse on the heavy rules (garudhamma) is found in the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya.
These should be understood in the manner already stated.
However, upon hearing these eight *garudhammas* being recited by the Elder after she had learned them in the presence of the Teacher,
Mahāpajāpatī’s immense dejection was instantly allayed by the water brought from Lake Anotatta.

As if her head had been sprinkled with a hundred jars of cool water, she became free from feverish distress and, being uplifted, uttered this inspired exclamation beginning with "Just as if, venerable sir," manifesting the rapture and joy born of accepting the heavy rules (*garudhamma*).
"By the 'water-pot thieves' (*kumbhatthenaka*)" means: having lit a lamp in a water-pot and searching for goods in another's house by its light.
"Thenakacorehi": "The disease called setaṭṭhikā" refers to a certain kind of parasite that pierces an arrowhead lodged in the middle of a shaft;
pierced by this, even an arrowhead that has emerged [from the body] is unable to draw up the sap from the top of a rice stalk.
"The disease called mañjiṭṭhikā" refers to the internal redness of sugarcane.
But by the phrase "a dam for a large lake beforehand," this meaning is shown:

just as some water remains in a large lake even when the embankment has not yet been built, and furthermore, when it has already been built, even that which would not have remained due to the lack of a dam now remains;
even so, those [faults] which exist when the basis has not yet arisen...
The heavy rules (garudhamma) were laid down precisely for the sake of non-transgression;
had they not been laid down, the True Dhamma would have endured for five hundred years after women had gone forth.
But because they were laid down beforehand, it will endure for another five hundred years as well—thus, it will endure for exactly the first-mentioned thousand years.
This "thousand years" is stated specifically with reference to those whose taints are destroyed and who have attained the various analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*);

furthermore, beyond that, there is another thousand years by way of those whose taints are destroyed through dry insight (*sukkha-vipassaka*), a thousand years by way of non-returners (*anāgāmin*), a thousand years by way of once-returners (*sakadāgāmin*), and a thousand years by way of stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*). Thus, there are five thousand years in total.
The True Dhamma of realization will endure; the Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyatti) will likewise endure for that same length of time.
For there is no realization in the absence of the scriptures, nor is it the case that realization does not occur when the scriptures exist.
However, the outward signs (liṅga) of the religion will continue to prevail for a long time even after the scriptures have disappeared.
2. Commentary on the Ovāda Sutta 52.
In the second [case], "one who is well-versed" (bahussuta) should be understood here as being well-versed by way of the entire word of the Buddha.

"A heavy offense" (garudhamma) refers to physical contact (kāyasaṃsagga). This is the summary here. However, the determination regarding the instructor of bhikkhunīs is found in the *Samantapāsādikā*.
It should be understood in the same manner as previously stated.
3. Commentary on the Short Discourse (Saṃkhittasutta).

53. In the third [discourse]: "For the sake of lust" means for the purpose of lust. "For the sake of dispassion" means for the purpose of becoming free from passion. "For the sake of bondage" means for the sake of the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa).

"For the sake of conjunction" means for the sake of being conjoined within the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*). "For the sake of disjunction" means for the sake of the state of being disjoined from the cycle of existence. "For the sake of accumulation" means for the sake of the increase of the cycle of existence.

"Not for the sake of diminution" means not for the sake of the destruction of the cycle of existence. "For the sake of difficulty in maintaining" means for the sake of being difficult to nourish. "Not for the sake of ease in maintaining" means not for the sake of being easy to nourish.
In this sutta, the cycle of existence is explained in the first section, and the turning away from the cycle (*vivaṭṭa*) in the second section.
It was thus spoken. And by this exhortation, Gotamī attained Arahatship.
4. Commentary on the Dīghajāṇu Sutta: 54.
In the fourth [sutta], "Byagghapajja"—this is an address to him by way of his lineage. For his ancestors...
"Born on the path of the tiger": because people in that clan were born there, they are called Byagghapajja (Tigers).
"By means of archery": by means of the work of an archer. "Appropriate to that": serving as a means for knowing, "At this time, it is proper to do such-and-such.
"Of mature virtue": those whose virtue has increased, whose conduct is mature. "Coming": arrival. "Not too deep": not excessively great. "Not too shallow": [not excessively small].
Not exceeding the head. "Having exhausted" means having taken and spent. In this context, for one whose income is twice their expenditure, their expenditure is unable to exhaust the income.
"A wise person living at home should divide his wealth into four parts..."
“One may enjoy wealth with one part, employ two parts in work,
and set aside the fourth as a reserve for times of misfortune.
For one who acts in this way, decline cannot possibly overcome income.

"Like one who eats figs": just as when someone wishing to eat figs shakes a ripe fig tree, many fruits fall all at once, and having eaten those fit for consumption, he leaves behind the rest which are more numerous;
even so, he who makes his future life short and squanders his wealth by scattering it about.
Thus, it is said: "This clansman consumes his wealth like one eating the fruit of the udumbara tree. "Death without an elder" means death without a leader.
"He leads a balanced life" means he maintains a right livelihood. "Balanced living" means a life lived for the sake of balance.
"Ways of ruin" means the grounds for destruction.
“Diligent in his own work” means endowed with the energy of exertion in the places where work is to be done. “A distributor” means one who is accomplished in distribution.
“Welfare in the life to come” means a state of security pertaining to the future world. “By his true name” means by the name “Buddha,” which is not false because he has indeed become enlightened.
“Generosity and merit increase” means that both generosity and the remaining types of merit increase. In this...
In the sutta, faith and the other factors are explained as mixed. The fifth [sutta] is self-evident.
6. Commentary on the Bhaya Sutta:

In the sixth, "the womb" (gabbha) means dwelling in the womb. "Belonging to this present life" (diṭṭhadhammika) refers to those things pertaining to the visible world that are similar to dwelling in the womb.
Furthermore, there are human wombs. "Belonging to the future life" refers to all wombs except for the human womb.
Both of these are called sensual pleasures (*kāma*): namely, fear and suffering; fear and disease; fear and a boil; fear and an arrow;
fear and attachment; fear and a mire; and fear and a womb. Thus, both are [sensual pleasures].
These are called sensual pleasures (*kāmā*). "In the form of gratification" means by way of sensual pleasure. "The path of mire" means the path of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa-palipatha*).
"Having transcended"—in this context, this refers to the state of that bhikkhu having attained *arahantship* by increasing insight (*vipassanā*).

"He observes such a generation, afflicted by birth and aging, quivering within the three realms of existence"—this is stated in the suttas after explaining the cycle of existence, and then in the verses...
"The turning away has been explained. The seventh and eighth [suttas] have their meanings already clarified.
9–10. Commentary on the Two Suttas on Persons (Puggala-sutta):
In the ninth, "straight" (*ujubhūta*) means straight because of the absence of crookedness of body and so forth. "Concentrated in wisdom and virtue" (*paññāsīlasamāhita*) means by means of wisdom...
"And endowed with virtue. "To those who sacrifice" means to those giving gifts. "Seeking merit" means looking toward or searching for merit.
"Consisting of acquisitions" means having the fruition of acquisitions; it is an immeasurable state that has become an acquisition.
"In the tenth, 'excellent'" means preeminent and supreme. "Of beings" means of all beings. The rest is clear throughout.
The Sixth Chapter: The Gotamī Chapter.
(7) 2. The Chapter on Earthquakes. 1.
Commentary on the Discourse on Desires.
61. Regarding the first [verse] of the seventh [chapter]: "Of one who is secluded" means secluded by physical seclusion (*kāyaviveka*).
"Living independent" means living without dependence on anything whatsoever, being engaged in the work of insight (*vipassanā-kamma*).

"For the sake of gain" means for the sake of obtaining the four requisites (*paccaya*). "Mournful and lamenting" means both mournful and lamenting; there is also a reading as *sociccā parideviccā*. "Fallen from the true Dhamma" (*saddhamma*)...
At that very moment, he fell away from the true Dhamma of insight. In this sutta, the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and its cessation (*vivaṭṭa*) are explained.
2. Commentary on the *Alaṃ* Sutta:
In the second [sutta], "Enough for oneself, enough for others," means one who is capable in the practice of what is beneficial for both oneself and others.
The mastery [of the teaching] is appropriate. "Quickly comprehending" means that one reflects quickly;

the meaning is that when the aggregates, elements, bases, and so forth are being explained, one understands those phenomena quickly. In this sutta, serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) are taught.
However, due to the inclination of the individual and the elegance of the teaching, this is explained by descending from the summit downward.
3. Commentary on the Saṃkhittasutta 63.
In the third [sutta], "evameva" means for no reason at all; or rather, it means exactly as this person requests.
"Moghapurisa" means deluded persons, empty persons. "Ajjhesanti" means they entreat or request. "Anubandhitabba" means by following after their modes of conduct (iriyāpatha).

They think, "He must be followed; he must not be abandoned. Speaking thus while failing to show respect for the purpose of understanding [the teaching], it is said that this monk, even when given exhortation, continues to indulge in negligence;
having heard the Dhamma, he remains right there and does not wish to practice the ascetic life.
Therefore, the Blessed One, having thus rebuked him, [spoke further] because he was [capable of attaining] Arahatship.
Being endowed with the necessary supporting conditions (*upanissaya*), he said to him while instructing him: "Therefore, bhikkhu, you should train yourself thus," and so forth.

Therein, by the instruction, "My mind will be established within, well-composed, and arisen evil unwholesome states will not persist by taking hold of the mind," he has first described the basic concentration (*mūlasamādhi*) consisting of one-pointedness of mind (*citt’ekaggatā*) by way of the internal (*niyakajjhatta*).
Then, in order to show that "one should not be satisfied with just this much, but rather that concentration must be developed in this way," it is said:

"When, bhikkhu, your mind is settled within, well-composed, and no arisen evil unwholesome states remain obsessing the mind, then you, bhikkhu, should train yourself thus: 'May my mind-liberation through loving-kindness...'"
"…will be developed… well undertaken. Having thus increased his development by way of loving-kindness (*mettā*), it was further said:

"When, O monk, this concentration has been developed and cultivated by you in this way, then, O monk, you should develop this concentration with applied thought and sustained thought (*savitakka-savicāra*)," and so forth. Its meaning is: when, O monk—
When this basic concentration has been developed in this way by means of loving-kindness, you should not be satisfied with that much alone;

rather, while bringing this basic concentration to the fourfold and fivefold jhānas upon other objects as well, you should develop it according to the method beginning with "with applied thought and sustained thought," and so forth.
Having said this, in order to show that one should also develop the fourfold and fivefold jhānas upon other objects preceded by the remaining divine abodes (brahmavihāras), he said:
"When, monk, this concentration has been thus developed and well-developed by you, then, monk, you should train yourself thus:
'May compassion be my mind-deliverance,'" and so forth. Thus [he spoke] preceded by loving-kindness (mettā).
Having shown the development of the fourfold and fivefold jhānas, [the text] speaks again in order to show the practice preceded by the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā*) and so forth:
"When, bhikkhu, this concentration has been thus developed and well-developed by you, then, bhikkhu, you should train yourself thus:
'Contemplating the body in the body,'" and so on, until: "When, bhikkhu, this concentration has been thus developed..."
"Once it has been well-developed, then, O bhikkhu, wherever you go," and so forth, he said. In this context, "gagghasi" means "you will go.
By the phrase "only in comfort" (*phāsuṃyeva*), he indicates *arahatta* (liberation). For one who has attained *arahatta* is said to dwell in comfort in all postures.
4. Commentary on the Gayāsīsa Sutta.

64. In the fourth [paragraph], he said this: in order to announce to the community of monks the thought that had arisen in his own sphere of striving, he spoke the words beginning with, “Formerly, monks. *Obhāsa* means the radiance of the knowledge of the divine eye.
*Ñāṇadassana* means the vision consisting of knowledge that has become the divine eye. *Sannivutthapubba* means having previously dwelt together.
[This] has been mastered before. However, in this sutta, these eight knowledges have appeared in the text itself:

the knowledge of the divine eye, the knowledge of the modes of psychic power, the knowledge of penetration of minds, the knowledge of the destiny according to deeds, the knowledge of future states, the knowledge of present states, the knowledge of past states, and the knowledge of previous births.
Along with those, there are the four knowledges of insight (vipassanā-ñāṇa).

By combining these knowledges—namely, the knowledges of the path, the four knowledges of the fruition, the four knowledges of review, and the four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā)—which constitute the six unique knowledges, it is in this way that this discourse is said to have been expounded. 5.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Bases of Mastery (Abhibhāyatana-sutta).
65. Regarding the "five bases of mastery" (*abhibhāyatanāni*), they are the causes for mastering. What do they master? Both adverse phenomena (*paccanīkadhamma*) and objects (*ārammaṇa*).
For they master adverse phenomena by way of being their opposites, and they master objects through the person’s preeminence in knowledge (*ñāṇuttariyatā*).
In the passages beginning with "perceiving forms internally," however, [it refers to] internal forms by way of preliminary work (*parikamma*).
One is said to be "perceiving form internally. For when practicing the preliminary work on blue, one does so upon the hair, the bile, or the pupil of the eye.
When practicing the preliminary work on yellow, one does so upon the fat, the skin, the palms of the hands, the soles of the feet, or the yellow parts of the eyes.
When practicing the preliminary work on red, one does so upon the flesh, the blood, or the tongue.
Or he applies it to the whites of the eyes. When performing the whitening treatment, he applies it to the bones, the teeth, the nails, or the white parts of the eyes.
However, that does not become beautifully blue, beautifully yellow, beautifully red, or beautifully white;
it remains simply unpurified.

"One sees forms externally": for one whose preliminary work (*parikamma*) has thus arisen internally, while the sign (*nimitta*) is external, he is said to be "percipient of forms internally, seeing forms externally" by way of the preliminary work being internal and the absorption (*appanā*) being external. "Limited" means unextended. "Beautiful and ugly" means...
Whether they be beautiful or ugly, it should be understood that this base of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*) is taught specifically by way of limited perception (*paritta*).
"Having mastered them" means: just as one who has a good appetite, upon receiving only a spoonful of food, gathers it together thinking, "What is there to eat here?
and makes it into a single mouthful—even so does one whose knowledge is supreme.
A person of clear knowledge thinks, "What is there to be attained here in this limited object?
This is no burden for me," and having mastered those forms, he enters into attainment; the meaning is that he reaches absorption (appanā) right along with the arising of the sign (nimitta).
By the words "I know, I see," his mental application (ābhoga) is described; and that, moreover, [occurs] from the attainment itself.

It is for one who has emerged [from attainment], not while within the attainment itself. "He perceives thus" means that he perceives thus both by way of the perception of mental application (*ābhoga-saññā*) and by way of the perception of jhāna.
For the perception of mastery exists even while within the attainment, but the perception of mental application belongs only to one who has emerged from the attainment.
"Infinite" (*appamāṇāni*) means having increased measure; the meaning is "vast. Regarding the word "having overcome" (*abhibhuyya*):
here, just as a gluttonous man, having received one large portion of food, does not regard it as something great, thinking, "Let there be more, let there be more!
What will this do for me?", even so is the person of supreme knowledge, whose wisdom is lucid.
“Why should one attain this? This is not immeasurable; there is no burden for me in achieving one-pointedness of mind,” thinking thus, he overcomes [the object] and attains absorption.
The meaning is that here, absorption is reached simultaneously with the arising of the sign (*nimitta*).
“Perceiving the formless internally” means being devoid of preparatory perception regarding internal form, either due to non-attainment or due to lack of interest.

"One sees forms externally": one for whom even the preliminary work (*parikamma*) or the sign (*nimitta*) has arisen externally is thus called "one who, being percipient of the formless internally, sees forms externally" by way of both the external preliminary work and absorption (*appanā*).
The rest here is exactly according to the method already stated regarding the fourth base of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*). Among these...

However, among the four, the limited is presented according to the temperament of one dominated by applied thought (*vitakkacarita*), the immeasurable according to the temperament of one dominated by delusion (*mohacarita*), the beautiful according to the temperament of one dominated by hatred (*dosacarita*), and the ugly according to the temperament of one dominated by lust (*rāgacarita*). For these [meditations] are suitable for these [temperaments].
And their suitability has been explained in the *Visuddhimagga* in the "Description of Temperaments" (*cariyaniddesa*).
In the context of the fifth base for mastery (*abhibhāyatana*) and the others, the term "blue" is stated in an all-inclusive sense.
"Blue-colored" is stated by way of color; "blue-appearing" is stated by way of appearance. What is meant is that they are seen as being entirely blue, with no visible gaps and with unmixed colors.
"Blue-luminous," however, is stated by way of radiance; it means "possessing a blue radiance."
The meaning is "endowed with blue radiance. By this, he shows their extreme purity; for it is precisely by way of their pure color that these spheres of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*) are described.

Furthermore, the method of forming the kasiṇa and the preliminary work (*parikamma*) herein—such as "one who is learning the blue kasiṇa takes up the sign (*nimitta*) in something blue, whether in a flower, a cloth, or a pigment"—is as follows.
And the entire procedure for absorption has already been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*.
6. Commentary on the Discourse on the Liberations (Vimokkha-sutta).
66. In what sense are they called "liberations" (*vimokkha*)? In the sense of being resolved upon (*adhimuccana*). But what is this sense of being resolved upon?
What is its meaning? It means being thoroughly liberated from opposing states (*paccanīkadhamma*), and it means being thoroughly liberated by way of delighting in the object (*ārammaṇa*).
What is meant is that it proceeds toward the object with a state of fearlessness and without constraint, like a child lying on his father’s lap with all his limbs relaxed.
However, this meaning does not exist in the final liberation (*vimokkha*).
It exists in the preceding liberations.
Regarding the phrase "possessing form, he sees forms": here, "form" refers to the form-jhāna produced internally with respect to the hair and so forth by means of the blue kasiṇa and others;
one who has this is "possessing form" (*rūpī*). Furthermore, he sees external forms such as the blue kasiṇa and others with the eye of jhāna.
By this, the four fine-material-sphere jhānas of a person who has produced jhāna upon the kasiṇas as internal and external objects are shown.
"Perceiving the formless internally" means not perceiving form internally; that is to say, one who has not produced fine-material-sphere jhāna regarding one's own hair and so forth.
By this, the fine-material-sphere jhānas of one who has performed the preliminary work externally and produced jhāna externally are shown.
“*Subhanteva adhimutto hoti*” (He is intent upon the beautiful): by this, the jhānas regarding the well-purified color-kasinas, such as blue and so forth, are shown.

Although within the actual absorption there is no mental application (*ābhoga*) thinking “beautiful,” nevertheless, one who dwells having made the well-purified beautiful kasina his object is rightly said to be “intent upon the beautiful.”
Because it occurs [in this way], the teaching is thus formulated. However, in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, it says:

“How is it that one is intent upon the beautiful? This is liberation. Here, a bhikkhu dwells with a mind imbued with loving-kindness toward one direction... [and so on]... Because loving-kindness has been developed, beings become non-repulsive. With a mind imbued with compassion... [and so on]...”
“He dwells with a mind accompanied by sympathetic joy …pe… accompanied by equanimity, pervading one quarter …pe….
Because equanimity has been developed, beings become non-repulsive. Thus, being resolved upon what is beautiful, this is liberation,” it is said.
Regarding the phrases “entirely transcending perceptions of form,” etc., that which ought to be said has already been stated in the *Visuddhimagga*. This is the eighth [liberation].
"Deliverance" (vimokkha): because of the complete relinquishing and liberation from the four aggregates, this is called the eighth and supreme deliverance.
7–8. Commentary on the Discourse on Noble and Unnoble Modes of Speech (Anariyavohārasutta):

In the seventh [discourse], "unnoble modes of speech" (anariyavohārā) means non-noble discourse, discourse that is defiled. This is the name for those volitions by which they engage in such speech. In the eighth, the meaning should be understood by way of the opposite of what was stated [in the seventh].
9. Commentary on the Discourse on Assemblies (Parisāsutta) 69.
Regarding the ninth [assembly], "the assembly of khattiyas" (*khattiyaparisā*) means the gathering or coming together of khattiyas. This same method applies everywhere.
"Many hundreds of assemblies of khattiyas" refers to gatherings such as those with Bimbisāra, gatherings with kinsmen, gatherings with the Licchavis, and so forth.
It can indeed be found in other world-systems as well. "Previously conversed" means that talk and discussion have been held before.
"Discussion" refers to having previously engaged in discussion on the Dhamma. "Whatever their complexion may be":
they may be white, black, or fair-skinned, whereas the Teacher is golden-hued. This, however, is said with reference to physical form. Physical form, too—

And it was only their own wisdom that appeared to them; however, the Blessed One did not appear like a barbarian, nor did he sit wearing earrings of loose gems, but rather sat in the very garb of a Buddha.
They saw him as having exactly the same physical form as themselves.
Whatever kind of voice they possessed—whether it was broken, gurgling, or like the cawing of a crow—the Teacher’s voice was like the Brahma-voice. This...
However, this was said with reference to another language. For even if the Teacher speaks while seated upon a royal throne, they think, "Today the king speaks in a sweet voice.
But when the Blessed One has finished speaking and departed, and they see the king returned, the inquiry arises: "Who is this? In that context, "Who is this? refers to [the Buddha].

The meaning is that even though they were investigating, thinking, "Who is this who has vanished while speaking just now in the Magadha language and the Sinhala language with such a sweet manner—is he a deva or a human?", they did not know.
But for what purpose does he teach the Dhamma to those who do not know this? For the sake of creating a latent impression (*vāsanā*). For even the Dhamma heard in this way will, in the future...

"It is a condition" means he teaches by depending on the future. Its occurrence should be understood through such instances as the meeting with Soṇadaṇḍa and others, involving hundreds of assemblies of brahmins, as well as through other world-systems.
10. Commentary on the Earthquake Sutta (Bhūmicālasutta).
70. "In this context, 'seating' refers to a piece of leather. 'Udena Shrine' refers to a monastery built at the dwelling place of the yakkha Udena.
The same method applies to the Gotamaka and other shrines. 'Developed' means increased. 'Cultivated' means practiced repeatedly.
'Made a vehicle' means made like a harnessed carriage. 'Made a foundation' means made a basis in the sense of a support."
"Made as it were": established. "Accumulated": gathered on all sides, well-increased. "Well-undertaken": properly undertaken.
Having thus spoken without specific restriction, he spoke the passage beginning with "Of the Tathāgata... in order to show it again by way of restriction.
Here, "for an eon" (*kappa*) means for the duration of a lifespan; that is, fulfilling whatever measure of human life exists at each respective time.
He might remain. "For the remainder of the aeon" means for more than the hundred years mentioned as "only a little longer. However, the Elder Mahāsīva said:

"There is no such thing as thundering in a place where Buddhas do not dwell; by repeatedly entering meditative attainment and suppressing the death-proximate sensations, he would remain for a fortunate aeon itself.
But why did he not remain? Because of the body subject to grasping (*upādinnaka-sarīra*)."

A person is overcome by decrepitude and the like, yet Buddhas, without falling into a state of decrepitude and so forth, attain *parinibbāna* precisely during the fifth portion of their lifespan while they are still beloved and esteemed by the multitude.

Furthermore, when the great disciples who have awakened after the Buddha (*buddhānubuddha*) have attained *parinibbāna*, one must remain alone like a solitary stump, or perhaps surrounded only by young novices; then [one reflects]: "Oh, the Buddhas!"

"He would incur contempt from the assembly; therefore, he does not stand. Even when this was said, that which is called "the duration of his life" is precisely what is determined by the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
Just as in the phrase "with a mind obsessed by Māra," the word *tanti* is merely a particle, so too [is it here] with "with a mind obsessed by Māra."
The meaning is that just as no other ordinary person (*puthujjana*) whose mind is overwhelmed would be able to penetrate [the truth], even so he was unable to penetrate it.
For Māra obsesses the mind of one in whom all twelve distortions (*vipallāsa*) have not been entirely abandoned.
And since four of the distortions had not yet been abandoned by the Elder, Māra therefore [obsessed] his mind.
It obsesses. But what does it do when it obsesses the mind? It displays a terrifying visual object or makes a terrifying sound audible.
Then, having seen or heard it, beings lose their mindfulness and their mouths gape open;
inserting its hand into their mouths, it crushes their hearts, and they consequently fall unconscious.
"Having offered, they remain standing. But how could he have been able to put his hand into the Elder’s mouth?

Instead, he displayed a terrifying object. Upon seeing it, the Elder did not penetrate the radiance of the sign (*nimittobhāsa*). Why did the Blessed One, though already knowing, address him up to three times?
Later, when [the Elder] requested, "Venerable Sir, let the Blessed One stay," [the Buddha said], "This misdeed is yours alone."
“This is your own fault,” he said, in order to make himself appear blameless by casting the blame upon others.
Regarding the term “Māra the Evil One”: here, he is called Māra because he kills (*māreti*) beings by leading them toward what is disadvantageous. “The Evil One” (*pāpimā*) is a synonym for him;
indeed, he is called “the Evil One” because he is possessed of evil qualities (*pāpadhamma*). He is also known as Kaṇha, Antaka, Namuci, and Pamattabandhu.

These are his names. As for the phrase "And this was said": on the eighth day after the Blessed One’s attainment of enlightenment, while still at the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa), [the deity] approached and said, "Blessed One, that purpose for which you fulfilled the perfections has now been reached;
omniscient knowledge has been penetrated. What is the use of wandering through the world? and spoke just as he does today.
“Venerable sir, may the Blessed One now attain final Nibbāna,” he entreated. The Blessed One rejected his request, saying to him, “Not yet,” and so forth.
With reference to that, he said, “But this was spoken, venerable sir,” and so on.
In that context, *viyattā* means skilled by way of the Path; likewise, they are disciplined (*vinītā*) and confident (*visāradā*). *Bahussutā* means...
They are "learned" (*bahussuta*) because they have heard much by way of the Three Baskets (*tipiṭaka*). They are "bearers of the Dhamma" (*dhammadhara*) because they retain that very Dhamma.
Alternatively, they are both learned in the scriptures (*pariyatti*) and learned through realization (*paṭivedha*);

they are "bearers of the Dhamma" because they retain the Dhamma of both scripture and realization—thus should the meaning be understood here. They are "practicing the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma" (*dhammānudhammapaṭipanna*) [of the Noble Dhamma].
They have practiced the Dhamma of insight (vipassanā) which is in accordance with the Dhamma. "Practicing in conformity" means practicing the appropriate course of training.
"Walkers in accordance with the Dhamma" means those whose habit is to conduct themselves in accordance with the Dhamma. "Their own teacher’s doctrine" means their own teacher’s teaching.
All terms beginning with "they will proclaim" are synonyms for one another. "By means of the Dhamma" means by means of that which is reasoned and possesses a cause.
By means of their speech. "With wonders" (*sappāṭihāriya*) means that they will teach the Dhamma in such a way as to lead to liberation.

"The holy life" (*brahmacariya*) refers to the entire holy life of the Dispensation, comprised within the three trainings. "Successful" (*iddha*) means fully accomplished by way of the flavor of meditative absorption (*jhāna*).
"Prosperous" (*phīta*) means having reached growth by way of the attainment of the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*), like a tree in full bloom.
"Spread abroad" (*vitthārika*) means extended, by way of being established in various directions.

"Widely known" (*bāhujañña*) means known or penetrated by many, by way of the realization of the great multitude. "Became widespread" (*puthubhūta*) means it reached a state of vastness in every respect.
How so? As far as it was well-proclaimed among gods and humans—that is, among all those of a discerning nature, whether gods or humans.
And it exists; the meaning is that it has been well-expounded by all. "Appossukka" means one who is free from concern.
For you, O Evil One, from the eighth week onwards, have wandered about crying out, "Venerable Sir, let the Blessed One now attain final Nibbāna;
let the Sugata now attain final Nibbāna. From this day forward, be devoid of hope; do not [seek] for the sake of my final Nibbāna.
"Exert yourself," he says.

"Mindful and clearly comprehending, he relinquished the life-formations": having established mindfulness well and delimited [the process] with knowledge, he released and abandoned the life-formations.
In this regard, the Blessed One did not relinquish the life-formations as one might throw a clod of earth with his hand.
He relinquished [the attainment]; however, having entered the fruition attainment (*phalasamāpatti*) for only three months, he gave rise to the thought, "Henceforth I shall not enter it again.
It is with reference to this that it is said, "he relinquished" (*ossaji*). There is also a reading, *ussajī*.

"A great earthquake" (*mahābhūmicālo*) means a massive shaking of the earth. At that time, it is said, the ten-thousandfold world system (*dasasahassī lokadhātu*) trembled. "Terrifying" (*bhiṃsanako*) means causing fear.
"And the divine drums resounded" means the celestial drums resounded; the sky thundered with a dry roar, lightning flashed out of season, and a momentary rain fell—this is what is meant.
"He uttered an inspired utterance": why did he utter it? Someone might say: "The Blessed One followed closely behind [the monk]..."
“‘May you attain final Nibbāna, venerable sir!’—thus, being distressed by fear, he relinquished the life-formations. Let there be no such occasion for that;
for one who is afraid, there is no such thing as an inspired utterance (udāna). Rather, he uttered an inspired utterance released by the surge of joy.
In this context, it is called *tula* because it is weighed and delimited, being evident to all, including even dogs, jackals, and the like.
What is that? It is sense-sphere karma (*kāmāvacara-kamma*). It is "incomparable" (*atula*) because there is no other worldly karma that is its equal or comparable;

thus it is incomparable. What is that? It is exalted karma (*mahaggata-kamma*). Alternatively, sense-sphere and fine-material-sphere karma are comparable, while immaterial-sphere karma is incomparable.
Or, karma with little ripening is comparable, while karma with much ripening is incomparable. It is "originating" (*sambhava*) because it is the cause for origination.
"Rāsikārakaṃ" means "one who forms a heap. "Bhava-saṅkhāraṃ" means "that which conditions renewed existence.
"Avassajī" means he relinquished. "Munī" refers to the Buddha-muni. "Ajjhattarato" means "delighting in his own internal [nature].
"Samāhito" means "composed through access and absorption concentration. "Abhindi kavacamiva" means "he broke it as if it were armor. "Attasambhavaṃ" means "arisen within himself."

The defilement. This is what is meant: he abandoned both the worldly karma known as "tulā" and "atulā"—which has received the names "sambhava" in the sense of being subject to fruition and "bhava-saṅkhāra" in the sense of forming existence—and he split asunder his own arising and the defilements, remaining inwardly delighted and concentrated, like a great warrior at the head of battle casting off his armor.

Alternatively, "weighing" means comparing; he weighed both the incomparable arising—namely, Nibbāna—and arising itself. "The formative activity of existence" refers to the karma that leads to existence.

"The Sage relinquished" means that the Buddha-Sage, by way of such a method as "the five aggregates are impermanent, the cessation of the five aggregates is Nibbāna, which is permanent," weighed the danger in existence and the benefit in Nibbāna.

Having seen that formative force of existence (*bhava-saṅkhāra*), which is the root of the aggregates, as "action" (*kamma*), he abandoned it by means of the Noble Path—which leads to the destruction of action—as described in the phrase "it conduces to the destruction of action.
How so? "Delighting within, composed, he shattered his own arising like a coat of mail.
For he, through insight (*vipassanā*), delighted within, and through serenity (*samatha*)...

"Concentrated": thus, having stood from the preliminary stage onwards, having enveloped his personal existence (attabhāva) like armor by the power of serenity and insight, he shattered the entire web of defilements known as "arising from self" because they originate within himself.
And because of the absence of defilements, the karma performed becomes "rendered useless," as it is incapable of producing rebirth.
Thus, by abandoning the defilements, he abandoned karma. For one whose defilements have been abandoned, there is no such thing as fear;

therefore, it should be understood that he relinquished the life-formations while entirely free from fear, and uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) for the purpose of making known his state of fearlessness.
"When great winds" means at whatever time or on whatever occasion great winds [arise]. "Blowing" refers to the winds that cause tossing and shaking.
When these winds arise, they cut off the wind that supports the water, which is nine hundred and sixty thousand yojanas thick;
then the water in the sky breaks apart, and as it breaks apart, the earth breaks apart.
Then the wind, by its own power, binds and seizes the water as if performing an internal function, and from that, the water rises up.
When that [water] rises up, the earth rises up. Thus, the water, when shaken, causes the earth to shake.
And this shaking occurs even until the present day; however, because it is so frequent, its rising and falling are not perceived.
"Of great power, of great majesty" means they are of great power due to the greatness of their success (*ijjhanā*), and of great majesty due to the greatness of what is to be experienced.
"Of great power" means powerful. "Limited" means weak. "Immeasurable" means strong.

"He makes this earth shake" means that having produced supernormal power (*iddhi*), he shakes the earth either to inspire awe—like Mahāmoggallāna—or to investigate it—like the novice Saṅgharakkhita, the nephew of the Elder Mahānāga. "He causes it to quake" means he makes it shake all around.
“Trembles” is a synonym for that very same thing. Thus, among these eight earth-tremblings: the first is by way of an elemental disturbance;

the second, by way of the power of psychic potency (*iddhi*); the third and fourth, by the splendor of merit; the fifth, by the splendor of knowledge (*ñāṇa*); the sixth, by way of the giving of applause;
the seventh, by way of the nature of compassion; and the eighth, by way of weeping. [These occur] when [the Bodhisatta] descends into his mother’s womb and when he emerges from it.
And at the Great Being, the earth shook through the power of his merit; it shook, being struck by the splendor of his wisdom at the time of his full enlightenment;
it shook, offering its applause while established in the state of acclaiming the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma;
and it shook, unable to endure the agitation of the mind while established in a nature of compassion at the relinquishing of the life-force.
"It shook" means that at the time of the Parinibbāna, being overwhelmed by the force of weeping, it shook.
This meaning, however, should be understood in terms of the earth-deity; for this does not apply to the great physical earth because it is insentient. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, the Chapter on the Earthquake.

73–79. In the third [verse], "should one cultivate" means "should one indeed cultivate. "The Dispensation" (*sāsana*) means the instruction. "For the destruction of the taints" (*āsavānaṃ khayāya*) means for the sake of the fruit of Arhatship.

In the fourth [verse], "having set out" (*paṭihitāya*) means having entered the path. "That would be an obstacle for me" (*so mamassa antarāyo*) means that it would be an obstacle to my life, as well as an obstacle to heaven and an obstacle to the Path for one who dies as an ordinary person (*puthujjana*).
*Assa*. "Satthakā" means those which cut the limbs like a knife; thus, they are called *satthakā*. The fifth and subsequent [terms] are exactly as explained by the method already stated.

80. Regarding the "ten grounds for indolence": this means the grounds, bases, or causes of indolence for one who is lazy.
"Work that ought to be done" refers to tasks such as the distribution of robes and so forth.

"Does not arouse energy" means he does not arouse either of the two kinds of energy. "Of what has not been attained" refers to the states of dhamma consisting of jhāna, insight, the path, and the fruit.
“For the attainment of the unattained”: for the sake of attaining that very thing not yet attained.

“For the realization of the unrealized”: for the sake of realizing that very thing not yet realized. “This is the first”: this sinking down, thinking “Come now, I shall lie down,” is the first basis of indolence.
In this manner, the meaning should be understood in all instances. *Māsācitakaṃ* (the month-long hoarder).
Regarding the term *maññeti*: here, "māsa-ācita" means a dried bean (*tintamāsa*). The intended meaning is that he is as heavy as a dried bean.

81–82. Regarding the first [type] of the ninth [chapter], it is exactly according to the method explained above. In the second, "possessing faith" means being endowed with two kinds of faith.

"But not approaching" means he does not attend upon [the teacher]. "Nor inquiring" means he does not inquire about what is meaningful and what is meaningless, or what is the reason and what is not the reason.

3. Commentary on the Mūlaka Sutta.
83. In the third [section], "all phenomena" refers to the five aggregates (*pañcakkhandhā*).

"Rooted in desire" (*chandamūlakā*): desire of inclination (*ajjhāsayacchanda*) and desire for action (*kattukamyatāchanda*) are their root; thus they are "rooted in desire. "Arising from attention" (*manasikārasambhavā*):
they originate from attention. "Originating from contact" (*phassasamudayā*): they emerge and form a mass from contact. "Converging in feeling" (*vedanāsamosaraṇā*): they meet together in feeling.
"Samādhi is their chief" means they have samādhi as their chief (*samādhippamukhā*). "Mindfulness is their dominant influence" means mindfulness is their sovereign (*satādhipateyyā*);

the sense is that mindfulness is their eldest [leader]. "Wisdom is their superior" means wisdom is their highest point (*paññuttarā*). "Liberation is their essence" means liberation is their very core (*vimuttisārā*).
And here, the four beginning with "rooted in desire" are said to be mundane; the remaining ones are a mixture of mundane and supramundane.
4. Commentary on the *Corasutta* (Discourse on the Robbers) 84.
In the fourth [verse], "a great robber" (*mahācoro*) refers to a great thief capable of causing unrest within the kingdom. "Is brought to an end" (*pariyāpajjati*) means it reaches its exhaustion.
"Does not endure for long" (*na ciraṭṭhitiko hoti*) means he is unable to remain protecting his domain for any length of time. For one who does not plunder...
"He strikes" means that he strikes those who do not strike back at him—those who are virtuous, the elderly, and young children—and those who are unfit to be struck.
"He takes without remainder" means he seizes everything without leaving anything behind. For this is the practice of skilled thieves:
of another's two garments, one must be taken; if there is only one, having given a weak substitute, [the other is taken].
It should be taken firmly. Regarding the rice in the cooking-pot and so forth, having given one portion, one [portion] should be taken.
"He works too close" means he commits acts of theft in places near villages, market towns, or royal capitals.
"And he is not skilled in storing" means he is not clever in depositing what he has acquired with those worthy of offerings; he does not clear the path to the next world.
5. Commentary on the Samaṇa Sutta 85.

In the fifth [verse], "that which by a recluse" (*yaṃ samaṇena*) refers to that collection of qualities which is to be attained by a recluse. "By one who has lived the life" (*vusīmatā*) means by one who has dwelt in the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
"Freed, I free others from bondage" (*mutto mocemi bandhanā*) means: having myself been freed from all bonds, I also free the great multitude from the bondage of passion and so forth.

I release. "Paramadanta" (the supreme tamer) means that, having been neither instructed nor exhorted by anyone else, he has penetrated [truth] through his own self-arisen knowledge (*sayambhuñāṇa*) and is thus called "supremely tamed" because he has been tamed by the supreme taming.
"Parinibbuto" means he is fully extinguished through the extinction of the defilements (*kilesaparinibbāna*).

86. Sixth: "And let not fame come to me" means: let fame not go along with me. "One who gains without difficulty" means one who gains extensively.

"Virtue and wisdom" (*sīlapaññāṇa*) means both virtue and knowledge. "Having gathered together" (*saṅgamma*) means having assembled. "Having come together" (*samāgamma*) means having met. "Dwelling in company" (*saṅgaṇikavihāra*) means dwelling in the company of a group.
"Indeed, they are not so" (*na hi nūna ete*) means: indeed, these [people] are not so; for thus...
"Panameti" means "makes them bend," for these [fingers] are indeed so. "With finger-taps" means by piercing after making a finger-tapping staff.
