Regarding the tenth "individual position" (*paccekaṭṭhāna*): this refers to a position of authority (*adhipatiṭṭhāna*), a senior position (*jeṭṭhakaṭṭhāna*).

For, having made him the senior [member], one is not permitted to perform any formal act of the Saṅgha (*saṅghakamma*). Nor should he be rehabilitated (*vuṭṭhāpetabba*) by means of that root; that is, making that [offense] the root [of his status].
He is not permitted to perform the act of rehabilitation (*abbhāna-kamma*). The remainder is clear in all respects.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, the Chapter on Mindfulness (*Sativagga*). (10) 5. The Chapter on Asceticism (*Sāmaññavagga*)
91. Hereafter, in the passages beginning with "Then the laywoman Bojjhā," [there are mentioned] the laywoman Bojjhā,
the laywoman Sirimā, the laywoman Padumā, the laywoman Sutanā, the laywoman Manujā, the laywoman Uttarā, the laywoman Muttā, the laywoman Khemā,
the laywoman Rucī, Princess Cundī, the laywoman Bimbī, Princess Sumanā, Queen Mallikā, and Tissā.
The female lay follower Tissā-mātā, the female lay follower Soṇā, the female lay follower Soṇā’s mother, the female lay follower Kāṇā,
the female lay follower Kāṇā’s mother, Uttarā Nanda-mātā, Visākhā Migāra-mātā, the female lay follower Khujjuttarā,
the female lay follower Sāmāvatī, Suppavāsā the Koliyan daughter, the female lay follower Suppiyā, and Nakula-mātā the housewife— of these [it is said] of so many...
Only the observance-day ceremony (uposathakamma) endowed with eight factors has been explained here. One who so desires may explain it in detail.
The remainder is clear in meaning throughout.
Thus ends [the section from] the Manorathapūraṇī, the commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya.
The commentary on the Aṭṭhakanipāta is completed.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
In the Aṅguttara Nikāya.
Commentary on the Book of Nines (Navakanipāta-aṭṭhakathā) 1.
The First Fifty (Paṭhamapaṇṇāsaka) 1.
The Chapter on Enlightenment (Sambodhivagga)
1. Commentary on the Sambodhi Sutta.

Regarding the first [sutta] of the Navaka-nipāta: "Of those pertaining to enlightenment" (*sambodhipakkhikānaṃ*) means of those existing on the side of enlightenment—which is comprised of the four paths—and which are its aids;
this is the meaning. He asks thus with reference to the nine qualities mentioned in the canonical text.
What is the *upanisā*? It is the condition of decisive support (*upanissaya-paccaya*). "Ablaze" means leading to effacement (*abhisallekhika*).

"Conducive to the opening of the mind" means they are suitable and helpful for the opening of the mind through serenity and insight (*samatha-vipassanā*). A discourse concerning fewness of desires is a "discourse on fewness of desires.
The same method applies to the remaining terms as well.
"The foul should be developed for the abandoning of lust"—this meaning is to be illustrated by the simile of the rice-gatherer:
A certain man, taking a sickle, began to reap the rice in a rice-field starting from the edge.
Then, cows broke down his fence and entered the field. He set aside his sickle, took up a staff, and having driven the cows out by that same path, [proceeded to continue his work].
Having made the fence ordinary, he again took up the sickle and began harvesting the rice. In this context, the field of rice should be regarded as the Buddha’s teaching;
the rice-harvester as the practitioner (*yogāvacara*); the sickle as wisdom (*paññā*); the time of harvesting as the time of performing the work of insight (*vipassanā*);
the staff as the meditation subject of foulness (*asubha-kammaṭṭhāna*); and the fence as restraint (*saṃvara*). Having broken through the fence...
The arising of lust through negligence, prompted by a lack of reflection and acting impulsively like entering a cow-pen;
and then, having set aside the food and taken up a staff, driving the cows out by the very path they entered, restoring the fence to its original state,
and once again leading them back from the starting point— this is like the subduing of lust by means of the meditation subject on foulness (*asubha-kammaṭṭhāna*).
Again, it is the time to begin the work of insight (vipassanā). It is with reference to this meaning that it was said: "The foul (asubha) should be developed for the abandoning of lust (rāga).

In this context, "of lust" means of the lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure. "Loving-kindness" (mettā) refers to the meditation subject of loving-kindness. "For the abandoning of ill-will" (byāpāda) means...
For the purpose of abandoning anger that has arisen in the manner already described. "Mindfulness of breathing" (*ānāpānassati*) refers to mindfulness of breathing with its sixteen bases.
"For the cutting off of applied thoughts" (*vitakkupacchedāya*) means for the purpose of cutting off applied thoughts that have arisen in the manner already described.

"For the uprooting of the conceit 'I am'" (*asmimānasamugghātāya*) means for the purpose of uprooting the conceit that arises as "I am. "The perception of non-self becomes established" (*anattasaññā saṇṭhātīti*) [refers to] the characteristic of impermanence.
When the characteristic of non-self is seen, it is indeed seen. For when one of these three characteristics is seen, the other two are likewise seen.
Therefore it was said: "Bhikkhus, for one who perceives impermanence, the perception of non-self becomes firmly established.
"Nibbāna in this very life" means that one attains the unconditioned final Nibbāna in this very life. In this regard—
In the sutta, the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) and its reversal (vivaṭṭa) are explained. 2. Commentary on the Nissaya Sutta:
In the second [sutta], "endowed with support" (nissayasampanna) means endowed with a foundation. "Faith" (saddhā) refers to faith as conviction (okappana-saddhā). "Energy" (vīriya) refers to...
Bodily and mental energy. "That which" means that which belongs to him. "By noble wisdom" means by the wisdom of the path together with insight (*vipassanā*).
"Having reckoned" means having known. "He pursues one thing" means he pursues that which is fit to be pursued.
"He endures" means he endures that which is fit to be endured. "He avoids" means he avoids that which is fit to be avoided. "He dispels" means [he dispels] that which is fit to be removed.
"He removes it. "In this way, monks"— in this way, indeed, a monk who, by means of both thorough learning and questioning and by means of the defining of the Dhamma,
has well penetrated and well realized what is to be practiced and so forth,
and who practices, endures, avoids, and dispels [the hindrances], is said to be "endowed with support."
3. Commentary on the Meghiya Sutta.
Third: “At Cālikā” means in the city of that name. It is said that because it was built along a shifting path, it appeared as if it were moving to those looking at it;
therefore, it became known as Cālikā. “At Mount Cāliya”: that mountain too...
Because it appeared as if it were moving to those looking at it during the dark fortnight of the full moon due to its total whiteness, it was called Cāliya-pabbata (the Moving Mountain).
There they had a great monastery built. Thus the Blessed One dwelt in dependence on that city in the Mahāvihāra on Cālikā-pabbata.
Jantugāma is another village belonging to that same monastery, serving as its alms-resort; it is also known as Jattugāma.

They recite [the following]. "One who desires striving" means one who performs the work of striving. "For the sake of striving" means for the purpose of performing the duties of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*).
Having heard the Elder’s words, the Teacher, reflecting and perceiving that "his knowledge is not yet mature," spoke thus in order to turn him back:
"First, while you are alone... This, moreover, was said to him because even though he had gone there in this manner, he was still engaged in his task.
He spoke thus for the purpose of generating gentleness of mind, thinking: "If [the goal] is not being accomplished, he will come again out of affection, remaining free from anxiety.
"There is nothing further to be done" means that because the four tasks regarding the four truths have been performed, there is no other task remaining to be done.
"Or the accumulation of what has been done" refers to the further accumulation of what has already been attained.
There is none. For a path that has been developed is not developed again, nor is there a further abandoning of defilements already abandoned.
Meghiya, when one says "exertion," what should we say? When one says "I am performing the duty of a recluse," what else indeed should we say?
"He sat for his midday rest" means he sat down for the purpose of his midday rest.

And as he was sitting, he sat upon that very auspicious stone slab where, in former times, he had successively sat for five hundred births while playing at garden games, surrounded by a threefold troupe of dancers.
From the moment he sat down, it was as if his state as a recluse had been abandoned.
Having assumed the guise of a king, surrounded by a select retinue of dancers, he became as if seated upon a magnificent couch beneath a white parasol.
As he relished that prosperity, a sensual thought arose within him.
At that very moment, he saw two thieves brought before him by great warriors, as if they had been placed there already. Of those two—
Through his ordering of the execution, a thought of ill will (*vyāpādavitakka*) arose; through his ordering of the binding of one person, a thought of cruelty (*vihiṃsāvitakka*) arose.
Thus, like a tree surrounded by a network of creepers, or like a honey-gatherer surrounded by honey-bees, he was encircled by unwholesome thoughts (*akusalavitakka*).
With reference to this, it was said: "Then, to the Venerable Meghiya... and so forth. *Anvāsatta* means...

“Followed and surrounded. “He approached the Blessed One”— meaning that, thus beset by evil thoughts and unable to perform his meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) as was suitable for him, he observed, “Indeed, having seen this, the long-sighted Blessed One has forbidden it,” and thinking,
“I shall inform the One of Ten Powers of this matter,” he rose from his seat and went toward [the Blessed One].
The Blessed One approached him.
4. Commentary on the Nandaka Sutta:
"In the assembly hall" means in the dining hall. "To where the assembly hall was" refers to where the Teacher [was] with the Elder Nandaka.
Having heard the sound of a Dhamma teaching begun with a sweet voice, he asked, “Ānanda, who is this teaching the Dhamma with such a sweet voice in the assembly hall?

When he heard, “Venerable sir, today is the turn of the Elder Nandaka, the preacher of the Dhamma,” he said, “Ānanda, that bhikkhu is preaching the Dhamma in an excessively sweet manner; we too shall go.”

Having said, "I shall listen," he approached the assembly hall. Standing outside the gateway, he remained there, his six-colored rays concealed within the folds of his robe, assuming the guise of a stranger.
"Waiting for the conclusion of the conversation" means that he stood right there listening to the discourse on the Dhamma, awaiting this end of the talk: "This is what was said. Then the Venerable...
When the first watch of the night had passed, Ānanda gave notice to the Teacher: "The first watch, Bhante, has elapsed;
please rest for a short while. The Teacher remained right there. Then, when the middle watch had also passed, the Venerable Ānanda said:
"Bhante, you were by nature delicate members of the Khattiya caste, and as the delicate sons of a Buddha, you are supremely delicate."
"The middle watch of the night has also passed; rest for a moment," he said. The Teacher remained standing right there.

While he was still standing there, the first light of dawn appeared. At the rising of the dawn, the Elder reached the conclusion of his discourse by saying, "This is what I said," and at that very same instant, the Dasabala released his six-colored bodily radiance.
"He struck the bolt" means he struck the door-panel with his fingernail.
"Appearing embarrassed" means being ashamed and feeling abashed; however, he had no mental distress or embarrassment.

For one who has attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), there is no such thing as a lack of eloquence; even for this much, he would not have been unable to speak. Even this much... [he did not].
He shows that [the Buddha] would have spoken. Saying "Excellent, excellent," he spoke thus, praising the Elder’s teaching of the Dhamma.

Herein, the meaning is: "Your teaching of the Dhamma has been well-grasped and well-spoken. "Of sons of good family" refers both to those who are sons of good family by conduct and those who are sons of good family by birth.
"The noble silence" was said with reference specifically to the attainment of the second jhāna.

"Insight into phenomena through higher wisdom" (*adhipaññādhammavipassanā*) refers to the knowledge of insight (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) that discerns conditioned formations (*saṅkhāra*). "A four-limbed [creature]" refers to such beings as horses, oxen, camels, and so forth.
"Having said this" means having spoken of this Dhamma endowed with these four factors. "He entered the dwelling" means he entered the Perfumed Chamber (*gandhakuṭi*).

"At times for hearing the Dhamma" means at various appropriate times for listening to the Dhamma. "Discussion of the Dhamma" (*dhammasākacchā*) refers to discourse consisting of questions and answers.
"A profound word of meaning" (*gambhīraṃ atthapadaṃ*) means a profound, hidden, and secret meaning.

"By wisdom" (*paññāya*) refers to the wisdom of the path together with insight (*vipassanā*); the wisdom of comprehension and penetration, as well as the wisdom of learning and inquiry, are also certainly included.
"Has attained or will attain" (*patto vā pajjati vā*) means that he esteems him by way of such appreciation for his qualities, thinking: "He has attained Arahantship, or he will reach it."
"Those who have not attained their hearts' desire" means those who have not attained Arahantship; or alternatively, "those whose minds have not attained [the goal]" are *appattamānasā*.
Regarding "a happy dwelling in this very life" (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra*): here, a happy dwelling in this very life may be either mundane or supramundane.
5. Commentary on the Sutta on Powers (*Balasutta-vaṇṇanā*)
5. In the fifth [section], the powers of wisdom and so forth are to be understood by way of their unshakability regarding ignorance, indolence, blamefulness, and lack of faith.
"Known as unwholesome" means they are recognized as unwholesome (*akusala*). This same method applies everywhere.

"Unfit for noble ones" (*nālamariyā*) means incapable of performing the state of a noble one (*ariya*), or unsuitable for noble ones. "Well-seen" (*voditṭhā*) means clearly seen. "Well-traversed" (*vocaritā*) refers to the mind-door.

"Attained to manifestation" means having reached the stage of active practice. "To one who has need" means to one who has need of the teaching of the Dhamma. "Fear regarding livelihood" is fear concerning the means of sustaining life.
"Fear of ill-repute" is fear of censure. "Fear of timidity in assemblies" is the fear of succumbing to timidity upon entering an assembly.
In this sutta, the cycle of existence and its cessation (vaṭṭa-vivaṭṭa) are explained.

6. Commentary on the Sutta of Cultivation (Sevanāsutta) In the sixth [sutta], "requisites for life" (*jīvitaparikkhāra*) means the equipment for life. "To be acquired" (*samudānetabba*) means to be gathered together.

"They are acquired with difficulty" (*kasirena samudāgacchanti*) means they arise with hardship. Regarding the phrase "either during the portion of the night or the portion of the day," here, during the portion of the night...
Having known [this] during the portion of the night, one should set out; but if there is danger from fierce beasts and the like on the way at night, one should wait until sunrise.
Having known [this] during the portion of the day, one should set out by day; but if there is danger from obstacles during the day, one should wait until sunset.
"Having understood" (saṅkhāpīti) means having understood the attainment of the fulfillment of the cultivation of the goal of asceticism. "That person" (so puggalo) refers to...
However, this [phrase] is connected with the word "should not be followed.
Regarding "without asking permission," the meaning here is that one should depart without having asked that person for permission. "Even while being expelled" means even while being driven out.
For such a person, even if they were to take a hundred bundles of wood, a hundred water-jars, or a hundred jars of sand as a staff...

If he causes [the offender] to be reinstated, or causes him to be expelled with the thought, "Let him not live here," then even after having asked his forgiveness, one must follow him for as long as life lasts; he must not be abandoned. 7.
Commentary on the Sutasoma Sutta. 7.
Regarding the seventh [sutta], "five grounds for transgression" means five reasons for overstepping. "A living being" means, at the very least...
"An ant or a tiny insect. "Not given" means even as little as a blade of grass belonging to another. "By way of theft" means with a mind of stealing.

"One who makes a hoard, unable to enjoy sensual pleasures" means one who, having made and kept a hoard, is incapable of enjoying the objects of desire (*vatthukāma*) and the defilements of desire (*kilesakāma*).
This was said with reference to unallowable strands of sensual pleasure (*akappiya-kāmaguṇa*). "Having renounced the Buddha" means...
"It is not the Buddha"—thus one may reject it. The same method applies to the Dhamma and the rest. This much, first of all, is what has come down in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).
However, in the Canon (*Pāḷi*), the "going on wrong ways" (*agatigamana*) are discussed in this Sutta.
8–10. Explanation of the Sajjha Sutta and others.

8–10. In the eighth [verse], the renunciation of the Buddha and others is explained. In the ninth, because he is mentioned together with the worldling (*puthujjana*), he is called "one worthy of offerings" (*āhuneyya*).

In the tenth, the *gotrabhū* is one endowed with a mind of powerful insight that has reached its culmination through the immediate condition (*anantarapaccaya*) of the path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimagga*).
The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
The First Chapter: On Full Enlightenment.
2. The Chapter on the Lion’s Roar. 1.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Lion’s Roar.

11. Regarding the first [case] for the second [person]: "He approached the Blessed One" means that the monk, thinking, "If the Teacher intends to set out on a journey, this would be the time to do so.
Come now, I shall ask the Teacher for permission to go on tour," approached him surrounded by the community of monks.
"Venerable sir, the Venerable Maṇḍissa..."—it is said that this monk addressed the Elder.
Seeing him departing with a large retinue of bhikkhus, [Devadatta] thought, "These bhikkhus have left the Tathāgata and gone forth surrounding Sāriputta;
I shall cause an interruption of his journey. Having harbored anger toward an unworthy object, he spoke thus.

In this context, *āsajja* means having struck or provoked. *Appaṭinissajja* means without relinquishing, that is, without being made to endure it or without confessing a transgression (*accaya*). In what?

But did he harbor resentment for a specific reason? It is said that as the Elder was rising and departing after paying homage to the One of Ten Powers, the corner of his robe brushed against the man’s body; others say it was a gust of wind.
Having harbored resentment on account of this much, and seeing the Elder proceeding with a great retinue, he became envious and thought, "I shall cause an interruption to his journey."
He spoke thus. Having heard the words of that bhikkhu, "Come, bhikkhu," the Teacher, perceiving,
"If it is said that the bhikkhu Sāriputta did not strike him, he might harbor malice toward me, thinking, 'Venerable sir,
you take the side of your own chief disciple alone, not mine,' and thereby be reborn in a state of misery," summoned Sāriputta.
Thinking, “I shall ask about this matter,” he addressed a certain bhikkhu and spoke thus:
“Having taken a key” means having grasped a lock. “A lion’s roar” means the best of roars, the foremost of roars, the irreversible roar.

Thus informed by the two great elders, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus abandoned their night-quarters and day-quarters and went into the presence of the Teacher. “A matter of censure” means a matter of reproach.
"Consisting of excrement" means it is simply excrement. The same method applies to the rest as well. "Equal to the earth" means equal to the earth in the sense of not becoming angry;
for the earth does not feel joy when one deposits something clean upon it, nor does it feel dejection when one deposits something unclean.
He shows that his own mind is also of such a nature. "Vipula" means not limited (aparitta).

"Exalted" (*mahaggata*) means having attained greatness. "Immeasurable" (*appamāṇa*) means having increased its measure. "Vengeless" (*avera*) means being free from unwholesome enmity and personal animosity.

"Unafflicted" (*abyāpajjha*) means being without suffering and devoid of mental distress. "He here" (*so idha*) refers to that bhikkhu who has not yet established the foundation of mindfulness through the contemplation of the body;
he thinks, "How could one like me do such a thing?"—thus he utters the first lion's roar.
A river. In this way, the application [of the explanation] should be understood everywhere.
A "dust-sweeper" (*rajo-haraṇa*) is a cloth for sweeping away dust; it is another name for a foot-wiper (*pāda-puñcha*). "With a basket in hand" means with a back-basket in hand or a mortar in hand.
"Wearing rags" (*nanta-kavāsī*) means one whose clothing consists of pieces of cloth cut from the edges. "Gentle" (*sūrato*)...
"Pure in virtue" means endowed with gentleness. "Well-tamed" means having thoroughly attained self-mastery. "Well-trained" means well-instructed.
"He harms no one" means that even when someone seizes him by his horns or rubs his back, he does not cause any injury.
"Like a bull whose horns have been cut off" means with a mind similar to that of a bull whose horns have been severed.
*Aṭṭīyeyya*: he would be distressed; *pīḷito* means oppressed. *Harāyeyya*: he would feel ashamed. *Jiguccheyya*: he would come to loathe it. *Medakathālikaṃ*:
a *medakathālikā* is called by butchers a pan with holes made here and there for the purpose of letting out the broth.
*Parihareyya*: having filled it with meat and lifted it up, he would carry it away. *Chiddāvachiddaṃ*: full of holes.
It is possessed of apertures both small and large. "Oozing" (*uggharanta*) means the lymph (*yūsa*) emerging from the upper-facing apertures.
"Dripping" (*paggharanta*) means the lymph emerging from the lower-facing apertures. Thus, his entire body would be smeared with lymph.
"Full of holes" (*chiddāvachidda*) means having small and large apertures by way of the nine openings of wounds. Thus it is here.
With the eighth and ninth factors, the Elder spoke of his own lack of desire and lust for his own body.
Then that bhikkhu... Thus, when the Elder had uttered this lion’s roar by means of these nine reasons, then that bhikkhu [spoke].
"Transgression" (*accaya*) means an offense. "Has overcome me" (*maṃ accagamā*) means it has occurred having passed over and overcome me. "May he accept it" (*paṭiggaṇhatu*) means...
"May it be forgiven. "For the sake of restraint in the future" means for the purpose of exercising restraint in the future, so as not to commit such an offense again.
"Truly" means certainly. "You make amends according to the Dhamma" means you act exactly as the Dhamma stands;
that is to say, you ask for forgiveness. "We accept that from you" means we accept that offense of yours.
Forgive me. This is growth, O Bhikkhu, in the Noble Discipline; this, O Bhikkhu, is what is called "growth" in the Noble Discipline, in the teaching of the Buddha, the Blessed One.

What is it? It is the seeing of a transgression as a transgression, making amends according to the Dhamma, and undertaking restraint for the future. Now, speaking with reference to the individual, he who sees a transgression as a transgression—
"Having seen [the fault], he makes amends according to the Dhamma and undertakes restraint for the future"—thus it was said.
"It bears fruit": for if the Elder had not forgiven him, that monk’s head would have split into seven pieces right then and there. Therefore the Blessed One spoke thus.
"If he says 'to me'": if this monk says, "Forgive me," then let him forgive me.
"May this venerable one also forgive me," [said the other]. Thus the Elder, having accepted his transgression, himself also asked forgiveness from the Teacher in person.
2. Commentary on the *Saupādisesa-sutta* (The Discourse on With a Remnant)

12. "With a residue remaining" (*saupādisesa*) means with a remainder of clinging (*upādāna*). "Without a residue remaining" (*anupādisesa*) means free from any remainder of clinging; it is a term of negation.

"One who acts moderately" (*mattaso-kārī*) means one who acts according to measure, not one who acts to full completion. "Sāriputta, this exposition of the Dhamma did not occur to you" (*na tāvāyaṃ...
paṭibhāsī*): the Blessed One has no lack of presence of mind (*appaṭibhāna*); rather, [the meaning is] "I have not yet spoken this exposition of the Dhamma."

This, however, is the meaning here: "May they not, having heard this discourse on the Dhamma, fall into negligence" means that they should not fall into negligence by failing to exert effort toward the goal of Arahantship, thinking, "We have indeed been liberated from the four states of misery.
"Spoken with the intention of answering questions" shows that it was explained according to the essential nature of the question asked by you. Of these...
However, for the purpose of dispelling desire and lust for existence among the nine types of persons, having made this very same occasion for discourse, he said:
"Just as even a tiny amount of excrement is foul-smelling, even so, monks, I do not praise even a trifling amount of existence, not even for the duration of a finger-snap. Thus [he spoke].

He spoke this Sutta. Not only is the destiny of these nine types of persons fixed, but the destiny is also fixed for those families that possess such established merits as the three refuges, the five precepts, a daily meal-offering, a fortnightly meal-offering, a rainy-season residence offering, a lotus pond, and a dwelling place. For them too, the destiny is fixed.
Those families are indeed like those of stream-enterers.
3. Commentary on the Koṭṭhika Sutta: 13.

In the third [sutta], "to be experienced in this very life" (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*) refers to karma that ripens within this very existence. "To be experienced in the future life" (*samparāyavedanīya*)...
Kamma that ripens in a second existence. "To be experienced as pleasant" means kamma that produces pleasant feeling.
"To be experienced as painful" means kamma that produces painful feeling. "To be experienced when fully matured" means having reached the stage of yielding its result.

"To be experienced when not yet matured" means not having reached the stage of yielding its result. "To be experienced much" means yielding abundant results. "To be experienced little" means not yielding abundant results.
"Avedanīya" means that which does not bring about the experience of karmic fruition (*vipākavedanā*). In this sutta, the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and its cessation (*vivaṭṭa*) are explained.
4. Commentary on the *Samiddhi Sutta*:

In the fourth [sutta], "Samiddhi" refers to the elder who was the co-resident pupil (*saddhivihārika*) of the elder [Mahā-Kaccāna]; he received this name because of the excellence of his physical form (*attabhāva-samiddhatā*).

"Having what as their object" (*kimārammaṇā*) means having what as their condition (*kiṃpaccayā*). "Apperceptions and thoughts" (*saṅkappavitakkā*) means thoughts that have become apperceptions (*saṅkappabhūtā vitakkā*).

"Having name-and-form as their object" (*nāmarūpārammaṇā*) means having name-and-form as their condition (*nāmarūpapaccayā*). By this, he shows that the four immaterial aggregates and the derived matter consisting of the primary elements are the conditions for thoughts.
"Where do they go to diversity? (*kva nānattaṃ gacchantīti*) means in what place do they go to a state of diversity, a difference in nature?

"In the elements" (*dhātu*) means in the form element (*rūpadhātu*) and so forth. For the thought of forms (*rūpavitakka*) is indeed one thing, while the thoughts of sounds (*saddavitakka*) and so forth are others. "From the arising of contact" (*phassasamudayā*) means by way of the associated condition of contact.
"Converging in feeling" (*vedanāsamosaraṇā*) means that the three feelings are the convergence. By this much, those that are wholesome, unwholesome, and mixed have been described.

However, those beginning with "headed by concentration" (*samādhippamukha*) should be understood as belonging to the side of diminution (*apacayapakkhika*). In that context, in the sense of being the forerunner...
They are "headed by concentration" (*samādhippamukhā*) because concentration is their chief in the sense of being the eldest.

They are "dominated by mindfulness" (*satādhipateyyā*) because mindfulness is their governing principle in the sense of being the primary cause. They are "surpassed by wisdom" (*paññuttarā*) because path-wisdom is their superior.
They are "having liberation as their essence" (*vimuttisārā*) because, having attained the liberation of the fruit, they reach the core. By way of their object, [they have] the deathless Nibbāna...
"Having plunged in and established themselves there" means they have reached the deathless (*amatogadha*). "And let him not be conceited because of that" means:
because of that answer, he should not give rise to conceit (*māna*) or arrogance (*dappa*), thinking, "I have answered the questions asked by the chief disciple.
5–6. Commentary on the Gaṇḍa Sutta and others.
15–16. In the fifth [case], three or four years constitute a "group of years. One who has many such groups of years arisen is called "one with many groups of years" (*anekavassagaṇika*).

"Tassa assu" means "they would belong to him. "Wound-openings not made by piercing" (*abhedanamukhāni*) refers to those wound-openings that have arisen solely from karma, and were not produced by anyone having pierced them.
"Only loathsome" (*jegucchiyam eva*) means only that which is to be shunned, only that which is repulsive.

"Of that which consists of the four great elements" means made of the four great elements. "Accumulated by means of boiled rice and sour gruel" means built up and increased by means of both boiled rice and sour gruel.
"Subject to the nature of being impermanent, to rubbing, to crushing, to breaking, and to destruction" means: subject to the nature of impermanence in the sense of ceasing after having existed;

subject to the nature of being rubbed with ointments for the purpose of counteracting foul odors; [subject to the nature of being crushed by contact]; subject to the nature of breaking; and subject to the nature of destruction.
The nature of being rubbed by means of gentle massage for the purpose of dispelling afflictions of the limbs and members;

or the nature of being rubbed by means of stretching, pressing, and so forth, for the purpose of perfecting the formation of various limbs and members that were deformed due to dwelling in the womb while lying on the thighs during infancy;
and likewise, even when thus maintained, the nature of breaking and disintegrating.

The meaning is: "having the very nature of breaking up and dispersal. Here, the term *anicca* (impermanence) and the terms *bhedana* (breaking up) and *viddhaṃsana* (destruction) express its passing away (*atthaṅgama*), while the remaining terms express its arising (*samudaya*). "Become disenchanted" means:
"be weary of it and abandon this body"—this is what he shows. Thus, powerful insight (*balavavipassanā*) is explained in this sutta. The sixth [sutta] is exactly as described above.
However, here it is knowledge itself that is spoken of by way of its characteristic of perception (*saññā*).
7–8. Commentary on the *Kulasutta* and others. 17–18.
In the seventh [sutta], "they do not rise up with what is pleasing" means from their seats with what increases the mind, in the manner of inclining the mind.
Having risen, they do not go out to meet them. They do not greet them respectfully means they do not pay homage by prostrating themselves on their five limbs.
They give without respect means they give without due consideration. Not respectfully means they do not give with their own hands.
They do not sit down near them to listen to the Dhamma means they do not sit close by with the thought, "We shall hear the Dhamma. They do not wish to listen means...

It proceeds by turning away [from objects], like water poured on the rim of a jar. In the eighth [chapter], having included the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettā*) according to the inclinations of those to be trained (*veneyya*), it is said that he is "endowed with the nine factors.
9. Commentary on the *Devatāsutta*.
19. "In the ninth [case], we were full of remorse" means we fell into a state of dejection due to our remorse.
"We went to a low state" means that, relative to the world of the devas above, the lower realm is called "low.
"But we did not share according to our ability and strength" means that we did not eat after having made a sharing with those possessed of virtue in accordance with our own ability and strength.
10. Commentary on the Velāma Sutta. 20.
Regarding the tenth [question]: "Householder, is alms given in your family? The Blessed One does not ask this with reference to giving to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
For in the house of the merchant, excellent alms were constantly given to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
The Teacher does not not know that; however, there is a gift being given by the common people of the world, and it is coarse, which does not satisfy the merchant’s heart.
He asks, "I shall ask about that. *Kaṇājaka* means rice with broken grains;
it is cooked with broken grains and even with husked rice-grains. *Biḷaṅgadutiya* means accompanied by sour gruel. *Asakkaccaṃ*...
"Gifts" means he gives without showing honor. "Without respect" means he gives without the reverence due to those worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*).

"Does not give with his own hand" means that instead of giving with his own hand, he gives through another's hand; the meaning is that he merely issues a command. "Gives what has been cast away" means he does not give continuously;
it is like an annual festival offering (*soṇḍabali*). He holds the view that there is no future life.
"He gives" means he does not give while believing in both karma and its fruit.
"In whichever [family]" refers to whichever among the three types of families endowed with excellence.

Regarding the phrase "not for the sake of enjoying excellent food," even when food consisting of various choice flavors and fragrant *śāli* rice is brought before him, his mind does not incline toward it; rather, he thinks, "Take this away, for it increases disease."
Having said this, he eats the rice with broken grains together with whichever *ḍāka* spirit may be present, relishing it as if it were the Deathless (*amata*).

When fine garments such as those from Kāsi are brought to him, he says: "Take these away; they cannot even cover one who wears them, nor do they fit upon the body," and instead accepts coarse cloth resembling the outer bark of the coconut tree.
Thinking, “While wearing these, one knows the state of being clothed, and while covering what ought to be covered, one does indeed cover it,” he puts them on with affection.
When elephant-vehicles, horse-vehicles, chariot-vehicles, golden palanquins, and so forth are brought forward, he says, “Take away these unstable things;
it is not possible to sit upon them. But when a dilapidated little cart is brought forward, he says, “This is stable; here it is comfortable.”
He consents to that [invitation] by saying, "Let us sit. Regarding "not in the five superior strands of sensual pleasure":
having seen well-adorned and prepared beautiful women, he thinks, "I suppose these are yakkhinīs who wish to devour me; what use have I for them? and thus passes his time as comfortably as possible.
"They do not wish to listen" means they do not desire to hear; the sense is that they do not have faith. "They do not lend an ear" refers to what has been spoken...
They do not lend an ear for the sake of hearing. "Sakkaccaṃ" (carefully) and the following terms are to be understood as the opposite of what was previously stated.
"Velāma": he received this name because he was endowed with sublime qualities that transcended the boundaries and limits (*velā*) of birth, clan, appearance, wealth, faith, wisdom, and so forth.
Regarding the statement, "He gave such a gift, a great gift," here is the sequential account (*anupubbīkathā*).
—It is said that in the past he took rebirth in the house of a chaplain in Bārāṇasī; they gave him the name Velāma-kumāra.
At the age of sixteen, he went to Takkasilā together with the prince of Bārāṇasī for the purpose of learning the arts.
Both of them began their studies under a world-renowned teacher. Just as...
And likewise, there were eighty-four thousand other royal princes in Jambudīpa.
In the place where he was taken, the Bodhisatta served as their tutor and instructed those eighty-four thousand princes;
he himself mastered in three years the crafts that would normally take sixteen years to learn. The teacher [declared], "The craft of Prince Velāma has become proficient."
Having understood this, he said, "Sirs, I have known Velāma; he knows everything.
All of you, going together in harmony, learn the craft from him. Thus he entrusted the eighty-four thousand princes to the Bodhisatta.
The Bodhisatta paid homage to the teacher and, departing with a retinue of eighty-four thousand princes, went to a nearby city.
Having reached the prince who was the master of the city and having had him take up the craft, once the prince had become proficient in that art,

he sent him back to that very place. By this same method, having traveled to eighty-four thousand cities and having made eighty-four thousand princes proficient in their respective crafts, he sent each one back to his own city, and finally [reached] the prince of Bārāṇasī.
Having taken [the prince], he returned to Bārāṇasī. When the prince had completed his training, the people consecrated him in the kingdom and gave the office of chief priest to Velāma.
Those eighty-four thousand royal princes, having received their respective consecrations in their own kingdoms, came every year to attend upon the King of Bārāṇasī. They [approached] the King...
Having seen this, they went into the presence of Velāma and said, "Teacher, we have been established in our respective kingdoms;

please tell us what you require," and then they departed. During their coming and going, the countryside was excessively harassed by people seizing carts, chariots, cows, bulls, chickens, pigs, and so forth;
the great multitude gathered together and wailed in the royal courtyard.
The king summoned Velāma and said, "Teacher, the countryside is being oppressed;
kings, on their journeys to and fro, commit great plundering, and the people are unable to endure it. Please devise a means to bring peace to this affliction of the countryside.
"Very well, Great King, I shall devise a means. Having demarcated whatever extent of countryside you require," he said.

"Take them," he said. The king did accordingly. Velāma, having administered justice over eighty-four thousand kings throughout the countryside, established them within the king's own realm like spokes upon the hub of a wheel.
From that time forth, whether coming or going, those kings traveled only through their own respective territories; they did not commit plunder, thinking, "This is our own territory."
They acted thus. Out of respect for the king, they did not even oppress the king’s realm.
The people of the countryside became peaceful, silent, and free from clamor. All the kings were delighted and joyful, and they invited him, saying, “Teacher, tell us whatever you require from us.
Velāma, having bathed his head, opened the doors of the chambers in his own residence, which were filled with the seven precious gems.
Having surveyed the wealth set aside for seven successive generations of his family and having calculated his income and expenditures,
he announced to the king, "It is fitting that I give alms by shaking the entire land of Jambudīpa. He then had twelve *yojana*-long rows of cooking hearths constructed on the banks of the Ganges,
and at each location, he established great storehouses for the purpose of storing ghee, honey, molasses, oil, sesame, rice, and other provisions.
Having established them, he assigned the people, saying, "In each location, you must provide for so many and so many persons;
whatever can be obtained from men, report it to me even if there is not a single item left.

Then, having caused a drum to be beaten throughout the city with the proclamation, "Starting from such-and-such a day, let the people eat the alms-food of the Brahmin Velāma," he set the matter in motion.

When those in charge of the gift announced, "The distribution of gifts is finished," he put on a garment worth a thousand [pieces of gold], draped over one shoulder a cloth worth five hundred, and adorned himself with all his ornaments.
Then, for the purpose of testing the recipients of the gift, he filled a golden pitcher with water the color of crystal and thought: "If in this world there are those worthy to receive this gift..."
"Since there are persons worthy of offerings, let this water come out and take hold of the earth. If there are none, let it remain just as it is.
Having made this declaration of truth, he turned the water-pitcher upside down. The water remained as if it had been caught by a strainer.
The Bodhisatta thought, "Alas, Jambudīpa is empty! Not even a single person worthy of offerings..."
Thinking, "There is no one worthy enough to receive it," he felt no remorse, but instead reflected:
"If this offering will be purified through the merit of the donor, let the water come forth and take the earth. Water resembling the color of crystal came forth and took the earth.
Then, thinking, "Now I shall give the gift," he reached the head of the assembly and surveyed the offerings.
He had rice-gruel served at the time for rice-gruel, solid food at the time for solid food, and a meal at the time for a meal.
In this very manner, alms were given day after day.
Furthermore, in that distribution of gifts, there was nothing that could be said such as, "This particular thing exists" or "That particular thing does not exist. Now...
Thinking that the gift would not reach its conclusion with just this much, he had red gold extracted and had golden bowls fashioned;
then he sent a message to eighty-four thousand kings for the purpose of providing eighty-four thousand golden bowls and other requisites.
The kings, thinking, "At long last we have been favored by our teacher," prepared everything and sent it back.
While the gift was being given, seven years and seven months passed by.

Then the brahmin, thinking, "I shall give a gift after dividing the gold," prepared the offerings on a vast scale. Having made the preparations, he gave gifts starting from eighty-four thousand golden bowls and continuing down to ten million pieces of gold.
In this context, "filled with silver" means filled with silver ingots, silver discs, and silver coins.
As for the bowls, they should not be considered small; they placed exactly four bowls on a patch of ground measuring one *karīsa*.

The bowl’s base was made of the nine precious gems, while from the rim upwards it was made of the eight precious gems; six yokes of a chariot drawn by thoroughbred horses were equal to the circumference of the bowl’s rim.

He went around distributing them; setting aside groups of recipients at the outer edge of each bowl, he first gave what had been placed in the bowl, and afterwards, having separated them joint by joint, he gave the bowls themselves. In this way, he gave eighty-four thousand bowls.
The same method applies to the silver bowls and so forth. And here too, "filled with gold" means [filled] with golden platters, golden spoons, and golden coins.
"Filled" means filled with the seven kinds of jewels. "Adorned with golden ornaments" means they were decorated with golden trappings.
"With bronze milking-basins" means they had silver milking-pails. Furthermore, the horns of those cows were covered with golden sheaths;
jasmine garlands were fastened around their necks; anklets were placed on their four feet; and fine linen cloths were spread upon their backs.
They fastened golden bells around their necks. Regarding the phrase "ten million garments":
according to worldly convention, twenty pairs of garments constitute one *koṭi*; however, here it is stated that ten robes [make up the amount].

In the passage beginning with "of fine linen," he gave whatever was most fine among linen and the other materials. As for those gifts of women, gifts of bulls, gifts of liquor, and gifts of festivals—

Even those things considered unsuitable for giving, he gave them as an entourage in order to cut off Velāma’s line of argument that "such a thing does not exist in the manner of Velāma’s giving. "As if rivers were overflowing" means they overflow like rivers.
Having thus described Velāma’s gift, the Teacher said, "Householder, no one else gave such a great gift; I [gave it]."
“I gave a gift. Yet, even while giving such a gift, I did not find a person worthy to receive it;
why then, while a Buddha like me is seen in the world, do you give a gift and think thus?

Thus, expanding his instruction to the merchant, he said, “It may be that for you...,” and so forth. And were not there at that time the aggregates of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?
Were those [aggregates] ceased? Why did he say, "At that time I was the brahmin Velāma"? Because the lineage was uninterrupted.

For those aggregates, such as form and so forth, having ceased after providing the conditions for these [present ones], spoke thus by maintaining an uninterrupted succession from one to another. "No one purifies that offering" means no ascetic or brahmin.
It could not be said that either a deva or Māra, having arisen, purifies that offering.
For one who purifies that offering, at the highest limit it would be the Buddha, and at the lowest limit a disciple such as the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma.
"One endowed with right view" means one endowed with vision, a stream-enterer. "This is more fruitful than that" refers to [the gift] to a stream-enterer.
The gift given to the great multitude of worldly people— who renounce such a quantity of gold and bullion for seven years and seven months—
is more fruitful than the gift given [to the former].
And as for the phrase "one who gives to a hundred perfected in view," here, by way of one *sakadāgāmī*, there are one hundred and one *sotāpannas*.

Having done so, the calculation for stream-enterers (sotāpanna) should be understood. By this method, in all instances, the calculation of individuals should be understood by multiplying each preceding number by one hundred with respect to the immediately following one.
Regarding the phrase "headed by the Buddha" (buddhappamukha): here, the Saṅgha seated with the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) as its senior member is "headed by the Buddha."
It should be understood as "the Saṅgha. Regarding the phrase "dedicating it to the Saṅgha of the four quarters":
here, a "monastery built for the Saṅgha of the four quarters" is one where a shrine (cetiya) has been established and where the hearing of the Dhamma is performed;
it is a place where monks coming from the four cardinal and intermediate directions may, without even being asked, wash their feet and [enter] through the door with a key.
Having opened the dwelling, looked after it, and dwelt there as long as convenient, they depart.
Even if it is merely a leaf-hut four *ratana* in size, it is called a monastery (*vihāra*) built for the Saṅgha of the four directions.
Regarding the phrase "one should go for refuge," what is intended here is a refuge from which one does not turn back once arrived by way of the path. However, others say:
It is said that because one has surrendered oneself and given it away, the going for refuge bears even greater fruit than that.

"One should undertake the training rules" means one should take up the five precepts (*sīla*). It is explained that even virtue (*sīla*) is described as having a non-retrogressive nature when it has been brought forth by the Path.
Others, however, say that because the gift of fearlessness toward all beings has been given, virtue bears even greater fruit than that.
It has been said. "The measure of smelling" (*gandhohanamatta*) means the mere act of sniffing; it refers to taking a lump of scented paste with two fingers and merely inhaling its fragrance.
Others, however, citing the reading "the measure of milking" (*gaddohanamatta*), explain the meaning as the mere act of stroking a cow's udder once.
"A mind of loving-kindness" (*mettacitta*) is a mind that radiates well-being toward all beings. That, moreover, occurs only by way of absorption (*appanā*).
"Taken. "The perception of impermanence" refers to powerful insight that has reached its culmination by serving as the immediate condition for the Path.
As for the similes, these merits such as giving should be understood as follows:
even if one were to make the whole of Jambudīpa level like the surface of a drum and, starting from the edge, have noble persons sit upon it after spreading out cushions; therein—

Suppose there were ten rows of stream-enterers, five of once-returners, two and a half of non-returners, one and a half of those whose taints are destroyed, one row of paccekabuddhas, and the perfectly enlightened Buddha alone.
Of a gift given to such a multitude of people, that given to the perfectly enlightened Buddha alone is of great fruit. As for the other—
“The gift of a monastery, prostration, and the cultivation of loving-kindness—these are not worth even a sixteenth part of one who comprehends [the nature of things] as their destruction.
For this very reason, at the time of his final nibbāna, the Blessed One said: “Practice in accordance with the Dhamma is the unsurpassed worship. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.

3. The Chapter on Abodes of Beings. 1.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Three Bases.
21. Regarding the first [section] of the third [chapter]: "Uttarakuruka" means those who dwell in Uttarakuru. "Adhiggaṇhanti" means they overcome;

they become superior, distinguished, and preeminent. "Amamā" means free from craving (*nittaṇhā*); however, in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), it is stated that they are "free from suffering" (*niddukkhā*).
"Apariggahā" means they are devoid of the sense of possession, such as "this is mine. "Niyatāyukā" means that their lifespan is fixed. For them, it is indeed settled.
Their lifespan is exactly one thousand years, and their destiny is fixed; having passed away from there, they are reborn only in the heavenly realms.
Regarding "possessing mindfulness": for deities who experience exclusively happiness, mindfulness is not firm; for those in hell who experience exclusively suffering, it is likewise not firm.
However, because these [beings] experience a mixture of pleasure and pain, their mindfulness is firm. Herein, "dwelling in the holy life" refers to the Buddhas and Pacceka-Buddhas in Jambudīpa.
Because it arises right here, the dwelling in the holy life of the Eightfold Path also occurs in this very place.
2. Commentary on the Assakhaḷuṅka Sutta 22.
In the second [sutta], "endowed with speed" means endowed with the speed of its stride. "Not endowed with beauty" means not [endowed] with the beauty of its physical form.
"Endowed. Regarding "endowed with speed among the wild colts of men": he is endowed with the speed of knowledge. "Not endowed with beauty":
he is not endowed with the beauty of virtuous qualities (*guṇavaṇṇa*). The remainder should be understood according to the method of the Canon itself.
Whatever needs to be said here has already been stated in the commentary on the *Tikanipāta*.
3. Commentary on the Taṇhāmūlaka Sutta 23.
Regarding the third [sutta], "dependent on craving" (*taṇhaṃ paṭicca*): there are two kinds of craving, namely, craving for seeking (*esanatāṇhā*) and craving for what is sought (*esitatāṇhā*).

That craving by which one, having set out upon paths such as those of goats or thorns, seeks and searches for wealth, is called craving for seeking. That [craving] which [arises] toward those things already sought and searched for...
Craving for what has been obtained is called craving for what is sought (*esanatṛṣṇā*). Here, however, it should be understood as craving for the act of seeking (*esanatṛṣṇā*).

Seeking (*pariyeṣaṇā*) is the seeking of objects such as visible forms; for that [seeking] occurs when there is craving for what is sought. Gain (*lābha*) is the acquisition of objects such as visible forms;
for that occurs when there is seeking.
Furthermore, discernment (*vinicchaya*) is fourfold by way of knowledge, craving, views, and applied thought (*vitakka*).
Among these, "One should know the discernment of pleasure; having known the discernment of pleasure, one should devote oneself to internal happiness"—this is discernment as knowledge.
As it has been handed down: "Discernment means two kinds of discernment: the discernment of craving and the discernment of views."
The determination of craving consists of the one hundred and eight modes of the wandering of craving. The determination of views consists of the sixty-two views.
However, in this sutta—“Desire, O Lord of Devas, has its source in thought”—it is thought itself that is presented as the "determination" here.
For having obtained gain, it is by means of thought alone that people determine what is desirable or undesirable, beautiful or ugly.
“‘This much will be for the sake of objects of form for me; this much for the sake of objects of sound;
this much will be mine; this much will be another’s; this much I shall consume; this much I shall store away. Therefore it is said:
‘In dependence on gain, there is discrimination.’”
"Lustful desire" (*chandārāga*) means that when one has thought with such an unwholesome thought (*akusalavitakka*), both weak lust and strong lust arise toward the object.
Here, "desire" (*chanda*) is a designation for weak lust. "Clinging" (*ajjhosāna*) is a strong conviction of "I" and "mine.
"Possessiveness" (*pariggaha*) is the act of grasping by way of craving and views. "Avarice" (*macchariya*)...
It is the inability to endure the sharing of one's possessions with others. For this very reason, the ancients explain its etymology thus:
"It is called *macchariya* because it functions with the thought: 'May this wonder belong to me alone; may it not become a wonder for another.
*Ārakkha* means guarding well by means of locking doors, securing chests, and so forth. *Adhikaroti* means...
*Adhikaraṇa* is a name for a cause (*kāraṇa*). *Ārakkhādhikaraṇa* is a neuter abstract noun; its meaning is "the cause of protection.
*Daṇḍādāna* is the taking up of a staff for the purpose of restraining another among such acts as taking up a staff.
*Satthādāna* is the taking up of a weapon, such as a sword with a single edge. *Kalahā* refers to both physical quarrels and verbal quarrels. The former is a compound (*viggaha*).
The final dispute. "Tuvaṃtuva" refers to the use of the word *tuvaṃ* (you) out of a lack of respect.
4. Commentary on the Sattāvāsa Sutta.
In the fourth [sutta], "seven abodes of beings" (*sattāvāsā*) means the dwellings of beings; the meaning is "places of residence. Therein, the Pure Abodes (*suddhāvāsā*) are also included.
It is indeed an abode of beings, but it is not included because it is not available at all times. For the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa) are like a military camp for Buddhas;
when no Buddhas have arisen for incalculable eons, that place remains empty. Thus, because it is not available at all times, it is not included.
The rest here should be understood according to the method already explained regarding the stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti).
5. Commentary on the Discourse on Wisdom (Paññāsutta) 25.
Regarding the fifth [verse]: "When" (*yata*) means at which time. "Well-accumulated" (*suparicita*) means well-heaped-up or well-increased.

"Fit to be spoken" (*kallaṃ vacanāya*) means suitable to say. "Free from lust" (*vītarāga*) means devoid of lust. "Not subject to lust" (*asarāgadhamma*) means not having a nature that is prone to passion.

"Of a nature not to return" means having the characteristic of not returning, being incapable of rebirth; the meaning is that its very nature is to cease without further re-linking of consciousness (*appaṭisandhika*).
In this sutta, only one whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*) is discussed.
6. Commentary on the *Silāyūpa* Sutta (The Rock Pillar Sutta)
26. In the sixth [case], Candikāputta refers to the Elder Candikāputta, who is known by his mother’s name.
"The mind is consolidated by the mind" means that, by way of the sequence of mental applications, the sequence of mental applications becomes consolidated—that is, it is built up and increased.

"The mind is well-consolidated by the mind" means that, by way of the sequence of mental applications, the sequence of mental applications becomes thoroughly consolidated and well-increased, one after another. His mind... [is not...]
"They exhaust" means that those objects, having seized and consumed the arising of consciousness of that one whose taints are destroyed, are unable to remain.
"Unmixed" means unmixed with them because of not clinging to those objects. "Attained to imperturbability" means attained to a state of non-shaking and a state of non-fluctuation.
“Stone pillar” (*silāyūpa*) means a stone column. “Sixteen cubits long” (*soḷasakukkuka*) means sixteen *hattha* in length. “Below the rim” (*heṭṭhānemaṅga*) means situated below the trench;
“above the rim” (*upari nemassa*) means above the trench. “Because it was well-planted” (*sunikhātatā*) means because it was repeatedly pounded with iron pestles and firmly fixed.
“In the same way” (*evameva kho*)—here, the one whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*) is to be regarded as the stone pillar, and the great winds...
Just as winds coming from the four directions are unable to move a stone pillar,
so too should it be understood that the defilements arising at the six sense-doors are unable to move the mind of one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava).
In this sutta as well, only one whose taints are destroyed is spoken of.
7–8. Commentary on the Two Verses on Enmity (Verasutta). 27–28.
In the seventh verse, "enmity gives birth to fear" means that one incurs both the fear of mental terror and the enmity of persons.

"Mental" (*cetasika*) means dependent upon the mind. "Suffering" (*dukkha*) refers to that which has the body as its basis. "Grief" (*domanassa*) refers to suffering associated with aversion (*paṭigha*).

In this sutta, the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*) is explained. It was stated that while the eighth [sutta] was addressed to the community of monks (*bhikkhu-saṅgha*), in this one, only the stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*) is discussed.
9. Commentary on the Āghātavatthu Sutta.
29. In the ninth [sutta], "bases for resentment" (*āghātavatthu*) refers to the causes of resentment. "One binds resentment" means one binds or arouses anger.
10–11. Commentary on the *Āghātapaṭivinaya-sutta* and others. 30–31.
In the tenth [sutta], "removals of resentment" (*āghātapaṭivinaya*) refers to the causes for the removal of resentment. "How could that be found here? [is the rhetorical question].
“Do not act for his harm”—how could this be obtained regarding such a person, and for what reason would it be possible to obtain it?
Having reflected thus, “Another indeed does harm to another according to their own mental inclination,” one dispels resentment.
Or alternatively: “If I were to give way to anger, how could that act of anger be found in this person? (It cannot be.)
The meaning is: "By what cause is it to be obtained? There is also a reading: "Whence is the gain? (*kuto lābhā*). The meaning is:
"If I were to become angry here, in that act of becoming angry, whence would there be any gain? What indeed could be called 'gain'? And in this sense, the particle *tan* is merely an expletive.
In the eleventh [chapter], "successive cessation" (*anupubbanirodhā*) means "cessation in successive order. The rest is everywhere of plain meaning.
The Third Chapter: The Section on the Abodes of Beings (Sattāvāsavagga).
4. The Great Chapter (Mahāvagga) 1–2.
Commentary on the Discourses on the Successive Abidings (Anupubbavihārasutta), etc.
32–33. Regarding the first [jhāna] of the fourth [tetrad], "successive dwellings" (*anupubbavihārā*) refers to the dwellings that are to be attained in successive order.

In the second [jhāna], "wherein sensual desires cease" (*yattha kāmā nirujjhanti*) means the place wherein sensual desires are stilled. "Having ceased" (*nirodhetvā*) means having rendered them non-recurrent.

"Free from hunger" (*nicchātā*) means free from hunger due to the absence of the hunger of craving and views. "Extinguished" (*nibbutā*) [refers to the extinguishing] of the defilements that torment oneself.
They are extinguished by way of non-existence. "Crossed over" means crossed over from sense-desires. "Gone to the further shore" means gone to the further shore regarding sense-desires.
"By that factor" means by that jhāna-factor. "Here sense-desires cease" means here in the first jhāna sense-desires cease.
And those who enter the first jhāna are said to dwell having repeatedly ceased sense-desires.
"With palms joined" means having placed the hands together in the gesture of reverent salutation (*añjali*). "He should attend upon" means he should serve.
By this method, the meaning is to be understood in all instances.
3. Commentary on the *Nibbānasukha Sutta* (The Discourse on the Bliss of Nibbāna)
34. In the third [case], "Udāyī" refers to the Elder Lāḷudāyī. "Etadeva khvettha" means "this very thing indeed here.
"Kāmasahagatā" means "associated with sensual desire" (dependent on sense-pleasures). "Samudācaranti" means "they operate" or "move about" at the mind-door.

"Ābādhāya" means "for affliction," that is, for oppression. "Pariyāyena" means "by way of" or "by reason of. The meaning should be understood in this same way for all sections. In this sutta, what is called "the bliss of the unexperienced" (*avedayitasukha*) is taught.
4. Commentary on the Simile of the Cow (Gāvīupamāsutta) 35.
In the fourth [simile], "mountain-dwelling" (*pabbateyyā*) means one that roams the mountains.

"Without having established it so that it stands well" means not having established it in such a way that it becomes well-established. "That sign" (*taṃ nimittaṃ*) refers to that which is reckoned as the first jhāna.
The sign. "He does not resolve it well-resolved" means he does not resolve it in the way that it would be properly resolved.

"Without harming" means without crushing or injuring. "The mind becomes supple and wieldy" means that just as the insight-mind at the moment of the supramundane path becomes supple, capable of action, and fit for action, so too does his [mind] become the basis for direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).
The fourth jhāna consciousness is pliant and wieldy. "Immeasurable concentration" refers to both the concentration of the four divine abodes and the concentration of the path and fruit;

however, here, by way of the expression "immeasurable with an immeasurable object," this highly refined concentration should be understood as "immeasurable concentration. By means of that immeasurable concentration...
"By being well-developed": at this point, this bhikkhu, having increased his insight (vipassanā), attained arahantship.
Now, showing the sequence of the higher knowledges (abhiññā) for one whose taints are destroyed, he said, "Of whatever...
and so forth. 5. Commentary on the Jhāna Sutta.
36. In the fifth [jhāna], "the destruction of the taints" refers to Arahantship.

Whatever there is therein that pertains to form (*rūpagata*) refers to the form that occurs at the moment of the first jhāna, either by way of the physical basis (*vatthu*) or by way of the matter originated by consciousness (*cittasamuṭṭhānika*), and so forth.

The categories beginning with "that which pertains to feeling" (*vedanāgata*) are to be understood by way of the associated feelings and so on. "Those phenomena" (*te dhammā*) refers to those five aggregates of phenomena, beginning with form.

Regarding the phrases beginning with "as impermanent" (*aniccato*): it is viewed as impermanent in the sense of non-existence after having existed; as suffering (*dukkhato*) in the sense of oppression; as a disease (*rogato*) in the sense of being afflicted;
as a tumor (*gaṇḍato*) in the sense of internal corruption; as a dart (*sallato*) in the sense of having entered [the body] and the sense of tearing;
as a misfortune (*agho*) in the sense of suffering; as an affliction (*ābādho*) in the sense of causing illness; as alien (*parato*) in the sense of not belonging to oneself; and as disintegrating...

As perishable, as empty in the sense of being ownerless, and as non-self in the sense of being subject to no mastery. "He contemplates" means he sees with the wisdom of powerful insight (*vipassanā*).
"By those phenomena" means by those phenomena consisting of the five aggregates. "He turns away" means he causes [the mind] to turn back toward Nibbāna.
"Into the deathless element" means into the Nibbāna-element. "He directs the mind" means that having seen the benefit through knowledge, he causes it to descend [into that state].
"Peaceful" means peaceful by way of being the opposite of the restless. "Exalted" means not subject to dissatisfaction.
"Abiding therein, he reaches the destruction of the taints" means that abiding in that first jhāna, he develops powerful insight and attains Arahantship.
According to another method: "by means of those states" refers to [the contemplations] such as "as impermanent," "as disintegrating," and so forth.
The characteristic of impermanence is explained by two terms; the characteristic of suffering by six terms beginning with "as suffering";
and the characteristic of non-self by three terms: "as other," "as empty," and "as non-self.
Therefore, having thus applied these three characteristics to the five aggregates as phenomena seen within meditative absorption, he turns back the mind—that is, he withdraws the mind.

"Releases" means he removes it. "He brings together" means that first, by way of hearing, by way of praise, by way of the scriptures (*pariyatti*), and by way of description, he brings the mind of insight (*vipassanā-citta*) toward Nibbāna as "this is peace";
thus he brings it toward the unconditioned, deathless element (*asaṅkhata-amata-dhātu*).
The path-consciousness (*magga-citta*) [brings it] toward Nibbāna solely by way of making it its object, thinking "this is peace, this is sublime," but not in that manner [as the preliminary stages].
He speaks. The meaning is that by penetrating it in this manner, he applies his mind to it.
"He stands firm therein" means he is established in that insight (vipassanā) which has the three characteristics as its object.

"He attains the destruction of the taints" means that by gradually developing the four paths, he reaches Arahantship. "By that very passion for the Dhamma" refers to the Dhamma of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā).

"By desire and lust. "Delight in phenomena" (*dhammanandi*) is a synonym for that same thing. For one who is able to completely exhaust desire and lust regarding both serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) attains Arahantship;
one who is unable becomes a Non-returner (*anāgāmī*).
"In a straw-man figure" means in a figure made of straw or cloth. "One who shoots arrows at a distance" means one who shoots from afar. "Unerringly."
"He pierces" means he is one who shoots at a moving target. Regarding the phrase "whatever there is there belonging to feeling," material form (*rūpa*) is not included here.
Why? Because it has been transcended. For he, having previously entered the fine-material-sphere jhāna and thus transcended material form, has now entered the immaterial-sphere attainment;
thus, by way of serenity (*samatha*), material form has been transcended by him. Below—
Having contemplated form, one now contemplates the formless by transcending it; thus, even from the perspective of insight (vipassanā), form has been transcended by this [jhāna].
Furthermore, since there is no form whatsoever in the formless realms (ārūpa), form was not included with reference to those.

Now, why was the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana) not included? Because of its subtlety. For in that state, all four formless aggregates (arūpakkhandha) are extremely subtle.

The subtle [perceptions] do not come within the range of comprehension. Therefore he said: "Thus, monks, as far as the attainment of perception extends, so far does the penetration of final knowledge extend.

This is what is meant: as far as there is any attainment involving consciousness, so far, for one who comprehends gross phenomena, there is the penetration of final knowledge, and Arahantship is attained. [This excludes] the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
However, because of their subtlety, they are not called "perception-attainments" (*saññāsamāpatti*). "By meditators" means by those who delight in meditative absorption (*jhāna*).
"Having emerged" means having emerged from that attainment. "Should be fully described" means they should be correctly proclaimed;
they should be merely pointed out as "peaceful and sublime," and thus announced, praised, and extolled.
6. Commentary on the Ānanda Sutta 37.
In the sixth [verse], "in the confinement" (*sambādhe*) means in the confinement of the five strands of sensual pleasure. "Attainment of space" (*okāsādhigamo*) means the attainment of space.

"For the purification of beings" (*sattānaṃ visuddhiyā*) means for the purpose of bringing about the purification of beings. "For the surmounting" (*samatikkamāya*) means for the purpose of transcending.
"For the sake of their disappearance" means for the purpose of going to destruction. "For the sake of attaining the method" means for the purpose of attaining the path together with insight.
"For the sake of realizing nibbāna" means for the purpose of making directly manifest the conditionless nibbāna.
"That very same eye will come to be" means that very same physical eye (pasādacakkhu) will remain undestroyed. Those...
"Visible forms"—that very same visible-object base will come into the range of his perception.
"He will not experience that base" means he will not cognize that visible-object base. The same method applies to the remaining [bases] as well.
"Udāyī" refers to the Elder Kāḷudāyī. "Is he indeed percipient?"—does this mean he is indeed possessed of mind? The letter *m* is merely for the purpose of euphonic junction (*padasaṃdhi*).
"Perceiving what? means having become percipient by means of which perception? Why is it stated, "By completely surmounting perceptions of form"?
Is there still a sensing of forms and so forth for one who possesses the first jhāna and the others? No, there is not;
however, as long as the kasiṇa-form remains the object, to that extent form has not yet been "surmounted. Because it has not been surmounted, it is able to serve as a condition.
It would be able [to act as a condition]. However, because it has been transcended, it is called "non-existent," and since it is non-existent, it cannot function as a condition;
this is what was taken up here to demonstrate.

Regarding the phrases "dwelling in Jaṭila" and "not leaning toward," [the former means] dwelling in the city of Jaṭila, while [in the latter] one does not lean toward [objects] by way of lust, nor by way of hatred...
"Not drawn back" (*anapanata*): having suppressed and restrained the defilements through volitional effort (*sasaṅkhāra*) and application (*sappayoga*), he stands;
yet because the defilements have been cut off at their root, he does not stand as one who merely restrains and suppresses them with effort. "Standing due to being liberated":
he stands precisely because he is liberated from the defilements. "Contented due to standing": because he stands, he becomes known as truly contented. "Due to being contented..."
“He will not be agitated” means that precisely because of his contentment, he does not fall into agitation. With the words, “Venerable Ānanda, what is the fruit of this concentration?
this elder nun, as if taking a palm fruit and asking, “What is the name of this fruit?
took hold of the concentration of the fruit of arahantship and asked, “Venerable Ānanda, what is the fruit of this concentration?”
He asks: "Was it spoken by the Blessed One? [The answer is: "It was spoken as 'the fruit of final knowledge' (*aññāphala*). Here, "final knowledge" (*aññā*) refers to *arahantship*;
the meaning is that this is called the concentration of the fruit of *arahantship* by the Blessed One. "Even one who perceives thus":
even one who perceives by means of this perception of the fruit of *arahantship* does not experience that sphere; thus, in this sutta, the concentration of the fruit of *arahantship* is explained.
7. Commentary on the Lokāyatika Sutta 38.
In the seventh [sutta], "Lokāyatikas" refers to those who propound the Lokāyata doctrine. "Satataṃ" means always. "Samitaṃ" means continuously.
"Tiṭṭhatetaṃ" means "let this stand aside"; do not set it forth; what use have you for this? "I shall teach you the Dhamma, O brahmins."
"I shall teach you the Dhamma of the Four Truths.
"One firm in the Dhamma" means one who stands having taken up a firm bow. "An archer" means a marksman. A "firm bow" is said to have a strength of two thousand [pounds].
A "strength of two thousand" refers to that which, when strung, has the weight of iron balls and so forth bound to its string upon the staff.
Having taken it up, it is released from the ground as soon as it has been raised to the height of a *kaṇḍa*.
"Trained" means one who has mastered a craft after ten or twelve years in the teacher’s household. "Skilled" (*katahattha*) refers to one who merely learns the craft but is not yet skilled;

however, this person is "skilled" because he has attained mastery through practice. "One who has performed service" (*katūpāsana*) is one who has demonstrated his craft in royal courts and similar settings.
"With a light seat" means with a very light chariot-pole that has been made hollow inside, filled with cotton-wool and the like, and finished with the work of polishing.
For such a one, though it is designed to carry one ox-load, it can carry two ox-loads... [and so on] ...though it is designed to carry eight ox-loads, it can carry sixteen ox-loads.
"Without difficulty" means without pain. "It would overtake" means it would pass beyond. This is what is meant:
"Just as that archer quickly passes over that shadow measuring four spans, so too he is endowed with a speed capable of traversing the entire world-system very swiftly.
'By means of running' means by running on foot. 'They said thus' means they spoke in this way."
8. Commentary on the Devāsurasaṅgāma Sutta 39.
In the eighth [verse], "drawn up in battle array" means they stood ready. "We shall engage in combat" means we shall fight or wage war.
"They indeed fled" means they simply ran away. "Facing northward" means having turned their faces toward the north.
"Abhiyantā" means they pursue or follow after. "Gone to a place of safety for the fearful" means having gone to a refuge that wards off fear.
"Incapable of being done" means there is nothing that can be accomplished by means of battle. But why does their conflict occur?
For the asuras were formerly inhabitants of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven; at the time when the Cittapāṭali tree flowers, [they desire] the flower of the divine Pāricchattaka tree.
They recollect [this]. Then, their anger having arisen, they cry out, "Seize the gods! and climb Mount Sineru right there where they stand, face to face;
the gods also emerge. A battle breaks out between those cowherd boys, like one where they strike each other with sticks.
Sakka, the king of the gods, having established a guard at five points below, [guards] the city of the gods above.
Having surrounded them, he had statues resembling himself, holding thunderbolts in their hands, installed.
When the asuras, having ascended after blocking the five lower positions, saw the statues of Indra, they turned back and returned to the city of the asuras itself.
"Facing south" means having turned toward the southern direction. "Having struck down the footless" means having rendered them footless, that is, completely without remainder.

"Having struck him down": "He has gone beyond sight" means that Māra knows the mind of one who has attained the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) by making it the basis for the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭapādaka*), and he also knows the mind of one who has attained that same state by making it the basis for insight (*vipassanāpādaka*).

However, whether the attainment of the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*) serves as a basis for the cycle of existence or as a basis for insight, Māra does not know the mind of one who has attained it.
Therefore it was said: "He has gone out of sight of the Evil One.
9. Commentary on the Nāga Sutta (Sutta 39) 40.

In the ninth [verse], "of one who dwells in the forest" (*āraññakassa*) means of one who lives in the wilderness. "Intent upon his range" (*gocarapasutassa*) means of one who goes for the purpose of taking up his feeding ground.
*Hatthikalabhā* means large, full-grown elephants. *Hatthicchāpā* means young calves. *Obhaggobhaggaṃ* means set up by bending it here and there.
*Ogāhaṃ otinnassa* means of one who has descended into a ford (*ogāha*), so called because it is a place where one may descend into the water.
*Ogāhā uttiṇṇassa* means of one who has emerged from the water-ford. *Vūpakaṭṭho* means having become secluded.

Now, since there was no need for the One Possessing the Ten Powers (the Buddha) to have a task with an elephant-king, this [simile] was brought forward in order to show a personage in the Dispensation who is his counterpart;
therefore, in order to show that personage, he said, "Just so," and so forth.
10. Commentary on the Tapussa Sutta.
41. *Dasame Malleṣu* means in the kingdom of the Mallas. "Right here, Ānanda, you shall be present" means that here the Blessed One spoke because he knew:
