"With Ānanda standing right here, there will be a conversation and dialogue with the householder Tapussa;
on that account, I shall teach a great discourse on the Dhamma. *Upasaṅkami* (he approached): it is said that after having eaten his morning meal, he [approached] the One Possessed of Ten Powers...
Thinking, “I shall go to attend upon him,” as he was departing, he saw the Elder from afar and approached the Venerable Ānanda.

“Renunciation appears like a precipice”—this renunciation, known as going forth, stands before us as if it were a great abyss into which one must plunge. “The mind leaps into renunciation” means [into] the state of going forth.
The mind leaps forward toward the object; having made that very object its focus, it gains confidence, becomes established, and is liberated from opposing states.
"Seeing this as peace" means for those bhikkhus who see this renunciation as peace, free from distress and feverish agitation.
"By many people it is of a different kind" refers to this...
"Along with many people"—the meaning is that it was unlike (visabhāga), or unequal, to the bhikkhus. "A source of talk" means the root of conversation.

"Even as I was thinking thus, Ānanda, my mind did not leap toward renunciation"—even while I was reflecting in this way, my mind did not enter into the state of going forth. "Seeing 'this is peace'"—[refers to the realization of the peace of Nibbāna].
"Excellent is renunciation"—even for one who perceives thus through the process of reflection, seeing that "this renunciation is peaceful.
*Anāsevito*: not practiced, not touched, not realized. *Adhigamma*: having attained, having reached, having realized.
*Tamāseveyyan*: I would practice, I would resort to, that benefit. *Yaṃ me*: by which reason for me. *Adhigamma*: having attained.
"Having attained": "It would be a source of affliction for me"—in the sense of being an affliction, it is an affliction for me.

"The mind does not leap forward into the thoughtless" means that the mind does not leap forward toward the second jhāna, which is without applied thought but with sustained thought (*avitakkavicāra*), by way of its object.
"In thoughts" means in applied and sustained thought (*vitakkavicāresu*). The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
The Fourth Chapter: The Great Chapter (Mahāvagga).
5. The Chapter on Asceticism (Sāmaññavagga). 1. Explanation of the Discourse on Distress (Sambādhasuttavaṇṇanā).
42. In the first [verse] of the fifth [chapter], "Udāyī" refers to the Elder Kāḷudāyī. "Avidvā" means he knew. "Bhūrimedhasa" means one of great wisdom.
"Yo jhānam abujjhī" means he who awakened to *jhāna*. "Paṭilīnanisabho" means one who is both withdrawn through solitude and preeminent in the sense of being supreme.
"Munī" refers to the Buddha, the Sage. "Pariyāyena" means by way of a particular reason. "Kāmasambādhassa" [means...]
For the attainment of the first jhāna is called an "attainment of space" merely by its non-existence [of the hindrances], not in every respect entirely.
In that regard, "there is still confinement": even in that first jhāna, there is indeed confinement and oppression.
There is also the reading *tatrāpi atthi*. And what is the confinement there? But what in that jhāna is called "confinement"? This, then, is the confinement here.
This state of non-ceasing of applied and sustained thought is called "congestion" and "oppression. The meaning should be understood in this same way for all instances.
"In the direct sense" means not by a single reason; rather, the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya) is called the attainment of space in its entirety because of the abandoning of all congestions.
2. Commentary on the Kāyasakkhi Sutta. 43.

Regarding the second [sutta], "In whatever way that base": by whichever cause and by whichever mode that base known as the first jhāna exists, in that very way he dwells having touched it with the body; by that respective cause and by that...
In that manner, having touched that attainment with the body consisting of the name-group (*nāmakāya*), he dwells; the meaning is that he enters it.

He is called a "body-witness" (*kāyasakkhi*) by way of a figurative expression (*pariyāya*); because the first jhāna has been realized by him through that body consisting of the name-group, he is therefore called a body-witness by this figurative method.
By way of the non-figurative expression (*nippariyāya*), however, it refers to as much as is to be realized by the body.
Because he has performed everything, he is called a "body-witness" (kāyasakkhi) in the absolute sense.
3. Commentary on the Discourse on Liberation by Wisdom (Paññāvimutta-sutta). 44. Regarding the third [discourse]:

"And he understands it through wisdom"—he knows that [first jhāna] by means of the wisdom of insight (vipassanā-paññā) regarding the first jhāna. Here too, the figurative and non-figurative senses are to be understood in the same manner as previously explained. And just as it is here, so it is in the sections following this as well.
4. Commentary on the Ubhatobhāgavimutta Sutta 45.

The fourth [type of person] is to be understood by way of both. Herein, "liberated in both ways" (ubhatobhāgavimutta) means liberated from the defilements that are the adversaries of both serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā).

At the conclusion [of this section], however, it is liberated from the form-body (rūpakāya) by means of meditative attainment (samāpatti), and from the name-body (nāmakāya) by means of the Noble Path (ariyamagga).
One who is liberated should indeed be understood as "liberated in both ways" (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*).
5–10. Commentary on the *Sandiṭṭhika-dhamma-sutta* and others, 46–51. Regarding the fifth and subsequent [suttas]:
"Visible here and now" (*sandiṭṭhika*) means that which is to be seen by oneself. "Nibbāna" refers to the nibbāna of the defilements (*kilesa-nibbāna*). "Parinibbāna" refers to...
This is a synonym for that very term. *Tadaṅganibbāna* (Nibbāna by way of its factors) is Nibbāna by means of each respective factor, such as the first jhāna and so forth.
*Diṭṭhadhammanibbāna* (Nibbāna in this very life) is Nibbāna within this very personal existence (*attabhāva*). The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, the Chapter on Asceticism (*Sāmaññavagga*).
The First Fifty [of the Vinaya Piṭaka] is concluded.
2. Commentary on the Second Fifty. 52. Regarding the subsequent sections:

"Security" (*khema*) means free from danger. "Attained to security" (*khemappatta*) means one who has reached the state of security. "Weaknesses of the training" (*sikkhādubbalyāni*) refers to those things that cause weakness in the training. In all other respects, the meaning is self-evident.
The commentary on the Navaka-nipāta (The Book of Nines) of the Manorathapūraṇī,
the commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya, is completed.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Ten-Fold Section (Dasakanipāta) of the Aṅguttara Nikāya: 1.
The First Fifty (Paṭhamapaṇṇāsaka)
1. Ānisaṃsavagga 1.

Commentary on the *Kimatthiya-sutta* In the first [sutta] of the Dasaka-nipāta, "wholesome virtues" (*kusalāni sīlāni*) refers to blameless virtues. [They lead] to a state of being unashamed and to freedom from remorse.
"They conduce to welfare" means they have non-regret as their purpose (*avippaṭisāratthāni*). "That is their benefit" means they have non-regret as their advantage (*avippaṭisārānisaṃsāni*).
Regarding the phrases "for the purpose of knowledge and vision according to reality," and so forth: "knowledge and vision according to reality" refers to nascent insight (*taruṇavipassanā*);

"disenchantment" refers to powerful insight (*balavavipassanā*); "fading away" refers to the Path; "liberation" refers to the fruit of Arhatship; and "knowledge and vision" [refers to the subsequent knowledge].
This is the knowledge of reviewing by name. "They proceed toward the summit" means they go for the sake of arahantship.
2. Commentary on the *Cetanākaraṇīya Sutta*.
In the second [sutta], "not to be done by volition" means it is not to be performed after having willed, fashioned, or planned. This is the natural law (*dhammatā*).
"Esā" means this is the intrinsic nature of phenomena (dhammasabhāva); "ayaṃ" refers to this fixed law of causes. "Abhisandenti" means they set in motion;

"paripūrenti" means they bring to fulfillment. "Apārā pāraṃ gamanāya" means for the purpose of going from the near shore, which is the round of existence in the three realms (tebhūmaka-vatta), to the further shore, which is Nibbāna.
3–5. Commentary on the Three Suttas on Conditions (Upanisa-sutta).

3–5. In the third [sutta], "one whose proximate cause has been destroyed" (*hatūpanisa*) means one whose cause has been destroyed. In the fourth and fifth, the distinction lies solely in the fact that they were spoken by two elders.
6. Commentary on the *Samādhi-sutta*.
In the sixth, "neither perceiving earth in earth" means not perceiving "earth" by taking earth as an object.
Thus, one would not be a percipient of the perception that has arisen. The same method applies to water and the other elements.
"Not this world" means one would not be a percipient of the perception of the fourfold and fivefold jhānas arising in this world.
"Not the other world" means one would not be a percipient of the perception of the fourfold and fivefold jhānas arising in the other world. And yet, one would still be a percipient. Now...
And furthermore, his attainment is said to be an attainment with applied thought (*savitakka*) itself.
For one who sits having entered upon it as "this is peaceful, this is sublime," even for a whole day, the arising of consciousness proceeds only as "peaceful, peaceful.
For one who sits having entered upon it as "sublime, sublime," even for a whole day, the arising of consciousness proceeds only as "sublime, sublime."

"This is called the stilling of all formations" refers to Nibbāna. When one has entered upon the thought, "Nibbāna, Nibbāna," and sits down, even for a whole day the arising of consciousness proceeds only as "Nibbāna, Nibbāna.
All of this is said with reference to the concentration of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti-samādhi*).
7. Commentary on the Sāriputta Sutta.

7. "And yet, friend, at that time I was percipient," means that at that time I was percipient by means of this perception of the attainment of fruition, namely, "Nibbāna is the cessation of existence.
This is said in reference to the reviewing [consciousness] which considers: "That attainment was accompanied by mind."
8. Commentary on the Jhānasutta:

In the eighth [sutta], "Samantapāsādika" means "beautifully serene on all sides" because of the presence of bodily actions and so forth that bring about serenity. "Sabbākāraparipūra" means "complete in all aspects," being fulfilled by all causal factors.
9. Commentary on the Santavimokkhasutta:
9. In the ninth [chapter], they are "continua" (*santati*) both by way of the continuity of the object and the continuity of the factors.
They are called "liberations" (*vimokkha*) because they are liberated from opposing states and because they are well-released through the absence of apprehension regarding the object.
"Having transcended form" means having proceeded beyond the fine-material jhānas. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
The First Chapter on Benefits.
2. The Chapter on the Protector. 1. Commentary on the Discourse on Lodgings.
11. Regarding the first [meditation subject] for the second [person], "endowed with five factors" means endowed with five qualities. "Neither too far nor too near":
for if it is too far, when one has gone there after wandering for alms, there is weariness of body and mind;
consequently, one is unable to produce unarisen concentration or to stabilize that which has already arisen.

It is too close and crowded with many people. However, for those dwelling in a place measuring forty *usabhas*, it is free from the faults of being either too distant or too near, and is well-suited for coming and going.
"Not crowded by day" means it is not thronged by the great multitude during the daytime.
2. Commentary on the Discourse on the Five Factors (*Pañcaṅgasutta-vaṇṇanā*)

12. In the second [verse], "an arahant" (*kevalī*) means one endowed with all (*kevala*) qualities in their entirety. "One who has lived the life" (*vusitavā*) means one who has completed the dwelling of the holy life (*brahmacariya-vāsa*).
"By the way of the one beyond training" (*asekhena*) means by that which is supramundane and included within the states of one beyond training.

"By the aggregate of virtue" (*sīlakkhandhena*) means by the mass of virtue. Regarding "the aggregate of liberation" (*vimuttikkhandhena*): here, excluding the three beginning with virtue, the remaining resultant states are called "liberation. The "knowledge and vision of liberation" (*vimutti-ñāṇadassana*) is the knowledge of review; that is purely mundane.
3–4. Commentary on the *Saṃyojana-sutta* and others. 13–14.
In the third [sutta], "belonging to the lower part" (*orambhāgiyāni*) means belonging to the lower portion; "belonging to the upper part" (*uddhambhāgiyāni*) means belonging to the upper portion.
In this sutta, only the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) is discussed. In the fourth, the "stumps and fetters" (*khilavinibandhā*) have already been explained in detail in the Pañcaka-nipāta.
"By height and circumference" means by length and breadth.
5. Commentary on the *Appamāda-sutta* 15.
Regarding the fifth [sutta], "In the very same way": just as the Fully Enlightened One is the foremost among all beings, so too...

It should be understood that diligence (*appamāda*), which causes wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*) to be performed, is supreme. But is it not this [diligence] alone that is mundane, whereas wholesome states can also be supramundane?
And is it not this [diligence] alone that belongs to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), whereas wholesome states belong to all four planes?
How, then, is it supreme among them? By way of being their producer. For it is through diligence that they are acquired; therefore, it is supreme among them. For this very reason...
It is said: "All these have heedfulness as their root.
"Of the forest-dwellers" means of those that move upon the surface of the earth. "Of living beings" means of four-footed creatures. "Footprints" refers to the tracks.
"They come together" means they enter into a common placement or collection. "Is declared the foremost" means it is declared the best.
"By its greatness" means it is declared to be the foremost by virtue of its magnitude, not by virtue of its excellence in qualities; such is the meaning.

"Vassika" refers to the jasmine flower (*sumana*). It is said that after hearing this discourse, King Bhātika, desiring to investigate the matter, prepared a chamber with a floor inlaid with the four kinds of fragrant substances, had fragrant flowers brought in, and [placed them] in a casket.
Having placed a handful of jasmine flowers in the center and arranged the remaining handfuls all around it, he closed the door and went outside.
After spending a short while outside, as he opened the door and was entering, the fragrance of the jasmine flowers struck his nose first of all. He [stood] right there on the great floor.

Having prostrated himself facing the Great Cetiya, he paid homage to the Cetiya, saying: "It was well-spoken by the Perfectly Enlightened One when he declared that the Vassika flower is their foremost.
*Khuddarājāno* means minor kings; there is also a reading, *kūṭarājāno*.
6. Commentary on the Āhuneyyasutta.
16. Sixth: One is endowed with the knowledge of change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū-ñāṇa*), which has Nibbāna as its object and consists of insight that has reached the summit (*sikhāpatta-vipassanā*).
7. Commentary on the First *Nāthasutta* 17.
Seventh: "With a protector" (*sanāthā*) means you should dwell having many groups of kinsmen as your relatives. They act as protectors, thus they are called "protectors" (*nāthakaraṇā*).
The meaning is: "those who provide one with a protector and a firm foundation. Regarding the terms *kalyāṇamitta* and so forth:

one who possesses friends (*mitta*) that are "good" (*kalyāṇa*)—meaning endowed with qualities such as virtue—is a "virtuous friend" (*kalyāṇamitta*). Because they walk together with him in standing, sitting, and other activities, they are his "virtuous companions" (*kalyāṇasahāya*).
And because he is inclined toward and bent over toward virtuous friends alone, both in mind and in body, he is "one who leans toward the virtuous" (*kalyāṇasampavaṅka*).
"He is easy to speak to" means he can be addressed with ease; he can be instructed with ease.
"He is patient" means that when spoken to harshly, roughly, or cruelly, he endures it and does not become angry.

"He receives instruction respectfully" means that whereas some, when being exhorted, grasp it wrongly, resist it, or go away without listening, he does not do so, but says, "Please exhort me, venerable sir."
“Exhort us! If you do not exhort us, who else will?”—thus he shows his deference. “High and low” means superior and inferior.
“Duties” (*kiṃkaraṇīyāni*) refers to tasks that must be performed after saying, “What shall I do?
Among these, “high work” (*uccakammaṃ*) consists of making robes, dyeing them, plastering work at a shrine (*cetiyakamma*), and [work] in the Uposatha hall, the shrine house, and the Bodhi-house.
"Tasks to be performed" refers to such things as these. "Minor duties" (*avaca-kamma*) means small tasks such as washing and anointing the feet.

"By means of that" (*tatrūpāyāya*) means by way of approaching that [place]. "Able to do" (*alaṃ kātuṃ*) means he is capable of doing it. "Able to arrange" (*alaṃ saṃvidhātuṃ*) means he is capable of deliberating upon it.

"One whose desire and affection are for the Dhamma" (*dhammakāmo*) means one who loves the word of the Buddha consisting of the Three Piṭakas; this is the meaning. "One whose speech is pleasant" (*piyasamudāhāro*)...
The meaning is that one listens attentively when another is speaking, and one desires to teach others oneself.
Regarding the terms *abhidhamme* and *abhivinaye*, a fourfold classification should be understood here: *dhamma* and *abhidhamma*, as well as *vinaya* and *abhivinaya*.
In this context, *dhamma* refers to the Sutta Piṭaka; *abhidhamma* refers to the seven treatises (*pakaraṇa*); and *vinaya* refers to the two Vibhaṅgas.
"Abhivinaya" refers to the Khandhaka and Parivāra sections. Alternatively, both the Sutta Piṭaka and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka are "Dhamma," while the paths and fruits are "Abhidhamma.
The entire Vinaya Piṭaka is "Vinaya," and that which brings about the pacification of the defilements is "Abhivinaya.
Thus, one should find sublime joy in all of this—herein, in the Dhamma and Abhidhamma, and in the Vinaya and Abhivinaya.
The meaning is "he becomes. Regarding the phrase "in wholesome states" (*kusalesu dhammesu*), the locative case is used in the sense of cause;
the meaning is that, for the sake of attaining those wholesome states belonging to the four planes, he does not abandon his duty.
8. Commentary on the Second Nātha Sutta:

18. Regarding the eighth [sutta], *therānukampitassa* means: of one who has been compassionately regarded by the elders (*thera*) through their compassionate concern for his welfare, which was inspired by their exhortation and instruction.
9. Commentary on the First Ariyavāsa Sutta (The Discourse on the Noble Abodes). 19.

Regarding the ninth [sutta], *ariyavāsā* means the abode of the noble ones (*ariya*). They are called "noble abodes" because the noble ones have dwelt, do dwell, and will dwell therein. *Yadariyā* means those noble ones who [dwell] in these abodes.
10. Commentary on the Second Discourse on the Noble Abodes (Dutiya-ariyavāsa-sutta). 20.

The tenth [discourse]: Since the monks dwelling in the kingdom of Kuru were possessed of profound wisdom and were appropriately engaged in their practice, this [sutta] is likewise profound and subtle, just as the Mahānidāna and other discourses were taught to them in the Dīgha Nikāya and elsewhere.

He spoke right there a sutta characterized by the three marks. In that context, "one who has abandoned five factors" means that, having become dissociated from five factors, one whose taints are destroyed dwelt, dwells, or will dwell [in those abodes].
Therefore, this state of having abandoned five factors is called a "dwelling of the noble ones. This same method applies everywhere. Thus, monks, a monk is endowed with six factors.
"He possesses" means he is endowed with the equanimity that has six factors. What are the states known as the "six-factored equanimity"?
They are knowledge and the rest. When "knowledge" is mentioned, four consciousnesses associated with knowledge are obtained by way of their activity;
when "constant abiding" is mentioned, the eight great types of consciousness are obtained; and when "there is no lust or hatred" is mentioned, ten types of consciousness are obtained.

Somanassa (mental joy) is obtained by way of repeated practice. Regarding the phrase "with a mind guarded by mindfulness": for one whose taints are destroyed, mindfulness performs the function of guarding at all times across the three doors.
For this very reason, it is said of him that whether walking or standing, sleeping or waking, his knowledge and vision are constantly and continuously present.
“Of many recluses and brahmins” means of numerous recluses and brahmins.
Here, “recluses” (samaṇā) refers to those who have gone forth into homelessness, while “brahmins” (brāhmaṇā) refers to those who address others as “sir” (bhovādino).

“Many individual truths” means many separate truths. The meaning is that there are many truths grasped individually, such as: “This view alone is the truth; this alone is the truth. “Confounded” means...
"Extracted" (*nīhaṭāni*). "Dispelled" (*panuṇṇāni*) means well extracted. "Abandoned" (*cattāni*) means relinquished. "Vomited out" (*vantāni*) means vomited forth.
"Released" (*muttāni*) means made free from their bonds. "Renounced" (*pahīnāni*) means abandoned.
"Reversed" (*paṭinissaṭṭhāni*) means relinquished in such a way that they do not ascend to the mind again. All of these are synonyms for the state of having relinquished what was previously grasped.

Regarding *samavayasaṭṭhesanā*: here, *avayā* means "unfailing," and *saṭṭhā* means "abandoned. Thus, one whose search (*esanā*) is completely (*sammā*) unfailing and abandoned is *samavayasaṭṭhesano*;

the meaning is "one who has thoroughly abandoned all searching. The accomplishment of the function of the Path is described by such passages as "the mind is liberated from lust" (*rāgā cittaṃ vimuttaṃ*).
The fruit of reflection (*paccavekkhaṇa-phala*) is described by such passages as "lust has been abandoned by me" (*rāgo me pahīno*).
The remainder is clear in meaning throughout. This is the second chapter, the Chapter on the Protector (Nāthavagga).
3. The Great Chapter (Mahāvagga).
1. Commentary on the Sīhanāda Sutta 21.
In the first [section] of the third [chapter], "gone to uneven places" means gone to uneven locations for grazing.
"They brought him to destruction" means they brought him to slaughter and killing. For, due to his intense radiance, he possessed compassion toward small living beings.

Therefore, having let out a lion’s roar—thinking, "Those who are able to stand their ground as adversaries will do so, while those who are weak and wish to flee shall flee"—he sets out for his range of action. This is a designation for the Tathāgata;
for if a lion is so called because of its endurance (*sahana*) and its striking (*hana*), the Tathāgata indeed endures all things, both desirable and undesirable.
He crushes and destroys the doctrines of all other proponents. This is his "lion's roar.
As for the "powers of a Tathāgata," these are powers belonging exclusively to the Tathāgata, not shared by others.

Alternatively, the meaning is that they are "powers attained" (āgatabala) in the same way that the powers of previous Buddhas were attained through the perfection of merit. In this regard, the Tathāgata’s [power] is twofold.
Power consists of physical power and the power of knowledge. Among these, physical power is to be understood according to the breeds of elephants. For this was said by the ancients:
“The black from Kālāva, the Gaṅgeyya, the white, the tawny-brown, The fragrant, the auspicious, the golden, the Uposatha, and the six-tusked—these are the ten.”
These are the ten breeds of elephants. Among them, "Kālāvaka" should be understood as the ordinary breed of elephant.
The physical strength of ten men is equal to that of one Kālāvaka elephant; the strength of ten Kālāvakas is equal to that of one Gaṅgeyya;
the strength of ten Gaṅgeyyas is equal to that of one Paṇḍara. The strength of ten...
That which is worth ten white elephants is the value of one tawny elephant. That which is worth ten tawny elephants is the value of one reddish-brown elephant.
That which is worth ten reddish-brown elephants is the value of one scent-elephant. That which is worth ten scent-elephants is the value of one auspicious elephant.
That which is worth ten auspicious elephants is the value of one golden elephant. That which is worth ten golden elephants...
That which is the strength of one Uposatha elephant is equal to that of ten Uposatha elephants; that which is the strength of ten Chaddanta elephants is equal to that of one Tathāgata.
This very thing is also called the "Nārāyaṇa compacted strength.
By the calculation of ordinary elephants, this is the strength of a thousand koṭis of elephants; by the calculation of men, it is the strength of ten thousand koṭis of men.
There is strength. This, first of all, is the bodily strength of the Tathāgata.

As for his power of knowledge (*ñāṇabala*), it is indeed already recorded in the Canon: the knowledge of the ten powers (*dasabala-ñāṇa*); the knowledge of the four grounds of self-confidence (*catuvesārajja-ñāṇa*) as found in the *Majjhima Nikāya*;

the unshakable knowledge regarding the eight assemblies; the knowledge that delimits the four modes of birth (*catuyoni-pariccheda-ñāṇa*); and the knowledge that delimits the five destinations (*pañcagati-pariccheda-ñāṇa*).

The seventy-three knowledges mentioned in the *Saṃyutta Nikāya* are called "the seventy-seven knowledges"; thus, there are many other such things as well that are termed "power of knowledge" (*ñāṇabala*).
Here too, it is specifically this power of knowledge that is intended. For knowledge is called "power" in the sense of being unshakable and in the sense of providing support.
"The place of the bull" (*āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ*) means the preeminent place, the supreme place; or alternatively, the "bulls" (*āsabhā*) are the previous Buddhas, and it is their place.
This is the meaning. Furthermore, a *usabha* is a bull that is the leader of a hundred cows;
a *vasabha* is one that is the leader of a thousand cows. Alternatively, a *usabha* is the leader of a hundred bulls; a *vasabha* is the leader of a thousand bulls.

A *nisabha* is the best of all cattle, capable of enduring all hardships, white, beautiful, a bearer of great burdens, and unshakable even by the sound of a hundred thunderclaps; it is this *nisabha* that is intended here by the term *usabha*.
This, too, is a figurative expression for it. "Āsabhaṃ" means "belonging to a bull (usabha). "Ṭhānaṃ" means a station that is immovable after pressing down upon the earth with all four feet.
Furthermore, this is called "āsabhaṃ" because it is like the āsabha;

for just as a bull known as a *nisabha* (leader), endowed with the strength of a bull, stands in an immovable station after pressing down upon the earth with all four feet, [so too does the Tathāgata].
In the same way, the Tathāgata, endowed with the ten powers of a Tathāgata and the four grounds of self-confidence,
having pressed down upon the earth of the eight assemblies, stands in an immovable state, unshakable by any adversary or enemy in the world including the devas.
Standing thus, he claims, approaches, and does not renounce that pre-eminent position (*āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ*).
He attributes [these qualities] to himself. Therefore it is said: "He claims the place of the bull.

"In assemblies" means in the eight kinds of assemblies. "He roars the lion’s roar" means he roars the best roar, he roars the roar of one who is fearless, or he roars a roar similar to that of a lion.
In this regard, there is this simile: just as a lion is endowed with the strength of a lion...

Confident in all respects and free from horripilation, he roars the lion’s roar; likewise, the lion-like Tathāgata, endowed with the powers of a Tathāgata, being confident and free from horripilation among the eight assemblies, roars the lion’s roar—endowed with the various graces of teaching such as "This is identity view" (sakkāya)—according to the aforementioned method.
Therefore it is said: "He roars the lion’s roar in the assemblies."

Regarding the phrase "he sets in motion the Brahma-wheel": here, *brahma* means supreme, most excellent, and distinguished. *Cakka* refers to the Wheel of Dhamma (*dhammacakka*). This, moreover, is twofold:

the knowledge of penetration (*paṭivedha-ñāṇa*) and the knowledge of teaching (*desanā-ñāṇa*). Of these, the knowledge of penetration is developed through wisdom and brings about the noble fruit for oneself;
the knowledge of teaching is developed through compassion and brings about the noble fruit for disciples.
The knowledge of teaching (*desanāñāṇa*). Therein, the knowledge of penetration (*paṭivedhañāṇa*) is twofold: that which is arising and that which has arisen.
For that [knowledge] is "arising" from the Great Renunciation up until the path of Arahantship; it is called "arisen" at the moment of the fruition (*phala*).
Or, it is "arising" from the Tusita heaven up until the path of Arahantship on the Great Bodhi Seat; it is called "arisen" at the moment of the fruition. From the time of Dīpaṅkara...
From the moment [the path] begins until the arising of the arahant path, it is called "arisen at the moment of the fruit.
Teaching-knowledge (*desanā-ñāṇa*) is also twofold: while it is occurring, it is called "occurring. That indeed occurs until the stream-entry path of Aññā Koṇḍañña;

at the moment of the fruit, it is called "occurring. Among these two, penetrative-knowledge (*paṭivedha-ñāṇa*) is supramundane (*lokuttara*), while teaching-knowledge is mundane (*lokiya*). Both of them—
This, moreover, is not shared by others; it is the very own wisdom of the Buddhas.
Now, in order to show in detail those ten powers endowed with which the Tathāgata claims his pre-eminent position, he asks:
"Which ten? Here, monks, the Tathāgata says: "The possible as possible," and so forth. Therein:
"As a cause and as a cause" means as a reason and as a reason. For a cause is called a "cause" (*ṭhāna*) because the fruit abides therein;
since it arises and proceeds in dependence upon that, it is therefore called a "cause. Regarding this, the Blessed One said:
"Whatever states are the causes and conditions for the arising of whatever states, those are the 'causes' (*ṭhāna*). Whatever states [are the results] of whatever states..."
Knowing that there are no causes or conditions for arising in this or that instance, one understands as it really is what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible.

Furthermore, this is explained in detail in the Abhidhamma by way of such passages as: "In this context, what is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible, according to reality? As for the phrase "whatever... [it refers to the following].
"By which knowledge": "This too, monks, is for the Tathāgata"—the meaning is that this knowledge of what is possible and impossible (*ṭhānāṭhāna-ñāṇa*) is called a power of the Tathāgata.
In this way, the application [of the formula] should be understood in all instances.
"Of the undertaking of kamma" (*kamma-samādānānaṃ*): it refers to wholesome and unwholesome kamma performed after having undertaken it; or, the undertaking itself is the kamma.

"From the standpoint and from the cause" means both by way of condition (*paccaya*) and by way of cause (*hetu*). In this context, destiny, the basis of existence (*upadhi*), time, and effort are the "standpoint" for the ripening of kamma, while the kamma itself is the "cause.

Furthermore, the detailed exposition of this knowledge has already been presented in the Abhidhamma in such passages as: "There are certain undertakings of evil kamma that, being obstructed by success in destiny, do not ripen."
"Leading everywhere" means leading to all destinations, both those that are good destinations and those that are bad destinations. "The way" means the path.
"He understands it as it really is" means that even among many people who are killing a single living being, he understands according to this principle: "The volition of this one will lead to hell;
the volition of this one will lead to the animal realm"—thus, even in the case of a single object, he understands the wholesome and unwholesome volitions.
He knows the intrinsic nature of the practices without error. Furthermore, the detailed exposition of this knowledge is found precisely in the Abhidhamma in the following manner:
"In that regard, what is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the way leading everywhere as it really is? Herein, the Tathāgata understands:
'This is the path, this is the practice leading to hell,'" and so forth.
"Many elements" (*anekadhātu*) means having many elements by way of the eye-element and so forth, or by way of the sense-sphere of desire and so forth.

"Diverse elements" (*nānādhātu*) means having various kinds of elements due to the distinct characteristics of those very same elements. "The world" (*loka*) refers to the world of aggregates, bases, and elements.
"He understands it as it really is" (*yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti*) means he penetrates the intrinsic nature of those elements without error. This too is knowledge.
“In this regard, what is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the world with its many elements and various elements as it really is?
Here, the Tathāgata understands the diversity of the aggregates,” and so forth; this has been explained in detail in the Abhidhamma.
“The diversity of inclinations” means the state of having diverse inclinations by way of inferior and other types of inclinations. This knowledge also [is included] therein...
What is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the various inclinations of beings as they really are? Herein, the Tathāgata understands:
"There are beings of inferior inclinations," and so forth; this has been explained in detail in the Abhidhamma.
"Of other beings" means of principal beings. "Of other persons" means of other inferior beings. These two terms have the same meaning.
Or rather, these two terms are stated in two ways according to the needs of those to be trained (*veneyya*).

"Knowledge of the higher and lower degrees of the faculties" (*indriyaparopariyatta*) means the superior state and the inferior state, as well as the increase and decrease, of the faculties such as faith (*saddhā*) and the rest.
Regarding this knowledge as well, the detailed exposition is: "In that regard, what is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the higher and lower degrees of the faculties of other beings and other persons?"
What is knowledge according to reality (*yathābhūtaṃ ñāṇa*)? It is as stated in the Abhidhamma in the following manner: "Here, the Tathāgata understands the inclinations of beings," and so forth.

Regarding "the meditations, liberations, concentrations, and attainments": this refers to the four meditations beginning with the first; the eight liberations beginning with "one possessing form sees forms";
the three concentrations beginning with "with applied thought and sustained thought" (*savitakka-savicāra*); and the attainments of the first meditation, and so on.
Of the nine successive attainments: defilement (*saṃkilesa*) refers to states conducive to decline; cleansing (*vodāna*) refers to states conducive to distinction.

Emergence (*vuṭṭhāna*)—as it is said: "Cleansing is emergence, and emergence from this or that concentration is also emergence"—refers both to familiar jhāna and to the fruition-attainments (*phalasamāpatti*) of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*). For each lower [attainment]...
Mastery in jhāna is the proximate cause for each successive higher stage; therefore, it is said that “purification is also emergence.
However, emergence from all jhānas occurs by means of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), and emergence from the attainment of cessation occurs by means of the fruition attainment.
With reference to this, it is said: “Emergence from each respective concentration is also emergence.”

This knowledge has also been explained in detail in the Abhidhamma according to the method beginning: "In this context, what is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the defilement, purification, and emergence of the jhānas, liberations, concentrations, and attainments as they really are? There are four types of meditators;
there is one kind of meditator who, while experiencing success, perceives it as failure. And so forth.
The detailed exposition and analysis of all the knowledges (*sabbañāṇa*) has been stated in the *Sammohavinodanī*, the commentary on the *Vibhaṅga*.

The discussion regarding the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa*) and the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*) is set forth in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*. The discussion regarding the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya*) has already been explained above.

In this regard, there is the argument of an opponent: "There is no such thing as a separate knowledge called the 'knowledge of the ten powers' (*dasabala-ñāṇa*); this is merely a part of the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*)."
"Such is the distinction. That should not be viewed in that way. For the knowledge of the ten powers (*dasabala-ñāṇa*) is one thing, and the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*) is another.
Indeed, the knowledge of the ten powers knows only its own respective functions, whereas the knowledge of omniscience knows those as well as what remains beyond them.
For among the knowledges of the ten powers, the first knows only what is a cause and what is not a cause; the second [knows] only the interval between karma and its result.
The third [chapter] concerns the delimitation of kamma; the fourth, the cause for the diversity of elements;
the fifth, the inclinations and resolutions of beings; the sixth, the sharpness or dullness of the faculties;
the seventh, their defilement and so forth together with the jhānas and other factors; the eighth, the continuity of the aggregates in past lives; and the ninth...
[The other powers] know only the passing away and rebirth-linking of beings, and the tenth [power] knows only the analysis of the truths.
However, the knowledge of omniscience understands both what is to be known by these [powers] and what lies beyond them; yet it does not perform all the functions of these [other powers].
For that [knowledge], being jhāna, cannot enter into absorption; being psychic power (*iddhi*), it cannot perform transformations; and being the path, it cannot [eradicate] defilements.
He is unable to dispel it.

Furthermore, the opponent himself should be asked: "Is this so-called knowledge of the Ten Powers with applied thought and sustained thought, without applied thought and with sustained thought alone, or without applied thought and without sustained thought;
is it of the sense-sphere, the fine-material sphere, or the immaterial sphere; is it mundane or supramundane? One who knows [the answer]...

“He will say: ‘In sequence, the seven knowledges are with applied thought and sustained thought (savitakka-savicāra); those following them are two that are without applied thought and sustained thought (avitakka-avicāra). He will say: ‘The knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsava-kkhaya-ñāṇa) may be with applied thought and sustained thought, may be without applied thought and with sustained thought only (avitakka-vicāramatta), or may be without applied thought and sustained thought.
Likewise, he will say: ‘In sequence, seven belong to the sense sphere (kāmāvacara), and following them, two belong to the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara).’”

At the conclusion, he will say, "One [knowledge] is supramundane. He will further say, "But omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa) possesses both applied thought and sustained thought (savitakka-savicāra) and is exclusively mundane.

Having thus understood the word-by-word commentary on this section, now, since the Tathāgata, from the very beginning, by means of the knowledge of what is possible and impossible (ṭhānāṭṭhānañāṇa)...

He sees the absence of the veil of defilements (kilesāvaraṇa) as being the proper and improper conditions for the attainment or non-attainment of the destruction of the taints (āsava-kkhaya) by beings susceptible to instruction;
this is because he sees their standing upon the basis of mundane right view and because he sees the absence of their standing upon the basis of fixed wrong view.

Then, through the knowledge of kamma and its result (kammavipāka-ñāṇa), he sees the absence of the veil of karmic result (vipākāvaraṇa) in them, because he sees their rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) as being endowed with three roots (tihetuka).

By means of the knowledge of the way leading everywhere (*sabbatthagāminīpaṭipadāñāṇa*), he perceives the absence of karmic obstructions, because he sees the absence of deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantariyakamma*).

Thus, for those who are without obstructions, by means of the knowledge of the many elements and the diversity of elements (*anekadhātunānādhātuñāṇa*), he perceives their specific temperaments (*cariyāvisesa*) for the purpose of teaching the Dharma in accordance with them, because he sees the variety of elements (*dhātuvematta*).
Then, by means of the knowledge of their diverse inclinations (*nānādhimuttikatañāṇa*), he perceives their inclination (*adhimutti*).
Even without employing a formal method, for the sake of teaching the Dhamma by way of his own inclination;

thus, in order to teach the Dhamma according to their capacity and strength to those who are inclined toward various views, he perceives the state of the higher and lower faculties through the knowledge of the penetration of others' faculties, because he sees the sharpness or dullness of faith and the other faculties. Having thus fully understood the state of the higher and lower faculties, however—

If they are far away, then because he has attained mastery over the jhānas and other states through the knowledge of the jhānas and so forth, he approaches them quickly by means of a specific supernormal power (*iddhi*). Having approached,

he perceives their former births and existences through the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa*), and he perceives their present mental states through the knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariya-ñāṇa*)— which is to be attained through the power of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*)—
and [he perceives their future] by the power of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa*).
Because he is free from delusion regarding the practice leading to the destruction of the taints (*āsava*), he teaches the Dhamma for the destruction of the taints.
Therefore, it should be understood that these powers are taught in this specific sequence.
2. Commentary on the *Adhivuttipada Sutta* (The Discourse on the Terms of Acceptance)
22. In the second [verse], "those states" (*ye te dhammā*) refers to those states consisting of the ten powers of knowledge (*dasabalañāṇa*) and the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
"Designation-terms" (*adhivuttipadānam*) means "synonym-terms" (*adhivacanapadānam*); the meaning is "the aggregates, bases, and elements.

For "designations" (*adhivuttiyo*) are called "synonyms" (*adhivacanāni*), because they are the terms that constitute the basis for the teaching. Indeed, even the Buddhas of the past [taught] these very same states.
They have spoken thus; those yet to come will also speak thus. Therefore, the aggregates and so forth are called "designative terms" (*adhivuttipada*).

Of these designative terms: alternatively, they are called "views" (*diṭṭhi*) because they proceed by overriding the actual reality and failing to grasp it according to its true nature; thus, "designative terms" are terms for views—terms that indicate views.

"Words" is the meaning. Of those designations and modes of expression of views. "For the sake of direct realization through higher knowledge" means for the purpose of making [the truth] manifest after having known it. "Confident" means having attained the joy of knowledge. "Therein" means among those phenomena;
"they teach the Dhamma in such and such a way" refers to those various proponents of views or others.
Or, having known their disposition, he may teach the Dhamma accordingly. "He will know the inferior as inferior" means he will recognize an inferior teaching as "an inferior teaching.
"Ñāteyya" means that which is to be known. "Daṭṭheyya" means that which is to be seen.
"Sacchikareyya" means that which is to be realized. "Knowledge of things as they really are in each case" refers to knowledge regarding those various teachings.

"Knowledge of things as they really are" (yathāsabhāvañāṇa). By this, he shows omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa). Having thus shown omniscient knowledge, and then wishing to show the knowledge of the ten powers (dasabalañāṇa), he says, "These ten," and so forth.
For even the knowledge of the ten powers is, in each respective case, simply knowledge of things as they really are (yathābhūtañāṇa).
3. Commentary on the Kāya Sutta 23.
In the third [case], "he has fallen into some offense" means he has fallen into some category of offense.
"Having investigated" means having entered into and scrutinized it. "Bodily misconduct" refers to the threefold bodily misconduct. "Vocal misconduct" refers to...
There are four kinds of verbal misconduct. "Evil envy" (*pāpikā issā*) means base jealousy.

"Having seen with wisdom" means having repeatedly seen with the path-wisdom accompanied by insight (*vipassanā*), [these qualities] are to be abandoned. "Succeeds" (*ijjhati*) means it is accomplished.

"Of one who dwells near" (*upavāsassa*) means of one who approaches and dwells in dependence [upon a teacher]. "Overpowering" (*abhibhuyya*) means having overwhelmed and crushed. "Proceeds" (*iriyati*) means it functions.
In this sutta, the path together with insight (vipassanā) is explained.
4. Commentary on the Mahācundasutta: 24.

In the fourth [verse], by the words "I know this Dhamma," the manner of speaking the proclamation of knowledge (ñāṇavāda) is stated. By the phrases "I am one who has developed the body" and so forth...
Regarding the doctrine of cultivation (*bhāvanāvāda*). In the third section, two doctrines are stated together; all three of these claim nothing less than *arahantship*.
"He might state a 'half-doctrine'" means he might state the doctrine: "I am half [of an *arahant*]. "To bring forward" means to take out and give.
5. Commentary on the Kasiṇa Sutta.

25. In the fifth [section], they are called *kasiṇāyatanāni* because the *kasiṇas* are so called in the sense of being "total" (*sakala*), while the bases (*āyatanāni*) are so called in the sense of being a "field" (*kheta*) or a "foundation" (*adhiṭṭhāna*) for those states that have them as their object.
*Uddhaṃ* means upwards, facing the expanse of the sky. *Adho* means downwards, facing the surface of the earth.
*Tiriyaṃ* means across, having delimitated it on all sides like a circular field. A certain person...
For one person develops the kasiṇa only upwards, another downwards, and another all around.
Or, for some other reason, he extends it in this way, just as one who wishes to see forms extends light. Therefore it is said:
"One perceives the earth-kasiṇa above, below, and across. Furthermore, the word "non-dual" (advaya) is stated for the purpose of showing that it does not partake of any other state.
For just as for one who has entered water there is only water in all directions and nothing else, even so the earth-kasiṇa is only earth-kasiṇa;
there is no admixture with any other kasiṇa. This same method applies everywhere.
"Immeasurable" (appamāṇa) is said with reference to the immeasurability of its pervasion; for when one pervades it with the mind—
It pervades everything entirely; it does not take a measure such as, "This is its beginning" or "This is its middle.

Here, "consciousness kasiṇa" refers to the consciousness that occurs in the space cleared by the kasiṇa. In this context, the directions—above, below, and across—should be understood with respect to the space cleared by the kasiṇa, and with respect to the consciousness occurring therein. This is the point here.
In brief, these earth-kasiṇas and so forth have been explained in detail according to the method of meditation on the meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*) precisely in the *Visuddhimagga*.
6. Commentary on the Kāḷī Sutta:
Regarding "in the sixth, the questions of the maidens," this refers to the inquiries of the maidens who were the daughters of Māra. [He spoke] for the attainment of the goal by the heart...
"Santi" (peace) is expressed by both terms as referring specifically to *arahatta* (arhatship). "Sena" refers to the army of defilements such as lust (*rāga*) and so forth.
"Piyasātarūpa" is a name thus acquired because it arises with respect to objects that are of a pleasant and agreeable nature.
"Alone, meditating, I realized bliss": having thus conquered the army of defilements, I, being all alone, while meditating, realized bliss.
I have realized it. "They can bear witness" means they have attained the state of being witnesses; [the phrase] "a Dharma-witness" refers to one who bears witness to the Dharma.
"There is no friendship for me with anyone" means that I have no so-called friendship with anyone whatsoever.
"Sister, some recluses and brahmins, having produced a self, claim: 'The earth-kasiṇa attainment is the supreme goal,'" refers to those for whom the earth-kasiṇa attainment is the highest limit.
Taking it as "the supreme goal," they were reborn. "To whatever extent, sister, there is the perfection of the earth-kasiṇa attainment" means:

to whatever extent there is the highest limit of the earth-kasiṇa attainment. "The Blessed One directly knew that" means: the Blessed One directly knew it by means of direct knowledge-wisdom (*abhiññā-paññā*).
"He saw the gratification" means: he saw the truth of the origin (*samudaya-sacca*). "He saw the danger" means: he saw the truth of suffering (*dukkha-sacca*).
"He saw the escape" means he saw the truth of cessation (*nirodha-sacca*). "He saw the knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path" means he saw the truth of the path (*magga-sacca*).
"The attainment of the goal": because these four truths were seen, there was the attainment of the goal known as arahantship;
it is the peace of the heart through the subsiding of all distress and fever.
7. Commentary on the First Mahāpaṇha Sutta 27.

Regarding the seventh [verse]: "Abhijānātha" means "having fully known," that is, having made it manifest through direct experience, "abide. "Abhiññāya" means "having fully known. "Idha" means "by this.
Or, "dhammadesanā" refers to the teaching of the Dhamma; that is to say, by this teaching of the Dhamma of the ascetic Gotama.

They say, "Let some distinction be stated regarding our own teaching of the Dhamma, or the teaching of the Dhamma of the ascetic Gotama, in comparison with ours—what indeed could that be? The same method applies to the second phrase as well.
Thus, like gold broken in the middle, they [compare] their own tenets with the Dispensation (sāsana) by means of mere words.
They set it down as being of equal weight. "Neither did they rejoice" means they did not accept it, thinking, "It is so.

"Nor did they reject" means they did not oppose it, thinking, "It is not so. Why? It is said that, knowing that "the followers of other sects are like the blind—they might speak either knowingly or unknowingly," they did not rejoice.
"‘They will not master it’ means they will not be able to explain it after having mastered it.

‘And further distress’ means that because they do not master it, they will encounter even greater suffering beyond that. For suffering arises for those who are unable to explain after having mastered [the teaching].
In the phrase ‘as if, monks, in what is not their domain,’ *taṃ* here is merely a particle; *yathā* is a word expressing a reason."
The meaning is that they have asked questions concerning what is not their proper domain.
Or, "having heard from here" means having heard from this teaching of mine. "From here" means from the Tathāgata or from the disciples of the Tathāgata.
"One would satisfy" means one would please; he shows that there is no way to satisfy [him] otherwise.
"Ekadhamme" means "in one dhamma. By this, the summary (uddesa) is shown. Further on, by the question "In which one dhamma?
the inquiry (pañha) is shown. "All beings subsist by nutriment"—this, however, is the explanation (veyyākaraṇa) here.

The same method applies to the others as well. But in such passages as "becoming completely disenchanted," etc., "disenchanted" refers to one who is becoming disenchanted through the contemplation of disenchantment by way of the correct cause and method.

Becoming weary, becoming dispassionate through the contemplation of fading away (*virāgānupassanā*), and making an effort for liberation through the contemplation of reflection (*paṭisaṅkhānupassanā*), he is being liberated;
or, the meaning is that he is being liberated by way of resolute confidence (*adhimokkha*) and is forming a firm conviction.

Having delimited [existence] by means of its arising and passing away, he is one who correctly sees the limits through the vision of the past and future ends. *Sammadaṭṭhaṃ*... [meaning "the rightly seen"].

"Having fully realized" means having approached correctly with knowledge for the sake of what is shared [with all beings]. "He becomes one who makes an end of suffering" means he becomes one who makes a limit and a boundary to the entire suffering of saṃsāra.
"All beings" means all beings in all states of existence, such as the sense-sphere existence and so forth, and the single-aggregate existence and so forth. "Sustained by nutriment" means...
"Those whose maintenance is by means of nutriment" are called *āhāraṭṭhitikā*. Thus, for all beings, nutriment is the single phenomenon that serves as the cause of their maintenance;
[the phrase refers to] within that one phenomenon. But if this is so, does it not contradict what was stated:

"The non-percipient beings are without root-cause, without nutriment, without contact," and so forth? It does not contradict it. For in their case, meditative absorption (*jhāna*) serves as nutriment.
Even if this were so, it might be argued that this contradicts the statement: “Bhikkhus, there are these four nutriments. But this too does not contradict it.

For in that sutta, phenomena characterized by the function of nutriment are called “nutriments” in an absolute sense (nippariyāya), whereas here, in a figurative sense (pariyāya), a condition is called a “nutriment.
Indeed, a condition must be obtained for all phenomena; and whatever fruit [arises], its condition...
It generates [them] and brings them forth; therefore it is called "nutriment" (*āhāra*). For this very reason it was said:

"Bhikkhus, I say that ignorance also has nutriment, not that it is without nutriment. And what, bhikkhus, is the nutriment for ignorance? It should be said: the five hindrances. This is what is intended here.
For when this nutriment as a condition is grasped, both the figurative nutriment and the non-figurative nutriment are included.
Everything is indeed included. In that context, nutriment as a condition is found in the state of non-percipient beings (*asaññī-bhava*).

For when the Buddha had not yet appeared, those who had gone forth in other religious orders performed preliminary work on the wind-kasina, attained the fourth jhāna, and upon emerging from it, [thought]: "Alas, this mind!"
"Intelligence is this mind; indeed, the mere absence of mind is good. For it is by depending on the mind that suffering conditioned by killing, binding, and so forth arises.

If the mind were absent, such things would not exist. Having thus developed conviction and preference, they pass away without falling away from their jhāna and are reborn in the non-percipient realm (*asaññībhava*).
Whatever posture was adopted by each individual while in the human world, [that remains their mode of being there].
Having been reborn with that mode of deportment, he remains for five hundred eons appearing like a mental form (*cittarūpa*).
For such a duration, he is as if asleep. Even for such beings, nutriment by way of conditions is obtainable;
for whatever jhāna they have developed to be reborn in, that very state becomes their nutriment. It is just like an arrow shot by the force of a bowstring.
As long as the force of the impulse exists, they continue to move. Likewise, as long as the condition for meditative absorption (jhāna) exists, they remain.

When that has ceased, they fall like an arrow whose momentum is exhausted. At the time of their passing away, that physical body of theirs vanishes, and sense-sphere perception (kāmāvacara-saññā) arises;
by the arising of that perception, those devas are known to have passed away from that realm.
But as for those denizens of hell who are said to subsist neither on the fruit of emergence nor on the fruit of merit, what is their nutriment?
Their nutriment is karma alone. Is it not to be said that there are five nutriments, or that there are not five?
Has it not been stated that "a condition is a nutriment"? Therefore, by whatever karma they are reborn in hell, [that is their nutriment].
That very [matter] becomes their nutriment because it is a condition for their maintenance. It is with reference to this that it was said:
"And one does not die so long as that evil kamma has not been exhausted.
Furthermore, no dispute should be raised here even regarding edible food; for even the saliva arising in the mouth is [a form of nutriment] for them.
It performs the function of nutriment. For in hell, saliva, being experienced as painful, serves as a condition; in heaven, it is experienced as pleasant.

Thus, in the sensual realm (*kāmabhava*), there are four nutriments in the direct sense; in the fine-material and immaterial realms (*rūpārūpabhava*), excluding the non-percipient beings, there are three;
and for the non-percipient beings as well as the rest, there is the nutriment that is a condition. In this manner, all beings subsist by means of nutriment.
They should be understood as follows. In this context, the four nutriments or whatever condition-nutriment there may be is the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*);

the prior craving that gives rise to the nutriment is the truth of the origin (*samudayasacca*); the non-occurrence of both is the truth of cessation (*nirodhasacca*); and the wisdom that understands cessation is the truth of the path (*maggasacca*).
In this manner, the application should be made according to the Four Noble Truths in all sections.
8. Commentary on the Second Discourse on the Great Questions (Dutiyamahāpañhasutta).
28. "In Kajaṅgalā" means in the city named Kajaṅgalā. "The people of Kajaṅgalā" refers to those residing in Kajaṅgalā.
"Regarding the great questions" means regarding questions that encompass great meanings. "As it appears to me here" means as it presents itself to me in this context.
"One whose mind is rightly well-developed" means one whose mind has been thoroughly developed by way of this cause and method. "This indeed is its meaning":

although the Blessed One answered questions such as "four things" and so forth by way of the method beginning with "four nutriments," nevertheless, when the four nutriments are fully understood, the four foundations of mindfulness are developed; and in those [foundations of mindfulness]...
When these are developed, the four nutriments are indeed fully understood. Therefore, due to the elegance of the teaching, there is only a difference in the phrasing here;
the meaning, however, is one and the same. This same method applies to the faculties and so forth as well. Hence it was said: "This is precisely its meaning.
For in terms of meaning, both of these are like gold that has been split down the middle.

9. Commentary on the First Kosala Sutta 29. In the ninth [sutta], "yāvatā" means as many as there are. "Kāsikosalā" refers to the districts of Kāsi and Kosala. "Attheva aññathattan" means that there is indeed "aññathatta" (alteration) of what is established;
it truly exists. "Atthi vipariṇāmo" means that there is indeed "vipariṇāma" (transformation), which includes death as well. In that too...

"He becomes disenchanted" means he grows weary even of that which has arisen as a success. "He becomes dispassionate toward the highest" means he becomes dispassionate toward the pinnacle of success, namely the status of King of Kosala.
"How much more so toward the inferior" means, even sooner, toward the inferior five strands of sensual pleasure belonging to ordinary humans.
"Mind-made" means produced by means of meditative absorption (*jhāna*). "Of Benares" means arisen in Benares. It is said that therein...
The cotton is soft; the spinners and weavers are skilled; and the water is pure and smooth.
"Polished on both sides" means it appears smooth, soft, and glossy on both surfaces. The four paths of practice are explained as being a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane.

Among the perceptions, the first is a perception of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), the second is a perception of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), and the third is a supramundane perception (*lokuttara*).

The fourth is the perception of the base of nothingness. Since that perception is described as "the foremost" (*agga*), and there is no further designation of perception beyond it, it is therefore called "the foremost.
"Of outsiders" means those who proceed outside the Teaching. "Neither shall I be, nor shall there be for me" refers to if I [had been] in the past...
"I shall not be; even now this selfhood of mine would not exist.

"I shall not be, nothing shall be mine"—if one thinks thus, "I shall not exist in the future, and nothing that constitutes a fetter shall arise for me," one becomes dispassionate toward the "foremost.

One becomes dispassionate toward the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*). For here, the state of peace (*santatā*) of Nibbāna is considered the "foremost" in contrast to the view of annihilationism.

"Ultimate purity of the goal" (*paramatthavisuddhi*) means the purity of the supreme goal; this is a designation for the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*).

For the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*) is called "foremost" because it is the basis for insight (*vipassanā*), while the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is so called because of its long duration.
"Supreme Nibbāna in this very life" (*paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbāna*) means the supreme Nibbāna within this very personal existence (*attabhāva*).
"Deliverance through non-clinging" (*anupādā-vimokkho*) means the deliverance of the mind by not grasping with the four kinds of clinging; this is a name for Arahantship.
"Full understanding" (*pariññā*) means transcendence. In this regard, the Blessed One demonstrates full understanding of sensual pleasures by means of the first jhāna;
he demonstrates full understanding of material forms by means of the formless-sphere attainments; and he demonstrates full understanding of feelings by means of Nirvana, which is free from clinging.
For Nibbāna is indeed called the full understanding of feelings because of the abandoning of all that is felt. "Parinibbāna through non-clinging" means parinibbāna without conditions.

Now, while speaking this sutta, the Blessed One saw five hundred bhikkhus oppressed by dissatisfaction and spoke it for the purpose of dispelling their dissatisfaction. And they, having dispelled that dissatisfaction...
Having directed their knowledge according to the teaching, they became stream-enterers; later, by increasing their insight, they attained arahantship.
10. Commentary on the Second Kosala Sutta: 30.
In the tenth [verse], "he returned from the battle" means he returned from the war. "He had obtained his desire" refers to the Great King of Kosala.
It is said that when [Bimbisāra] gave his daughter in marriage, he granted her a village in Kāsī called Satasahassuṭṭhāna, situated between the two kingdoms.
When Ajātasattu had his father killed, his mother also died shortly thereafter from the grief of separation from the king.
Thereupon, King Pasenadi of Kosala thought, "Ajātasattu has killed both his mother and father; my father’s..."
“Village” means he waged war for its sake; Ajātasattu also [waged war] for the sake of that village, thinking, “It belongs to my mother.
Both the uncle and the nephew arrayed a fourfold army and went to battle. Therein, Pasenadi of Kosala was defeated by Ajātasattu twice and entered his own city.
On the third occasion, [he thought], “How indeed might I achieve victory?”
Having understood the manner in which he could be countered through eavesdropping, saying, "He might [succeed]," he drew up a battle formation, surrounded him on both flanks, and captured Ajātasattu.
At that very moment, because his objective was achieved, he became known as "one who has attained his purpose" (*laddhādhippāya*).
He went toward the monastery; having established his victorious headquarters outside the city, [he waited] until they had decorated the city.

“I shall pay homage to the One of Ten Powers before [the city]. For from the moment of entering the city, there is much distraction,” he said, and surrounded by his retinue of ministers, he set out for the monastery and entered it. At what time did he enter?

It was when the monks had returned from their almsround, after the Fully Enlightened One had given them exhortation and entered the Fragrant Chamber, and the Saṅgha of monks had also received their exhortation.
Having accepted [the invitation], they went each to their respective night-quarters and day-quarters. When do they walk back and forth (*caṅkamanti*)? At what time do they walk?
It is for the purpose of dispelling the sloth and torpor caused by rich food, or because they are practitioners of daytime meditation (*divāpadhānika*).
For such persons, having walked back and forth after the meal, bathed, and allowed the body to take on its natural temperature, they sit down.
The minds of those performing the duties of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*) become one-pointed. As for the phrase "those monks": it is said that he, thinking, "Where is the Teacher?

Where is the Sugata? I shall enter only after asking from cell to cell," was looking about when he saw two *paṃsukūlika* monks walking on the great cloister-walk like forest elephants; he then approached them.
He arrived. It was with reference to him that this was said. "Desirous of seeing" means wishing to behold.
"The dwelling" (vihāra) refers to the Perfumed Chamber (gandhakuṭi); thus they spoke. "Without haste" means not hurried;

it means placing his foot with due measure at each step, performing the proper etiquette, and not disturbing the well-swept sand which resembled a network of pearls or a sinduvāra flower. "The porch" (ālinda)—
"Pamukhaṃ" means the front. "Aggaḷaṃ" means the door-panel (the door). "Ukkāsitvā" means having made the sound of knocking.
"Ākoṭehi" means strike it slightly with the tip of your fingernail near the keyhole; this is what is meant. It is said that non-humans knock too high up, while long-tailed snakes knock too low.
Without knocking in those places, one should knock in the middle, near the keyhole; this is the rule for knocking at the door.
They say: "The Blessed One opened the door. It was not that the Blessed One rose and opened the door himself; rather, he extended his hand, saying, "Open it.

Then, thinking, "For many millions of eons you have been giving gifts, yet you have never performed the act of opening a door with your own hands," the door opened by itself. And that occurred because of the Blessed One’s mental power.
It was opened; therefore, it is appropriate to say, "The Blessed One opened the door.
"An offering of loving-kindness" means a physical or verbal offering associated with loving-kindness (*mettā*). Regarding "gratitude":
formerly this king had a stout body and ate a *doṇa* measure of cooked rice. Then, day after day, the Blessed One gave him only a small amount...
For the purpose of reducing [intake] slightly:
“For a person who is always mindful,
who knows the proper measure regarding food obtained...”
“Sensations will arise for one whose body is frail;
he ages slowly while preserving his life.
Having given this exhortation, [the Blessed One] remained in this instruction, reducing [his intake] little by little day after day, and gradually...
He remained content with a mere measure of boiled rice in a hollowed palm; his limbs also became thin yet firm. Referring to the benefit bestowed upon him by the Blessed One, he said:
"Venerable sir, it is because I perceive my gratitude and thankfulness.

"In the noble knowledge" means in the path accompanied by insight (*vipassanā*). "Of increased virtue" means one whose virtue has grown. "Noble virtue" means [virtue] distinct from that of ordinary worldlings.
"Endowed with virtues": "possessed of wholesome virtue" means endowed with blameless virtues.

"Forest-dweller": he was born in the forest when being born; he attained full awakening in the forest when attaining enlightenment; and even while dwelling in the fragrant chamber—which is like a celestial palace—he dwelt as if in the forest itself.
It is with this in mind that he spoke thus. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
The Third Chapter: The Mahāvagga.
4. The Chapter on Upāli.
1. Commentary on the Upāli Sutta.

31. Regarding the first [offense] of the fourth [Saṅghādisesa], concerning the phrases beginning with "for the welfare of the Saṅgha" (*saṅghasuṭṭhutāya*): "welfare of the Saṅgha" (*saṅghasuṭṭhutā*) means the state of being well-disposed toward the Saṅgha;
it is the manner of accepting the words, as in the expression "Very well, Lord" (*suṭṭhu, bhante*), similar to the usage found in the phrase "Very well, O gods" (*suṭṭhu, devā*).
And for one who accepts the word of the Tathāgata, that leads to their welfare and happiness for a long time.

Therefore, in order to show the fault in not accepting and the benefit in accepting the Saṅgha’s words of “Very well, venerable sir,” and to reveal the meaning that this was prescribed for the purpose of receiving those words—not by force or by overpowering—he said:
“for the welfare of the Saṅgha. “For the comfort of the Saṅgha” means for the state of ease and for the communal life of the Saṅgha.
The meaning is: "for the sake of dwelling in happiness.
Regarding "for the restraint of difficult persons": "difficult persons" refers to immoral individuals who, even when being exhorted, enter upon [wrongdoing] with difficulty;
or those who, while committing a transgression or having committed one, feel no shame. It is for their restraint.

For if those training rules did not exist, they might harass the Saṅgha, saying: "What have you seen? What have you heard? What have we done? On what basis, having charged us with what offense, do you seek to restrain us?
But when the training rules exist, the Saṅgha, having pointed out the training rule, will restrain them in accordance with the Dhamma. Therefore it was said:
“For the restraint of persons who are difficult to correct.
“For the well-behaved” means for the sake of the comfortable dwelling of monks of amiable character.

For monks of amiable character, not knowing what should and should not be done, what is blameworthy and blameless, or the proper time and boundary, become weary while striving for the fulfillment of the three trainings.
But those who, having understood what is blameworthy and blameless, as well as the proper time and the boundary, strive for the fulfillment of the training, do not become weary.

Therefore, the laying down of these training rules leads precisely to their comfortable dwelling. Or rather, the restraint of individuals who are difficult to manage is itself their comfortable dwelling;
for, depending on an immoral person, the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies cannot take place.
[The monks] remain [idle], communal acts (*saṅghakamma*) do not proceed, there is no harmony, and the monks, being distracted, are unable to apply themselves to the recitation and other duties.
However, when those of immoral conduct have been restrained, all this affliction ceases;
consequently, the well-behaved monks dwell in comfort. Thus, [it is said]: "for the comfortable dwelling of well-behaved monks."
Here, the meaning should be understood in two ways.

Regarding "for the restraint of taints pertaining to the present life" (*diṭṭhadhammikānaṃ āsavānaṃ saṃvarāya*): taints pertaining to the present life are those to be experienced in this very existence by one who stands in non-restraint;
they include being struck with the hand, struck with a staff, struck with a weapon, having hands cut off, having feet cut off, ill repute, and remorse.
The meaning is: for the sake of the specific kinds of suffering, for their restraint, covering, and blocking the path by which they arrive.

Regarding "those pertaining to future lives" (*samparāyikānaṃ*): the so-called "taints pertaining to future lives" refers to the specific kinds of suffering to be experienced in the hells and other realms in a future existence, rooted in evil deeds committed by one who stands in non-restraint;
[the training is] for the purpose of counteracting and pacifying them.

"Those who lack confidence": for when a training rule has been laid down, there are wise people who lack confidence because they either know of the laying down of the training rule, or because they have seen monks practicing according to what was laid down. They think:
"Indeed, those things in the world which are grounds for the common people's passion, hatred, and delusion—far removed from these, these recluses dwell, having abstained from them."
"Alas, they are performing what is difficult!"—thus they develop confidence upon seeing the manuscript of the Vinaya Piṭaka, like those brahmins who hold wrong views but possess Vedic knowledge.
Therefore it is said: "for the sake of inspiring confidence in those who lack it.

Regarding "those who have confidence": even those sons of good family who have confidence in the Teaching, once they have learned the formulation of the training rules or [have understood] how they are formulated...
Seeing monks practicing accordingly, they become increasingly confident, thinking: "Oh, these venerable ones perform what is difficult;
they maintain the restraint of the Vinaya by taking but one meal throughout their lives. Therefore it is said: "for the increase of those who have confidence.

Regarding "for the stability of the true Dhamma": the true Dhamma is threefold—the true Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyatti), the true Dhamma of practice (paṭipatti), and the true Dhamma of realization (adhigama).

In this context, the entire word of the Buddha is called the True Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-saddhamma*). The thirteen ascetic qualities (*dhutaguṇa*), as well as conduct, restraint, virtue, concentration, and insight—this is called the True Dhamma of practice (*paṭipatti-saddhamma*).
The nine supramundane states (*navalokuttara-dhamma*) are called the True Dhamma of realization (*adhigama-saddhamma*).

All of these exist because, when there is the formal proclamation of the training rules (*sikkhāpada-paññatti*), monks [observe] both the training rule and its analysis (*vibhaṅga*) for the purpose of illustrating its meaning.

Furthermore, they master the word of the Buddha; and by practicing according to what has been prescribed, fulfilling that practice, they attain the supramundane Dhamma to be attained through practice.
Therefore, through the laying down of the training rules, the True Dhamma endures for a long time. Hence it is said: "for the endurance of the True Dhamma."

"For the support of the Vinaya" means that when a training rule (sikkhāpada) has been laid down, the fourfold Vinaya—namely, the Vinaya of restraint (saṃvara-vinaya), the Vinaya of abandonment (pahāna-vinaya), the Vinaya of settling disputes (samatha-vinaya), and the Vinaya of formal enactment (paññatti-vinaya)—is supported and well-sustained. Therefore it is said:
"for the support of the Vinaya."
2. Commentary on the Sutta on the Suspension of the Pātimokkha (Pātimokkhaṭṭhapanāsutta) 32.

Regarding the second [case]: "One who has committed a pārājika offense" means one who has fallen into an offense involving defeat. "The discussion regarding the pārājika is unfinished" means that having begun the discussion in this way—"Has such-and-such a person committed a pārājika offense, or not?"—it remains uncompleted. This same method applies everywhere. 3.
Commentary on the Sutta on the Committee (Ubbāhikāsutta)
33. "In the third [case], by means of a committee" means for the purpose of taking up a legal issue that has arisen and, having been set aside or extracted from the Saṅgha, resolving it.
"But he stands firm in the Vinaya" means he is established in the characteristics of the Vinaya.
"Irreversible" means he does not relinquish his own position merely because of another's words. "Capable" means capable both by the power of the body and by the power of knowledge.
"Endowed with. "To inform" means to make known. "To explain" means to make clearly understood. "To cause to reflect" means to cause to look upon. "To cause to behold" means to cause to see.
"To inspire confidence" means to produce confidence. "Legal issue" (*adhikaraṇa*) refers to the fourfold [issues], beginning with the legal issue of dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*).
"Origin of the legal issue" refers to the causes of the legal issue, such as the root of dispute. "Cessation of the legal issue" refers to the cessation of those legal issues.
"Quiescence" (*vūpasama*) refers to the sevenfold method for settling legal disputes (*adhikaraṇa-samatha*), which is the path leading to the cessation of such disputes.
4. Commentary on the Discourse on Ordination (*Upasampadā-sutta*):

In the fourth [section], "discontent" (*anabhirati*) means a state of longing or dissatisfaction. "To dispel" (*vūpakāsituṃ*) means to remove it. Regarding "higher virtue" (*adhisīla*), this same method applies to the mind (*citta*) and wisdom (*paññā*) as well.
7. Commentary on the Saṅghabhedasutta 37.
"By seven grounds" means by seven reasons. "They draw away" means they pull the assembly toward themselves, disentangle it, and draw it off to one side.
