"They draw apart" means they pull excessively; they act in such a way that [the assembly] becomes completely separated.
"Performing separate acts" means performing sangha-acts individually.
9–10. Commentary on the Two Ānanda Suttas, 39–40.
In the ninth [verse], "lasting for an eon" refers to the cause for remaining in hell for the duration of a lifespan. "Produces evil" means...
He incurs evil. "One bound for the states of misery" (*āpāyika*) means one who is destined to go to the states of misery. "One bound for hell" (*nerayika*) means one who will be reborn in hell.

"One who delights in factionalism" (*vaggarata*) means one who delights in schism. "He falls away from the security from bondage" (*yogakkhemā padhaṃsati*) means he falls away and departs from the state of Arahantship, which is secure from the bonds.
In the tenth [chapter], "assistance" (*anuggaha*) refers to mutual support and assistance. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.

5. The Section on Abuse. 4.
Commentary on the Kusināra Sutta.
44. In the fourth [section] of the fifth [chapter], "In Kusinārā" refers to the city of that name.

It is called *baliharaṇa* because offerings (*bali*) are brought there for the sake of the deities; [it means] "in that *baliharaṇa*. Regarding the phrases "unblemished, with meatless [meat]," and so forth:
by whatever [means] he has been struck, or medical treatments and the like have been performed, his bodily conduct [is affected] by things such as gadflies.
It is "perforated" (*chiddo*) like a palm leaf that has been gnawed through, and it is "defiled" (*paṭimaṃso*) because it can be grasped anywhere and dragged along;
the opposite of this is called "unperforated" (*acchiddo*) and "undefiled" (*appaṭimaṃso*).
As for verbal conduct, however, it is "perforated" and "defiled" by way of false speech, malicious speech, slander, groundless charges, and so forth.
It is "reversed," "unbroken," and "without flaw. Regarding "my mind is loving" (*mettaṃ nu kho me cittaṃ*):

having severed the impediments through application to the cultivation of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna-bhāvanā*), my mind has attained loving-kindness. "Free from malice" (*anāghāta*) means devoid of resentment; the meaning is that resentment has been destroyed by suppression (*vikkhambhana*).
"Where was this spoken?"—in which city was this training rule (*sikkhāpada*) spoken?
Regarding the phrases "I shall speak at the proper time" and so forth: one who reproves after having requested an opportunity from another is said to speak at the proper time.

One who reproves in the midst of the Saṅgha, or in the midst of a group, or in places such as the hall for voting slips, the hall for deliberation, the refectory, the path to alms-gathering, or the assembly hall, or at a moment when surrounded by attendants, is said to speak at the improper time. Speaking with truth means speaking what is factual.

Regarding the term *nāma*: when one says, "This appearance of yours is like that of a youth, an elder, one who wanders in assemblies, a wearer of rag-robes, or a preacher of the Dhamma," one speaks harshly.
However, if one speaks based on a specific reason, saying, "Venerable sir, you have the appearance of an elder;
you have the appearance of one who wanders in assemblies; you have the appearance of a wearer of rag-robes; you have the appearance of a preacher of the Dhamma," [one does not speak harshly].

"He speaks gently" means he speaks with gentleness. "He speaks for the benefit [of others]" means speaking by way of a specific purpose that is connected with the welfare of others. "I will speak with a mind of loving-kindness, not with a mind of hatred" means:
having established a mind of loving-kindness (*mettacitta*), I will speak; I will not speak while being possessed of a corrupt mind. 5.
Commentary on the Discourse on Entering the Royal Palace.
45. "In the fifth [case], 'done or will be done' means they have committed or will commit an act of sexual misconduct.

'Jewel' (ratana) refers to anything among the jewel-treasures, such as the mani-jewel and so forth. 'Seeks' (pattheti) means he desires to kill. 'Crowded with elephants' (hatthisambādha) means crowded by elephants.
Or there is the reading 'crushed by elephants' (hatthisammadda); its meaning is: 'wherein there is a crushing by elephants.'"
The crushing of elephants. The same method applies to the remaining [perils] as well. Regarding "forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles that are provocative":
these forms and so forth, which give rise to lust, are present there in their entirety.
6. Commentary on the Sakka Sutta.
46. In the sixth [verse], *sokasabhaye* means "in that which is accompanied by sorrow. Alternatively, there is the reading *sokabhaye*, which has the same meaning.
The same method applies to the second word as well. *Yena kenaci kammaṭṭhānena* means "by whatever work," such as agriculture, trade, and so forth.
*Anāpajja akusalam* means "without falling into any unwholesome state. *Nibbiseyya* means "one would produce" or "one would accumulate."
*Dakkho* means clever. *Uṭṭhānasampanno* means endowed with the energy of exertion. *Alaṃ vacanāya* means fit for discourse.
*Ekantasukhapaṭisaṃvedī vihareyya* means he would dwell experiencing exclusively physical and mental happiness through knowledge.
*Anicca* [means] because of not existing after having come to be. *Tuccha* means devoid of essence. *Musā* means [devoid of] permanence, beauty, and pleasure.
"Though they appear as if being eaten, they do not exist in that way; thus, they are false (*musā*). 'Subject to decease' (*mosadhammā*) means having the nature of perishing.
Therefore, he demonstrates that suffering arises dependent upon them. Here, however, *vo* is merely a particle.

Or, "one who has entered the stream" (*sotāpanna*) is "unfailing" (*apaṇṇaka*), meaning one who is certainly and unerringly a stream-enterer. He too produces meditative absorption (*jhāna*) and [is reborn in] the Brahma-world."
Or, having gone [to the Brahma-world], he might dwell experiencing absolute happiness in the six celestial realms of sensual pleasure.
In this sutta, the Teacher spoke of the virtue of the eightfold uposatha.
7. Commentary on the Mahāli Sutta.

47. "Misdirected" (*micchāpaṇihita*) means wrongly placed. "Unrighteous conduct and uneven conduct" (*adhammacariyā-visamacariyā*) refers to conduct termed unrighteous by way of the unwholesome courses of action (*akusala-kammapatha*);
the other [type of conduct] should be understood by way of the wholesome courses of action. Thus, here only the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) is discussed.
8. Commentary on the *Pabbajita-abhiṇha-sutta* (The Discourse on the Frequent Visits of the One Gone Forth).
48. In the eighth [verse], "by one who has gone forth" means by one who, having abandoned the household life, has entered the going-forth (pabbajjā) into the Teaching.
"Frequently" means constantly, repeatedly; it should be reviewed, observed, and examined.
"Discoloration" (vevaṇṇiyaṃ) means the state of being discolored. Furthermore, this discoloration is twofold: discoloration of the body and discoloration of the requisites.

In this context, the discoloration of the body should be understood by way of shaving off the hair and beard. For previously, even though one had been dressed in garments of various colors and fine textures,
had eaten food of various superior flavors from vessels of gold and silver, had reclined or sat upon excellent couches and seats in the inner chamber,
and had prepared medicinal treatments with ghee, fresh butter, and so forth, from the time of going forth...
One should wear robes that have been cut into strips and sewn together, dyed with a decoction of kasāva;
one should eat mixed rice from either an iron bowl or an earthenware bowl; one should lie down on beds such as the root of a tree, using a spread of muñja grass and so forth;
one should sit on a piece of hide, a mat of split bamboo, or similar items; and one must prepare medicine from fermented urine and other such substances. Thus it is here.
The description of the requisites should be understood in this way. For one who reflects thus, anger and conceit are abandoned.
"My livelihood is dependent on others" means that my life, sustained by the four requisites, is bound to others and reliant upon them.
For one who reflects thus, the livelihood becomes purified, and alms-food is honored among the four requisites.

There is no such thing as "enjoyment without reflection. Regarding the thought, "I must adopt a different deportment," there is a manner of walking that involves thrusting out the chest, holding up the neck, and moving with a graceful, unsteady gait;
[the monk thinks], "A different deportment from this must be adopted by me—one with tranquil faculties and a tranquil mind, looking only a yoke's length ahead, like a water-cart on uneven ground."
One should reflect: "I must go with a slow, measured pace and stride.
For one who reflects in this way, the posture becomes appropriate and the three trainings are fulfilled. *Kaccinukho* is a combination of particles used in the sense of a specific characteristic.

*Attā* refers to the mind. *Na upavadati sīlato* means that he does not criticize his virtue on account of virtue, [thinking], "Your virtue is impure. He does not find fault with the condition of virtue.
For when one reflects in this way, a sense of shame (*hirī*) arises within; that shame accomplishes restraint at the three doors.

Restraint at the three doors constitutes the fourfold purification of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*). Established in the fourfold purification of virtue, one increases insight (*vipassanā*) and attains *arahantship*.
"Wise fellow-celibates after having investigated" refers to wise fellow-celibates.
Having reflected thus. For one who reflects in this way, moral dread (*ottappa*) is established toward external things;
it should be understood through the immediately following method that this brings about restraint at the three doors.
"Separation" and "disappearance": separation from birth and disappearance through death. For one who reflects in this way...
There is no lack of restraint at the three doors; mindfulness of death (*maraṇassati*) is well-established. Regarding the phrases "I am the owner of my karma" and so forth:
"owner of karma" (*kammassaka*) means that karma is one's own, belonging to oneself.
"Karmic inheritance" (*kammadāyāda*) means that the fruit to be given by karma is the inheritance (*dāya*); one who takes that inheritance is a karmic heir. Karma is my source, my cause.
Kamma is my womb. "Kamma is my kinsman and relative" means one has kamma as a kinsman (*kammabandhu*).
"Kamma is my refuge and support" means one has kamma as a resort (*kammapaṭisaraṇo*). "I shall be its heir" means I shall be the heir to that kamma, the receiver of the fruit bestowed by it.
Thus, for one who reflects upon this ownership of action (*kammassakata*), the performance of evil deeds indeed does not [occur].
"How are my days and nights passing? Is it for me while performing my duties, or while not performing them;
while reciting the Buddha’s word, or while not reciting it;
or while applying wise attention, or while not applying it?"—in this way he considers, "How are my days and nights passing?"
The meaning is "they turn back. For one who reflects in this way, heedfulness (*appamāda*) becomes fulfilled.
"I delight in empty huts" means: having become alone in secluded places during all postures, does one indeed take delight?
For one who reflects in this way, physical seclusion (*kāyaviveka*) becomes fulfilled. "Superhuman states" (*uttarimanussadhamma*) refers to [states] beyond those of ordinary humans.

The meaning is: "Does there exist, or does there indeed exist, in my own continuum, a state superior to and more distinguished than the human quality—namely, the qualities such as *jhāna* belonging to those who have become sublime humans, both meditators and noble ones—or even the human quality consisting of the ten courses of wholesome action?

"Exalted distinction of noble knowledge and vision" (*alamariyañāṇadassanaviseso*) refers to the vast and supramundane wisdom; it is "knowledge" (*ñāṇa*) in the sense of understanding, and [it is] "vision" (*dassana*) by way of the eye.
Because it makes the Dhamma directly present as if it were already seen, it is "vision" in the sense of seeing; thus it is "knowledge-vision.

It is "noble knowledge-vision" because it is noble, pure, and supreme. It is "one possessed of sufficient noble knowledge-vision" because he possesses here that noble knowledge-vision which is sufficient, adequate, and capable of destroying the defilements.
This refers to the superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma) distinguished by the jhānas and so forth.
"Superiority in noble knowledge and vision" (*alamariyañāṇadassanaviseso*) means that it is both "noble knowledge and vision" and "superiority," hence "superiority in noble knowledge and vision.
Alternatively, the very pure knowledge and vision capable of destroying the defilements is itself the "superiority," hence "superiority in noble knowledge and vision.
"Attained" (*adhigato*) means: "Has this been acquired by me? "I am one who has attained" (*soham*) means: "I am that person who has acquired that superiority. In the latter [verse]:
"At the time" means at the time when one is lying on the bed of death. "Questioned" means being asked by fellow celibates about the specific qualities he has attained.

"I shall not be dejected" means: "I shall not be one whose backbone has collapsed and who is devoid of spiritual luster. For one who reflects in this way, there is no such thing as a vain passing away.
9–10. Commentary on the *Sarīra*, *Attha*, *Dhamma*, and *Sutta* Suttas (49–50).

In the ninth [sutta], "leading to renewed existence" (*ponobbhavika*) means that which produces renewed existence. "Volitional formations of existence" (*bhava-saṅkhāra*) refers to the kamma that constructs existence.
In this sutta, only the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) is discussed. In the tenth [sutta], virtue, learning, energy, mindfulness, and wisdom are mixed with both mundane and supramundane qualities.
It has been explained. The remainder is clear in meaning throughout.
The fifth chapter on Abuse is finished.
The first fifty-section division is completed.

51–54. In the first [section] of the second [chapter], "skilled in the course of one's own mind" (*sacittapariyāyakusala*) means skilled in the various states of one's own consciousness.

"Stains" (*raja*) refers to adventitious defilements. "Blemishes" (*aṅgaṇa*) refers to those such as moles, black spots, and the like that arise thereon. "For the destruction of the taints" (*āsavānaṃ khayāya*) means for the sake of *arahantship*.

Herein, [it is] "without residue remaining" (*anupādisesa*). For one who has attained the state without residue remaining, all phenomena are said to have reached their final consummation.

9. Commentary on the *Pabbajjā-sutta*.
59. Ninthly, "therefore" means: because the goal of recluseship (*sāmaññattha*) is not accomplished for one whose mind is thus unaccustomed [to it], therefore [one should train].
"And so that our mind will become accustomed according to our going-forth" means: accustomed in a manner befitting the going-forth.
For whoever indeed goes forth does so having aspired to *arahantship*. Therefore, that mind which is for the sake of attaining *arahantship*...
"Familiarized and developed" should be understood as that which was familiarized at the time of going forth.
One should train oneself thus: "May my mind become such as this. "The even and uneven of the world" refers to the good conduct and misconduct of the world of beings (*sattaloka*).
"The existence and non-existence of the world" refers to its growth and destruction, as well as its prosperity and decline.

10. Commentary on the *Girimānandasutta*
60. "Out of compassion for the Elder Girimānanda" means out of regard for the Elder Girimānanda.

"Eye disease," and so forth, should be understood according to their physical basis (*vatthu*). For there is no such thing as "disease" in the case of the translucent matter (*pasāda*) that has been produced [at the sense bases].

"Ear disease" is a disease of the external ear. "Nasal catarrh" is a disease of the external nose. "Worms in the nails" is a disease in the places scratched by the nails. "Arising from bile" [and so forth].
Those arising from bile (*pitta-samuṭṭhitā*). It is said that there are thirty-two of them. The same method applies to those arising from phlegm (*semha*) and so forth.

Those born of seasonal change (*utu-pariṇāma-jāti*) are diseases produced by seasonal changes such as excessive heat or extreme cold. Those born of improper conduct (*visama-parihāra-jāti*) are those produced by improper conduct, such as standing or sitting for too long.
Those caused by external trauma (*opakkamikā*) are those produced by such means as execution or imprisonment. Those born of karmic fruition (*kamma-vipāka-jāti*)...
It is produced from the ripening of powerful kamma. It is "peaceful" (santa) because of the pacification of lust and other defilements. It is "sublime" (paṇīta) in the sense of being insatiable.
The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
Thus ends the first chapter, the Chapter on the Mind (Sacittavagga).
(7) 2. Yamaka-vagga 1.
Commentary on the *Avijjā-sutta* and others, §§61–62.

In the first [sutta] of the second [chapter], "with its nutriment" (*sāhāraṃ*) means "with its condition" (*sapaccayaṃ*). "Knowledge and liberation" (*vijjāvimuttiṃ*) refers to both the knowledge of the fruit (*phalañāṇa*) and the remaining associated mental states (*sampayuttadhamma*).
And "enlightenment factors" refers to the factors of the path. In the second [sutta], "of craving for existence" means of the aspiration for existence.

Thus, in both suttas it is the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) alone that is described; and herein, in the first sutta, the round rooted in ignorance is described, while in the second, the round rooted in craving is described.
3–4. Commentary on the *Niṭṭhaṅgata-sutta* and others (63–64).
In the third [sutta], "attained to the goal" (*niṭṭhaṃ gata*) means those who are free from doubt. Here, "the goal" (*niṭṭhā*) refers to final nibbāna in this very world.
"Having left here" (*idha vihāya*) means having departed from this world for the Suddhāvāsa Brahma-world. In the fourth [sutta], "those with verified confidence" (*aveccappasanna*).
They are endowed with immovable confidence. "Stream-enterers" (sotāpannā) means they have entered the stream of the Noble Path.
5–7. Commentary on the First Discourse on Happiness, etc. (Suttas 65–67).
In the fifth [discourse], happiness and suffering rooted in the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) are asked about; in the sixth, those rooted in the Dispensation (sāsana); in the seventh...
“Naḷakapāna” is the name of a town so designated because in the past, a troop of monkeys, abiding by the Bodhisatta’s advice, drank water from reeds at that location.
“Becoming silent, becoming silent”: in whichever direction he looked, it was entirely silent there. “Having looked around”: having looked here and there. “My back aches.”
Why was he ill? For while the Blessed One was exerting himself in the Great Struggle for six years, there was great physical suffering;
subsequently, in his later years, a wind ailment arose in his back.

It is impossible for anyone to remain free from even a slight affliction due to the postures of standing, sitting, and so forth, within a body that has been grasped by clinging. Even taking this into account, it was for the sake of making way for the Elder...
He spoke thus. Having spread out his outer robe (saṅghāṭi) and laid it over a suitable couch that had been prepared in a secluded place.
9–10. Commentary on the Two Discourses of the *Kathāvatthu*. 69–70.
Regarding the ninth [discourse], "animal talk" (*tiracchānakathā*): because it does not lead to the paths of heaven or liberation, it is like something belonging to the animal realm.

How so? In that regard, talk concerning kings—such as the discourse proceeding by way of [mentioning] Mahāsammata, Mandhātā, Dhammāsoka, and others, saying, "He was so great in power"—is called talk about kings.

The same method applies to talk about thieves and so forth. Among those, talk based on worldly attachment, such as "That king was handsome and beautiful to behold," constitutes frivolous chatter (*tiracchānakathā*); for even he was indeed so great in power.
However, when it occurs in the form, "He has reached destruction," it remains within the state of being a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).

Even regarding thieves, talk such as "Mūladeva was so powerful" or "Meghadeva was so powerful"—based on their deeds and saying, "Oh, what heroes!"—is merely worldly talk and thus frivolous chatter (*tiracchānakathā*).

Even regarding battles such as the Mahābhārata war, talk such as "So-and-so was killed by such-and-so in this way" or "So-and-so was pierced in that way" is likewise based solely on a delight in action.
Idle talk is talk concerning animals; however, when it proceeds with the thought, "Even they have surely passed away," it becomes a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) in every respect.

Furthermore, regarding food and so forth, it is not permissible to speak by way of relishing the taste of sensual pleasure, thinking, "We ate, we enjoyed, we drank, we consumed such beautiful, flavorful, and well-textured [food]," but it is permissible when it is purposeful.
It is appropriate to say, "In the past, we gave food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, and perfumes endowed with such qualities as beauty to those possessed of virtue,
and we made offerings at the cetiya.
Even in conversations regarding kinsmen and the like, one may say, "Our kinsmen were brave and capable," or "In the past, we [traveled] in such diverse vehicles..."

It is not permissible to say, "We have wandered," out of a sense of attachment (*assāda*); however, it may be said for a purposeful reason, such as, "Those relatives of ours have also met their end," or, "In the past, we gave such sandals to the Saṅgha.

Regarding talk about villages, it may be spoken by way of whether they are well-situated or ill-situated, or abundant in food or lacking in food, or [referring to] those who dwell in such-and-such a village...
It is not permissible to say, "They are brave and capable," merely by way of attachment (*assāda*);

however, it is permissible to say, "They are faithful and confident" or "They have reached destruction and passing away," provided one does so for a purposeful reason. The same principle applies to talk concerning cities, towns, and provinces.

Even regarding talk about women, it is not permissible to speak by way of attachment based on their complexion, shape, and so forth; rather, [one may say], "They are faithful and confident, [and have reached] destruction..."
The same applies to talk of heroes: it is not permissible to say, "The warrior named Nandamitta was a hero," by way of relishing [the past];
rather, it is permissible only in the manner of saying, "He was faithful; he has passed away.
Regarding talk of liquor, however, it is not permissible to speak of various kinds of intoxicants by way of relishing them in the Pāli; one must speak of them only by way of their danger (ādīnava).

It is permissible. Regarding talk about streets (*visikhākathā*), it is not permissible to speak with a sense of gratification, such as, “That street is well-settled,” “That street is ill-settled,” “They are brave,” or “They are capable”;
however, it is permissible to say, “They are faithful, confident, and have reached destruction [of the defilements].

Talk about a water-pot stand (*kumbhaṭṭhānakathā*) refers to talk about a peak, a place for water, or a bathing ford; or it refers to talk about a water-carrier woman (*kumbhadāsī*). That too, such as saying, “She is pleasing, skilled in dancing and singing,” is not permissible.
It is not appropriate [to speak] by way of gratification; it is only appropriate in the manner beginning with, "Faith is serene," and so forth.
"Talk about departed relatives" refers to talk concerning deceased kinsmen. The method of determination (*vinicchaya*) therein is the same as for talk concerning living kinsmen.
"Miscellaneous talk" refers to all other kinds of animal talk of various natures that are excluded from both the former and latter types of talk.
“Speculations about the world” (*lokakkhāyikā*) refers to such Lokāyata sophistry and contentious talk as: “By whom was this world created? “It was created by such-and-such a person.
“The crow is white because its bones are white; the crane is red because its blood is red,” and so forth.

“Speculations about the ocean” (*samuddakkhāyikā*) refers to [questions such as]: “Why is the ocean called ‘Sāgara’? “It is called ‘Sāgara’ because it was dug up by the god Sāgara; it was dug up (*khata*).”
Because it is communicated by means of a hand gesture such as "meti," talk that merely reports the ocean and so forth is useless talk about the ocean.

"Bhava" means growth; "abhava" means decline. Talk that proceeds by stating some such useless reason as "thus is existence" or "thus is non-existence" is called talk about existence and non-existence.
“By their own splendor they outshine the splendor of others; you should consume, seize, and overcome their splendor.
Regarding this, there is this story: A certain alms-collector asked a great elder, “Venerable sir, what do monks do when they are consuming splendor with splendor?
The elder replied, “Friend, it is just as if one were to place something in the sun and the shadow [of that object] were to fall beneath it.”
It does not descend; it goes only upwards—thus they act. "Ten grounds for praise" means ten reasons that bring about praise.
The rest is everywhere of obvious meaning.
This is the second chapter, the Yamaka-vagga.
(8) 3. The Chapter on Yearning (Ākaṅkhavagga). 1. Commentary on the Discourse on Yearning (Ākaṅkhasuttavaṇṇanā). 71.
Regarding the first [sutta] of the third [chapter]: "Possessed of virtue" (*sampannasīla*) means having perfected virtue, or the sense is "having become endowed with virtue."
In this regard, perfection of virtue arises through two causes: by seeing the danger in the failure of virtue and by seeing the benefit in the perfection of virtue.
Both of these have been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*.
Therein, after the Blessed One had indicated the fourfold purification of virtue with the words "possessed of perfected virtue," he stated, "restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha."
The Elder Sumana, who dwelt at Dīpa Vihāra, said that by this [passage] the Master has shown the precept of the foremost (jeṭṭhaka-sīla) in detail.
However, his pupil, the Elder Cūḷanāga, who was versed in the Three Piṭakas, said: "In both instances, the Blessed One spoke only of restraint according to the Pātimokkha.
For restraint according to the Pātimokkha alone is 'virtue' (sīla); as for the other three, they are merely mentioned as places where virtue exists."
Not granting that "it exists," he said: "What is called restraint of the faculties is merely the guarding of the six doors;

purity of livelihood is merely the arising of requisites through what is lawful and righteous; and dependence on requisites is merely the use of requisites obtained after reflecting, 'This is for this purpose.
In the ultimate sense, however, virtue is simply the restraint of the Pātimokkha. Of whom...
Thus being broken, he is like a man whose head has been severed; it cannot be said that he will protect his remaining hands and feet.
But for one who is healthy, he is like a man whose head has not been cut off; he is able to restore his life and the rest to their former state.
Therefore, having indicated the restraint of the Pātimokkha by the phrase "perfect in virtue," [the text continues with] "perfect in the Pātimokkha."
Having stated synonyms for this very term and showing them in detail, he said: "restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha," and so forth.
In that context, the meanings of "restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha" and the other terms have already been explained. Why was it begun with the words "If he should desire"?
It is for the purpose of showing the benefits of virtue (*sīla*). Even if it should occur thus to those who have recently gone forth or to those who are dull-witted:
“The Blessed One says, ‘Fulfill virtue! Fulfill virtue! What, then, is the benefit in fulfilling virtue?
What is its distinction? What is its increase? Thus he spoke in order to show them these ten benefits, thinking:
“Perhaps, having heard this benefit—beginning with being dear and pleasing to one’s fellow celibates and ending with the destruction of the taints—they might fulfill virtue.”
In this context, "if he should wish" means if he should desire. "And dear" means he should be looked upon with eyes of affection; he should become a basis for the arising of endearment.
"Charming" means one who increases their mental delight, or one who is to be attained by their mind;

the meaning is that he is to be pervaded by a heart of loving-kindness (*mettā*). "Venerable" means one who occupies a position of honor among them, like a stone parasol. "Worthy of cultivation" means...
“Surely this venerable one knows what should be known and sees what should be seen”—thus he is to be honored.

“He is one who fulfills the precepts” means that he would be one who fulfills the fourfold purification of virtue (*cātupārisuddhisīla*) alone; it is said that he would be endowed with them in their entirety, without deficiency.
“Devoted to internal mental tranquility” means intent upon the tranquility of his own mind. “One who has not cast aside meditative absorption” means...
"One whose jhāna is not brought out externally" means one whose jhāna has not been lost.
"By means of insight" means by means of the sevenfold contemplation (*anupassanā*). "One who cultivates empty huts" means one who increases [the practice] in empty huts.

And herein, a bhikkhu who, having taken up a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) by way of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), enters an empty hut and sits there day and night, is said to be "one who cultivates empty huts."
This should be understood. This is the summary here; however, one who desires a detailed account should consult the commentary on the *Ākaṅkheyya Sutta* in the *Majjhima Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā*.
Regarding the word "attainer" (*lābhī*):
here, the Blessed One does not speak of fulfilling virtue and so forth for the sake of gain. For the Blessed One [said]: "The seeking of food..."
"Having cut off talk, one should not utter connected speech"—thus he exhorts his disciples.
How could he speak of the fulfillment of virtue and so forth for the sake of gain? However, this was said with reference to the inclinations of certain individuals;
for there might be those whose inclination is such that they think, "If we were not burdened by the four requisites, we would be able to fulfill the precepts."
He spoke thus according to their inclinations. Furthermore, this is the natural benefit (*sarasānisaṃsa*) of virtue, namely, the four requisites.
For wise people take out what has been stored in granaries and the like, and rather than consuming it themselves, they give it to those possessed of virtue;
thus, this was said for the purpose of showing the natural benefit of virtue.

In the third instance, "yesāhaṃ" means "of whom I am. "Tesaṃ te kārā" means "those acts performed by them"—that is, those acts consisting of the giving of requisites performed toward me by those gods or humans.

"May they be of great fruit and great benefit": through the worldly happiness that constitutes their fruit, may they be of great fruit; through the supramundane [attainment], may they be of great benefit. Or rather, both of these terms have the same meaning. [This applies] to one endowed with qualities such as virtue (sīla) and so forth.

For even a mere ladleful of alms-food, or even a leaf-hut built on ground the size of five ratanas, when given as a gift, protects one from the miserable states and the abyss for many thousands of eons;
and at the end, it becomes a condition for final nibbāna in the element of the Deathless.
There are illustrative examples here such as, "I gave milk-rice," and so forth. Alternatively, the entire *Petavatthu* and *Vimānavatthu* serve as proof.
In the fourth section, "petas" refers to those who have gone to the state of the departed. "Relatives" (*ñātī*) refers to those on the side of one's mother’s or father’s family.
"Blood relations" (*sālohitā*) refers to those bound by the same blood, such as paternal grandfathers and so forth. "Deceased" (*kālaṅkatā*) means dead.

"Their [thought]" (*tesaṃ taṃ*) refers to their thought of confidence toward me, or the recollection performed by them with a confident mind. For when a monk’s father or mother has passed away, thinking, "Our..."
Having a mind full of confidence, thinking, “The Elder Ñātika is virtuous and of beautiful character,” he recollects that bhikkhu;
for him, both that mental confidence and even that mere recollection become of great fruit and great benefit.

“Enduring aversion and delight” means one who, through the practice of renunciation, endures, overcomes, and masters aversion toward the practice of renunciation as well as delight in the strands of sensual pleasure. “Enduring fear and terror”: here, *bhaya* (fear) refers both to mental trepidation and to the object [that causes it], while *bherava* (terror) refers only to the object.
2. Commentary on the Kaṇṭaka Sutta 72.
In the second [verse], "by those well-known" means by those who are renowned and manifest, like the full moon or the sun in the midst of the sky.
"Into the enemy's city": "enemy" refers to the rear part, and "city" refers to the front part; [it means] by one running from the front toward the rear.
"Followed by a great retinue"—this is the meaning. "Thorn" (*kaṇṭaka*) means a thorn in the sense of piercing. "Frivolous sight" (*visūkadassana*) means a sight that is frivolous.
"Haunting the company of women" (*mātugāmūpacāra*) means the practice of moving about in the vicinity of women.
3–4. Commentary on the *Iṭṭhadhamma-sutta* and others.
73–74. In the third [verse], "color" (*vaṇṇa*) refers to the color of the body. "Dhammas" refers to the nine supramundane dhammas (*lokuttara-dhamma*).
In the fourth [verse], "noble" (*ariyāya*) means not of the ordinary person (*puthujjana*); it is stated thus because of its being mixed with virtue (*sīla*) and the other factors.

"He is a taker of the essence and a giver of the excellent" means he is a receiver of both the essence and the excellent; the sense is that he takes whatever is the essence of the body and whatever is its excellence.

5. Commentary on the Migasālā Sutta Regarding what must be said at the beginning of the fifth [sutta], that has already been stated in the *Chakkanipāta*. As for the phrases "he is immoral" and so forth: "immoral" (*dussīla*) means devoid of virtue (*nissīla*).
"Liberation of mind" (*cetovimutti*) refers to the concentration of the fruit (*phalasamādhi*). "Liberation by wisdom" (*paññāvimutti*) refers to the knowledge of the fruit (*phalañāṇa*).
"He does not understand" means he does not know by way of formal study and inquiry. "Immorality ceases without remainder":
here, first, the five types of immorality are abandoned by the path of stream-entry, and the ten by the path of Arahantship.
At the moment of the fruit, they are said to be abandoned. It is with reference to the moment of the fruit that it is stated here, "it ceases. [This refers to] the worldling.

Virtue is broken by five causes: by committing an offense involving defeat (pārājika), by renouncing the training, by joining the faction of other sectarians (titthiya), by attaining Arahantship, and by death.
Among these, the first three lead to a decline in development; the fourth leads to growth;
and the fifth leads neither to decline nor to growth. But how is it that virtue is broken by attaining Arahantship?
For the virtue of an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) is exclusively wholesome, and the path to *arahantship* leads to the destruction of both wholesome and unwholesome kamma;
thus, by that [path], his virtue is broken. "Not even heard through listening" means that which is worthy of being heard has not been heard.
"Not even accomplished through great learning" (*bāhusacca*): here, "great learning" refers to energy (*vīriya*). That which is worthy of being performed through energy...
It remains undone; because it is undone, one falls away from both heaven and the path.
"The view has not been penetrated" means that what ought to be penetrated by view has not been penetrated and has not been made manifest.
"One does not obtain even temporary liberation" means that one does not obtain rapture and gladness based on hearing the Dhamma from time to time.
"It goes toward decline" means it proceeds toward decline.
"He understands it as it really is" means he knows—by way of formal learning and inquiry—that "having attained the fruit of stream-entry, the fivefold immorality ceases without remainder.
"Even by his hearing it has been accomplished" means that what is worthy of being heard has been heard.

It is accomplished through great learning; that is to say, even the minimum requirement of effort—that which is to be performed by energy—has been performed, down to at least a degree of weak insight.
It is also well-penetrated through right view; that is to say, even by means of mundane wisdom, the penetration of conditions has been effected.
For in this person, wisdom cleanses his virtue, and he attains distinction through virtue cleansed by wisdom.
"Pramāṇikā" means those who take the measure of persons. "Pamiṇanti" means they are worthy to measure or weigh.

"One is inferior" means one is inferior in virtues. "Exquisite" means one is exquisite or superior in virtues. "That" refers to that act of measuring. "More excellent" means more beautiful. "More exquisite" means more supreme.
"The stream of Dhamma carries him away" means [the stream] proceeding as something courageous.
Insight-knowledge carries one across and brings one to the plane of the Noble Ones. "Who would know that interval?"—who indeed would know such a cause?
"He is virtuous" means he is virtuous by way of mundane virtue (*lokiyasīla*).

Regarding the point where that virtue of his ceases without remainder upon attaining the liberation of Arahantship, the logical connection there has already been stated. In the two [sections] following this...
In the [first] five [realms], the fruit of non-returning is called "liberation," while in the fifth, it is indeed arhatship itself.
The rest here should be understood according to the method already explained. The sixth [sutta] has its meaning already evident. 7. Commentary on the *Kākasutta* (Crow Sutta).
77. "Dhaṃsī" means one who destroys virtues. Without acknowledging anyone's virtue, he even voids excrement upon his head when seized by the hand.
"Pagabbho" means possessed of impudence. "Tintiṇo": "tintiṇa" is said to be craving;
one who is possessed of that, or one who is full of suspicion. "Luddo" means cruel. "Akāruṇiko" means devoid of compassion.
“Weak” means lacking strength and lacking power. “One who roars” means one who is prone to roaring; he wanders about while roaring. “A hoarder” means one who makes a store of possessions. 9.

Commentary on the Discourse on the Bases of Resentment (Āghātavatthusutta) In the ninth [verse], “in an improper place” means without cause. For in the occurrence of a state involving the mind, such as “He has done me harm,” and so forth, there is a cause.
It would [occur] in cases such as being struck by a stump; that is not present here. Therefore, resentment in such a case is called "resentment in an improper place.
The rest is clear in meaning throughout. The third chapter, the Chapter on Longing, is concluded.
(9) 4. Theravagga 1–3.
Commentary on the *Vāhana-sutta* and following, §§81–83.

In the first [sutta] of the fourth [chapter], "by one who has made it boundless" (*vimariyādīkatena*) means by one who, having broken the boundary of the defilements (*kilesa*), has made it boundless. The second is of plain meaning. In the third, "but not attended upon" (*no ca payirupāsito*) means it does not stand before him.
4. Commentary on the Byākaraṇa Sutta 84.

In the fourth [verse], "one who meditates and is skilled in attainments" means one who is perfected in the jhānas and expert in meditative attainment (*samāpatti*). "Irīṇa" means a state of emptiness.
"Vicinati" means to discern the absence of qualities, that is, the state of being devoid of virtues. Alternatively, it refers to the wilderness known as *irīṇa*.
He is as if he has entered a great thicket known as "vicina. *Anaya* means lack of progress; *byasana* means ruin.
*Anayabyasana* means lack of progress and ruin. *Kiṃ nu kho* means for what reason. 5–6.
Commentary on the Katthī Sutta, etc.

85–86. In the fifth [verse], "one who is boastful" (*katthī*) means one whose nature is to boast (*katthana-sīla*); "one who is self-exalting" (*vikatthī*) means one whose nature is to self-exalt (*vikatthana-sīla*), speaking by making [his faults] manifest.

"One who does not act continuously" (*na santatakārī*) means one who does not act constantly (*na satatakārī*). In the sixth [verse], "one who is conceited" (*adhimānika*) means one who is possessed of the conceit that he has attained what he has not attained.
"One who speaks of conceit as truth" (*adhimānasacca*) means he speaks of that very conceit of attainment as being true.
7. Commentary on the *Nappiyasutta* 87. Regarding the seventh [verse]:
"He becomes one who creates legal disputes" means he becomes a maker of litigation. "Not for the sake of being dear" means not for the state of being beloved.

"Not for the sake of being respected" means not for the state of being held in high esteem. "Not for the sake of the ascetic life" means not for the state of the qualities of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*). "Not for the sake of unity" means...

"Not for continuous existence. "Not of a nature to attend to phenomena" means not having the disposition to attend to, nor the disposition to comprehend, the nine supramundane states (*lokuttara-dhamma*). "Not secluded" means not being secluded.
"Deceitfulness" means the state of being deceitful. "Cunningness" means the state of being crafty. "Crookedness" means not being upright. "Curvature" means the state of being bent.
8. Commentary on the Akkosaka Sutta (88).
Regarding the eighth [sutta], the phrase "one who reviles, one who insults, one who slanders noble ones, a fellow practitioner of the holy life" (*sabrahmacārī*):

here, the word *sabrahmacārī* should be construed with the words "reviler" and "insulter," as in "a reviler of fellow practitioners of the holy life, an insulter of fellow practitioners of the holy life."
One who reviles the Noble Ones is called an "accuser of the Noble Ones" when, with the final charge, he slanders them, thinking, "I will destroy their virtues.
"The true Dhamma does not purify him" means that the true Dhamma of the Dispensation, consisting of the three trainings, does not reach purification within him.
Regarding the term "disease and affliction": here, the disease itself should be understood as the "affliction" because it causes a state of miserable living.
9. Commentary on the Kokālika Sutta 89.
Regarding the ninth [sutta], "The monk Kokālika approached the Blessed One": who was this Kokālika, and for what reason did he approach?
It is said that he was the son of the merchant Kokālika in the city of Kokālika in the district of Kokālika, and having gone forth into homelessness...
One named Cūḷakokālika was residing in a monastery built by his father, but he was not a disciple of Devadatta. For that son of a brahmin was actually named Mahākokālika.

Now, while the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, the two chief disciples, together with about five hundred bhikkhus, were wandering on a journey through the countryside when the time for the rains retreat drew near.

Having dismissed those bhikkhus who desired to dwell in seclusion, and taking their own bowls and robes, they reached that city in that country and went to the monastery. There, Kokālika performed the duties for them.
They, having exchanged greetings with him, said: "Friend, we shall dwell here for the three months of the rains; do not inform anyone of our presence."
Having obtained their formal consent, they stayed there. After staying and performing the *pavāraṇā* ceremony on the day of the invitation, they said to Kokālika, "Friend, we shall depart.
Kokālika replied, "Friends, stay for one day today and you may go tomorrow.
On the second day, having entered the city, he addressed the people: "Friends, you two chief disciples..."
“Even though they have come here and are living here, you do not know them; no one even invites them with the four requisites.
The city-dwellers asked, “Venerable sir, where are the Elders? Why did you not tell us? [The Elder replied: “Friends, what is the use of telling you?
Do you not see these two monks sitting in the seats of honor? These are the Chief Disciples. They quickly assembled and prepared ghee, molasses, and other offerings.
They brought robes and cloths.
Kokālika thought: "The supreme few-in-desires, the Chief Disciples, will not accept gains arising from directed speech;
since they do not accept them, they will say, 'Give these to the resident monk. Having thus caused that gain to be taken, he went into the presence of the Elders.
They arrived. Upon seeing them, the elders thought, "These requisites belong neither to us nor to Kokālika," and having refused them, they departed.
Kokālika became resentful, thinking, "How is it that they are departing without taking anything for themselves and without even giving any to me?
They too went into the presence of the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and again [spoke] to themselves...
Taking their retinue, they traveled through the countryside and eventually returned to that very city in that kingdom.
Recognizing the Elders, the citizens prepared alms together with requisites, erected a pavilion in the center of the city, and gave the offerings;
they also presented requisites to the Elders, whom the Elders then entrusted to the Saṅgha of monks.
Seeing this, Kokālika thought: "In the past these were of few desires; now they have become evil-desiring.

Yet, even in the past, I think they were just like those who are of few desires, contented, and secluded. Approaching the elders, he said, "Friends, you were like those of few desires in the past, but now you have become evil monks," and he established them right where they stood.
Thinking, "I shall split [him]," he went out in great haste and approached the Blessed One.
It should be understood that this was Kokālika, and it is for this reason that he approached.
Seeing him approaching in such a hurried manner, the Blessed One, reflecting, knew: "This man wishes to revile the two chief disciples."
"He has arrived; is it possible to turn him back? Then, seeing that "it is not possible to turn him back;

he has come having offended against the Elders, and he will certainly be reborn in the Paduma Hell," [the Buddha] spoke for the purpose of clearing his reputation—lest people say, "Even upon hearing someone reviling Sāriputta and Moggallāna, he does not stop them"—and for the purpose of showing the great culpability of insulting noble ones (*ariya*).
"Do not say so," he refused three times. In this context, "mā heva" means "do not speak thus.
"Saddhāyiko" means one who acts according to faith, one who inspires confidence, or one whose words are to be trusted. "Paccayiko" means one whose words are to be relied upon.
"He departed" means that, being urged by the power of his own karma, he departed; for it is impossible to ward off karma when it has found its opportunity.
"Shortly after he had departed" means that not long after he had gone.
"His entire body was covered" means that, leaving not even a space the size of a hair-tip uncovered, his whole body was overspread with boils that had arisen by breaking through the bones.
However, because of the power of the Buddhas, such karma is unable to yield its result in the presence of the Buddhas.
He was unable [to give it]; having left the vicinity of sight, he gave it. Therefore, not long after he had departed, boils broke out on him.
"The size of a *kalāya* bean" means the size of a chickpea (*caṇaka*). "The size of a young *beluva* fruit" means the size of a tender *beluva* fruit.
"They burst open" means they split. When they had burst open, his entire body became like a ripe jackfruit. He...
With his body putrefying, he lay upon the leaves of a plantain tree at the gateway of the Jeta Grove like a fish that had swallowed poison.
Then, the people who had come and gone for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma cried out, "Shame on Kokālika! Shame on Kokālika!
You have done what was improper; you have met with ruin and disaster solely because of your own mouth. Hearing their voices, the protective deities...
They raised a cry of reproach; from the guardian deities to the deities of the sky, by this means a single universal reproach arose as far as the Akaniṭṭha realm.
As for Turu, Kokālika’s preceptor named the Elder Turu, having realized the fruit of non-returning, was reborn in the Brahma-world.

Thus, beginning with the earth-dwelling deities, the sound reached as far as the Brahma-world through successive transmission: "What Kokālika has done is improper, in that he slanders the two Chief Disciples with a final charge.
Hearing this, [the deity] thought, "Lest this wretch perish even while I am looking on, I shall admonish him for the sake of inspiring faith in the Elders' hearts. He came and stood before him.
With reference to him, this was said: “Turū the Independent Brahmā. “Of good character” means of lovely virtue.
“Who are you, friend?”—saying this, even while still seated, he opened his wide-open eyes and spoke thus. “See how far you have gone astray! he said;
that is, seeing how much you have erred, you think it right to reprove me for a pimple the size of a mustard seed, while failing to see the great tumor upon your own forehead.

Then, knowing that "this Kokālika has reached a state of wrong view; like one who has swallowed poison, he will not heed the words of anyone," the Blessed One spoke the verse beginning with "For a man...
and so forth. Therein, "an axe" (*kuṭhārī*) refers to harsh speech, which is like an axe. "Cuts" means it cuts right at the roots, known as the roots of wholesome merit (*kusalamūla*).
"One who should be censured" (*nindiya*) refers to a person of immoral conduct who deserves censure. "Praises" means...
Having honored one who has attained the highest goal, he says, "He is one whose taints are exhausted.

Or he reviles him who should be praised—that is, he accuses that one whose taints are exhausted and who is worthy of praise by means of some final matter, saying, "This man is immoral. He searches for misfortune with his mouth;
that is, he searches for that transgression with his mouth. By means of that misfortune, [he finds] no happiness.
He finds nothing. For the result of praising those who deserve blame and blaming those who deserve praise is indeed equal.
"Even with all, even with oneself" means that the loss of wealth at dice—even with all one's own property and even including oneself—is but a minor offense.
But as for [offense] against the Sugatas... refers to the mental state directed toward persons who have attained the right path.
This corruption of the mind is a far greater misfortune than that.
Now, demonstrating its status as a greater misfortune, he said: "A hundred thousand... and so forth.
Therein, "a hundred thousand" refers to one hundred thousand *nirabbudas* according to the *nirabbuda* calculation. "Thirty-six" refers to another thirty-six *nirabbudas*.

"Five" means five *abbuda* according to the *abbuda* reckoning. "He who reviles the noble ones" means that for one who reviles the noble ones and is reborn in hell, this is the measure of his lifespan there—this is the meaning.

"He passed away" means that he passed away after his preceptor had departed. Regarding "the Paduma hell": there is no separate hell named Paduma; rather, he was reborn in a certain location within the great Avīci hell itself, where one must be cooked according to the *paduma* reckoning.
Twenty *khāris*—measured by the Magadhan *pattha*—make four *patthas* in the kingdom of Kosala. By that *pattha*, four *patthas* make one *āḷhaka*;
four *āḷhakas* make one *doṇa*; four *doṇas* make one *mānikā*; four *mānikās* make one *khārī*;
and twenty such *khāris* make a *tilavāha*. A *tilavāha* is a cartload of fine sesame seeds from Magadha.
Regarding "the Abbuda hell": there is no separate hell named Abbuda; rather, this is the name for a place within Avīci itself where one must be cooked according to the calculation of *abbuda*.
The same method applies to the Nirabbuda and other hells as well.
Furthermore, the calculation of years here should be understood in this way: just as one hundred times one hundred thousand makes a *koṭi*, so too...
In this way, one hundred times one hundred thousand *koṭis* is called a *pakoṭi*; one hundred times one hundred thousand *pakoṭis* is called a *koṭipakoṭi*;
one hundred times one hundred thousand *koṭipakoṭis* is a *nahuta*; one hundred times one hundred thousand *nahutas* is a *ninnahuta*;
one hundred times one hundred thousand *ninnahutas* is one *abbuda*; twenty times that is a *nirabbuda*; and this is the method [for the subsequent numbers].
"In all cases": the tenth [case] is to be understood according to the method already stated below. The remainder is clear in meaning throughout.
The fourth chapter, the Chapter on Elders, is concluded. (10) 5. The Chapter on Upāli.
1–2. Commentary on the *Kāmabhogīsutta*, etc. (91–92).
In the first [sutta] of the fifth [chapter], "by violence" (*sāhasena*) means by a violent deed. In the second, "fears" (*bhayāni*) refers to fears consisting of mental terror;
"enmities" (*verāni*) refers to unwholesome enmities and personal enmities. "The noble method" (*ariyo cassa ñāyo*) is the path together with insight (*vipassanā*). Thus...
"When this exists, that comes to be": thus, when this cause—beginning with ignorance—exists, this result—beginning with volitional formations—comes to be.
"With the arising of this, that arises": when one thing is a co-nascent condition for another, with the arising of the former, the latter is said to arise.
"When this does not exist": when the cause—beginning with ignorance—does not exist, the result—beginning with volitional formations—does not come to be.
"Of this cessation": through the non-occurrence of the cause, there is the non-occurrence of the fruit.
3. Commentary on the *Kiṃdiṭṭhika-sutta* (93).
"In the third [sutta], they restrained": they restrained both their physical posture (*iriyāpatha*) and their mode of speech (*vacanapatha*). "Trained in being quiet": [they were so trained].
"Trained by the Teacher who speaks with little noise and in moderation. "On account of another's voice" means because of the speech of another.
"Intended" means planned. "Becoming abashed" means having fallen into dejection and losing one's spirit. "With drooping shoulders" means with shoulders slumped down.
"By means of the Dhamma" means by means of a reasoned statement possessing a logical cause.
4. Commentary on the Vajjiyamāhita Sutta 94.
In the fourth [sutta], "Vajjiyamāhita" is his name. "All austerity" means every kind of difficult practice.
"All those who practice austerity" means all those who rely upon such asceticism. "A life of harshness" refers to the pursuit of a livelihood based on difficult practices.
*Anuyuttaṃ*: devoted. *Gārayhaṃ*: worthy of censure; that which is fit to be blamed. *Pasaṃsiyaṃ*: worthy of praise; that which is fit to be commended. *Venayiko*:
one who is himself undisciplined and must be disciplined by others. *Apaññattiko*: incapable of establishing anything as a rule. Alternatively, *venayiko* means a destroyer of beings.
*Apaññattiko* refers to one who establishes a *nibbāna* that is not directly perceptible (*apaccakkhaṃ*), [as well as those who hold views] such as "made by oneself" (*sayaṃkata*) and so forth.

He is unable to explain anything. "That Blessed One is not a mere destroyer" means that the Blessed One, having understood things as they truly are and explaining what is wholesome and unwholesome, cannot be led by another nor taught by another.
Furthermore, because he explains those phenomena based upon which a "being" is designated, he is not a destroyer of beings; rather, being well-disciplined and well-trained, he is a leader of beings.
This is the meaning. And he shows that its designations are indeed designations of wisdom (*paññā*). Regarding "unwholesome states increase for one who is being liberated from liberation":
this refers to the fact that unwholesome states increase for one who is intent upon a mental inclination (*adhimutti*) consisting of wrong view;
it is with reference to this that it was said. However, in the Dispensation, liberation—which consists of the mind's liberation—is a condition for wholesome states alone.
5. Commentary on the Uttiya Sutta 95.
Regarding the fifth [verse], "he remained silent": standing upon the [wrong] view of a self (*sattūpaladdhi*), he remained silent because he was asking what he had not yet asked.

"Indeed, I have been questioned by the ascetic Gotama regarding the most excellent of all questions" means: "I have been questioned by the ascetic Gotama concerning the supreme question among all questions."
"He confuses me but does not answer; surely he is unable, he is incapable of answering"—lest he should thus acquire such an evil view.
"Tadassa" means that such a course of views might arise for him.
"Paccantimaṃ" (borderland) is so called because, in the Middle Country, the fortifications of a city—such as its ramparts and so forth—are either firm or weak, or perhaps entirely absent.
"Let there not be [fear]; there is no apprehension of thieves. Therefore, without taking that [fear] into account, he said, 'a frontier city.
'With strong foundations' means having firm bases for its walls. 'With strong walls and gate-towers' means both firm walls and firm door-frames.
Why did he say 'with a single gate'? For in a city with many gates, there must be many wise gatekeepers; but in one with a single gate..."
Only one is suitable. There is no other equal to the Tathāgata in wisdom.

Therefore, in order to provide an illustration for the Teacher’s state of being wise, he said "a single door" in order to show only one gatekeeper. "Wise" (paṇḍita) means endowed with wisdom (paṇḍicca).
"Clever" (byatta) means endowed with proficiency (veyyattiya). "Intelligent" (medhāvī) means [endowed] with intelligence (medhā), which is defined as situational wisdom (ṭhānuppattikapaññā).
“Endowed with. “A path for circumambulation” means a road called a circumambulatory path.
“A breach in the wall” means a place where two bricks have fallen away. “A gap in the wall” means a broken section of the wall.
“He asked that very same question” means he asked again that very same question to be set aside, which had been previously asked in the manner beginning with “Is the world eternal? All...
And by this, he shows that [the interlocutor] asks in another manner while remaining precisely within the apprehension of a "being" (*sattūpaladdhi*) as "the world.
6. Commentary on the Kokanuda Sutta: 96.
Regarding the sixth [verse], *pubbāpayamāno* means making them like the previous ones, i.e., rendering them waterless. *Kvettha, āvuso* means "Who is there, friend?"
In this context, friends: "To whatever extent there is view" means all the sixty-two kinds of views that exist.
"To whatever extent there is a basis for views" refers to the eightfold basis as follows: "The aggregates are a basis for views;
ignorance, contact, perception, thought, improper attention, evil friends, and the voice of another are also bases for views. To whatever extent there is this [eightfold basis]...
There is what is called the basis for views (*diṭṭhiṭṭhāna*) and the cause of views (*diṭṭhikāraṇa*). "The foundation of views" (*diṭṭhādhiṭṭhāna*) means the foundation of views;
it is the name for a view that proceeds by being established upon and dominated by [other factors]. Regarding "the obsession of views" (*diṭṭhipariyuṭṭhāna*):
"What are the eighteen obsessions of views? It is that view which is a state of views (*diṭṭhigata*), a thicket of views (*diṭṭhigahana*), a wilderness of views (*diṭṭhikantāra*)..."
The disfigurement of views, the vacillation of views, the fetter of views, the dart of views, the confinement of views, the obstruction of views,
the bond of views, the precipice of views, the underlying tendency of views, the fever of views, the burning of views, the knot of views,
the clinging to views, the dogmatic adherence to views, and the misapprehension of views— these are the eighteen obsessions of views.”
Thus has the obsession of views been described. "Origin" (*samuṭṭhāna*) is a synonym for the basis of views. For this has been said:
"The aggregates are the condition for views in the sense of being their origin"; all of this should be expanded in detail.
Furthermore, the path of stream-entry is called the "eradication of views" because it eradicates all views. "All that" (*tamahaṃ*) means "all that, I [know]."
"I know. Why should I speak? What shall I say? 7–8. Commentary on the *Āhuneyyasutta* and others, 97–98.
In the seventh [sutta], "one of right view" means one who sees things as they truly are (*yāthāvadiṭṭhika*).

In the eighth, "skilled in the arising and subsiding of legal issues" means that by grasping the root of the four types of legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*), one becomes skilled in their arising and their pacification through subsiding.
9. Commentary on the Upāli Sutta 99.
Regarding the ninth [verse], “difficult to master” (*durabhisambhavāni*) means they are painful to master and hard to endure; it is said that they cannot be plunged into by those of little power.
“Forest and jungle tracts” (*araññavanapatthāni*) refers to forests (*araññāni*) and jungle tracts (*vanapatthāni*). By the accomplishment of the forest-dweller’s practice (*āraññaka-aṅga*),...
“Forests” (*araññāni*) refers to those places beyond the vicinity of villages, being locations where people do not frequent.

“Remote” (*pantāni*) means situated on the outskirts or at a great distance. “Solitude is difficult to practice” (*dukkaraṃ pavivekaṃ*) means that physical seclusion (*kāyaviveka*) is difficult to achieve. “Hard to enjoy” (*durabhiramaṃ*) means it is not easy to take delight in.
“In solitude” (*ekatte*) means in a state of being alone. What does this show? Even when physical seclusion has been established, it is [difficult] to cause the mind to find delight therein.
It is difficult. For this world delights in pairs. "They carry off," it is said, meaning they carry off as it were, devour as it were.

"Mind" (*mano*) means consciousness (*citta*). "Of one who does not obtain concentration" means of one who does not obtain either access-concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*) or absorption-concentration (*appanā-samādhi*).
What does this show? That for such a bhikkhu, the forests—by means of various sounds of grass, leaves, wild animals, and so forth, and by means of terrifying things—[are a source of distraction].
"They distract the mind, thinking 'I am conceiving. "He will sink" means he will sink through sensual thoughts (*kāmavitakka*).
"He will float up" means he will float upward through thoughts of ill-will and cruelty (*byāpādavihiṃsāvitakka*).
"Ear-cleanser" refers to what should be played while washing the ears. "Back-cleanser" refers to [what is done] while washing the back.
It should be played with. Therein, taking water with the trunk and pouring it over both ears is called "washing the ears";
pouring it over the back is called "washing the back. "He finds a footing" means he gains a support.
"Who am I and who is the elephant-king? means: "Who am I? Who is the elephant-king? I too am an animal, and he too is."
"I have four feet, and he has four feet; are we not both exactly equal?
*Vaṅkaka* is a small plough used as a toy for children. *Ghaṭika* is a game played by striking a short stick with a long stick.
*Mokkhacika* is a game of tumbling, where one takes hold of a stick in the air and [rolls] upon the ground.
Or, having placed a lead weight [on one end], they play by turning it upside down; this is what is meant.
A *ciṅgulaka* is a spinning wheel made of palm leaves and such, which revolves when struck by the wind. A *pattāḷhaka* is called a leaf-measure (*paṇṇanāḷi*);
they play by measuring sand and so forth with it. A *rathaka* is a small chariot. A *dhanuka* is simply a small bow.
"Idha kho pana" (here indeed) is merely a particle (*nipātamattaṃ*); the meaning is "idha kho panā" (here indeed).

In the phrase "Iṅgha tvaṃ, Upāli, saṅghe viharāhi" ("Come now, Upāli, dwell in the Saṅgha"), the word *iṅgha* is a particle used in the sense of an exhortation (*codanatthe*). By this, he exhorts the Elder to dwell in the midst of the Saṅgha;
he does not permit him to live in the forest. Why? Because it is said that for one dwelling in a forest lodging, the very duty of residence (*vāsadhura*) [is fulfilled].
"It will not fulfill the duty of the scriptures; however, while living in the midst of the Saṅgha, he will fulfill both duties and attain Arahatship, and he will become a leader in the Vinaya Piṭaka.

Then, having explained his former aspiration and former resolve in the midst of the assembly, I shall establish this bhikkhu in the foremost position among those who uphold the Vinaya. With this purpose...
While observing [the situation], the Teacher did not grant permission for the elder to dwell in the forest. The tenth [section] has its meaning already explained.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, the Upāli-vagga.
The second fiftieth section is completed.
3. The Third Fifty (11). 1.
The Chapter on the Perception of Ascetics (Samaṇasaññāvagga). 1.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Perception of Ascetics (Samaṇasaññāsutta-vaṇṇanā).

101. In the first [section] of the third [chapter], "perception of recluses" (*samaṇasaññā*) means the perception arising in recluses. "One who acts continuously" (*santatakārī*) means one who acts without interruption.

"Free from affliction" (*abyāpajjha*) means free from suffering. "This purpose occurs to him" (*idamatthaṃ tassa hoti*) means that regarding these requisites of life, the thought "this is the purpose, these are the conditions" occurs to him;
the meaning is that he makes use of them with reflective awareness (*paccavekkhitaparibhoga*). The second [section] has a self-evident meaning.
3. Commentary on the *Micchatta-sutta* (Sutta 103):

In the third [verse], "there is failure" (*virādhanā*) means there is a falling away from heaven and from the Path. "Not attainment" (*no ārādhanā*) means there is no accomplishment or bringing to fulfillment. "It occurs" (*pahoti*) means it proceeds. 4–5.
Commentary on the *Bīja-sutta* and others:
104–105. In the fourth [case], "fully undertaken according to one's view" means that it is undertaken, fulfilled, and grasped entirely in accordance with one’s own view.
"Volition" refers specifically to the volition produced through the three doors.
"Aspiration" is the longing, "May I become such a person. "Resolve" is the fixing of the mind, thinking, "I shall become a deity or some other kind of deity."
"Volitional formations" (*saṅkhārā*) refers to the associated volitional formations. In the fifth [verse], they are "preceding" in the sense of being a precursor.
"Following right after" means following immediately upon that. 6. Commentary on the *Nijjara-sutta* (The Discourse on Wearing Away)
106. Regarding the sixth [section], "the bases for wearing away" (*nijjaravatthu*) means the causes for wearing away. "Wrong view is worn away" (*micchādiṭṭhi nijjiṇṇā hoti*):
this has already been worn away—even by insight (*vipassanā*)—and thus abandoned below. Why, then, is it mentioned again? Because it has not yet been completely eradicated (*asamucchinna*).
For although it was worn away by insight, it was not yet completely eradicated. However, when the Path (*magga*) arises, it eradicates that [wrong view] completely.
But it does not allow one to emerge [from that state]. Therefore, it is taken up again. This should be applied to all the passages in this manner.
And herein, sixty-four states reach the fulfillment of their development by way of right liberation. Which sixty-four?

At the moment of the stream-entry path, the faculty of faith reaches fulfillment in the sense of resolution; the faculty of energy, in the sense of exertion; the faculty of mindfulness, in the sense of establishment... [and so on].

It fulfills the faculty of mindfulness; through the sense of non-distraction, it fulfills the faculty of concentration; through the sense of seeing, it fulfills the faculty of wisdom; through the sense of cognizing, it fulfills the faculty of mind;
through the sense of delighting, it fulfills the faculty of mental joy; and through the sense of predominance over the continuity of the process, it fulfills the faculty of vitality...
[and so on] ...at the moment of the fruit of Arhatship, through the sense of resolve, it fulfills the faculty of faith... [and so on].
The life-faculty is fulfilled in the sense of being the dominant factor for the continuity of the process of existence.
Thus, occurring eight times each in the four paths and the four fruits, sixty-four factors reach fulfillment.
7. Commentary on the Dhovana Sutta (The Washing Sutta)
107. "Washing in the seventh" refers to the washing of bones. For in that country, people do not cremate their deceased relatives;
instead, having dug a pit, they bury them in the earth.

Then, once they have become putrid, they extract the bones, wash them, arrange them in order, honor them with perfumes and garlands, and set them aside. When a festival arrives, they [display] those...
Having taken the bones, they weep and lament; thereafter, they play at the festival.
8–10. Commentary on the *Tikicchaka-sutta* and others, 108–110.
In the eighth [sutta], "purgative" (*virecana*) refers to medicine for the removal of humors (*doṣa*). "She has been purged" (*virittā hoti*) means she has been cleared out and cleansed.
In the ninth [section], "emetics" refers to medicinal substances that induce vomiting. In the tenth, "to be expelled" means those things which ought to be cast out;
"expelled" means those things already cast out. 11. Commentary on the First Discourse on the Non-Trainee (Asekha-sutta):

In the eleventh [section], right view itself is called "right knowledge" for the purpose of fulfilling the factors [of the path]. Thus, all these qualities of the fruit of arahantship are non-trainee states (*asekha*); because they occur in one who is a non-trainee, even the reviewing knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa*) is said to be a non-trainee state.
12. Commentary on the Second Discourse on the Non-Trainee (Asekha) 112.

Regarding the twelfth [discourse], "of the non-trainees" (*asekhā*) means those who are indeed non-trainees (*asekhā*), or those belonging to the category of the non-trainees. By this discourse, it is the one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) who is described.
The first chapter, the Chapter on the Perception of Ascetics (*Samaṇasaññāvagga*), is concluded.
(12) 2. Paccorohaṇivagga 1–2. Commentary on the Two Discourses on What is Not Dhamma (Adhammasutta). 113–114.
In the first [discourse] of the second [chapter], both the question and the answer are presented separately; in the second, they are presented together.
3. Commentary on the Third Discourse on the Non-Dhamma (Tatiya-adhamma-sutta) 115.
"Having recited the summary" means having set forth the matrix (mātikā).

"Praised by the Teacher himself" means praised by the Teacher when he established [the Bhaddiya monks] in the "Foremost Among" (etadagga) category in five instances. "Held in high esteem" means held in high esteem through the recognition of their virtues.
"Pahoti" means "is able. "Atisitvā" means "having transcended. "Jānaṃ jānāti" means "he knows what is to be known. "Passaṃ passati" means "he sees what is to be seen.
"Cakkhubhūto" means "become like the eye," arisen or produced as such. "Ñāṇabhūto" means "having the nature of knowledge.
"Dhammabhūto" means "having the nature of the Dhamma. "Brahmabhūto" means "having the nature of the Supreme (Brahmā). "Vattāti" means "he speaks."
“Capable” means capable of setting [the wheel] in motion. “One who leads to the goal” means one who extracts and demonstrates the meaning.
“As the Blessed One would for us” means as the Blessed One would explain it for us.
4. Commentary on the *Ajita Sutta*.
116. In the fourth [case], "Ajita" is one who has such a name. "Hundreds of mental positions" means hundreds of arisings of consciousness (*cittuppāda*).

"By which" means by those hundreds of mental positions while they are being engaged [in debate]. "They know themselves as overcome, thinking 'we are overcome'" means that when they have failed and been refuted, they know thus:
"We have failed; we have been refuted; the fault has been laid upon us. "Bases for the wise" means...
The causes for the state of being wise. 5–6.
Commentary on the *Saṅgāravasutta* and others, 117–118.
In the fifth [sutta], "this shore" (*orimaṃ tīraṃ*) refers to the mundane; this is the "near shore. "The further shore" (*pārimaṃ tīraṃ*) refers to the supramundane; this is the "far shore."
"Those who go to the further shore" means those who go to Nibbāna. "He runs only along the shore" means he runs only along the shore of the view of personal existence (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*).

"Those who follow the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma" means those who follow the Dhamma in accordance with the ninefold supramundane Dhamma well-expounded, proceeding by way of the preliminary practice consisting of virtue and so forth that is appropriate to that Dhamma. [They cross] the realm of Death.

"Having crossed over that which is very difficult to cross"—having crossed over the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) consisting of the three realms, which is the domain of death and exceedingly hard to traverse.
"They will reach the further shore" means they will attain *nibbāna*.

"Coming from home to homelessness" means coming from the cycle of existence to the state beyond the cycle (*vivaṭṭa*). "Wherein seclusion is far-reaching" refers to that seclusion of body, mind, and acquisitions (*upadhi*).
Difficult to delight in, yet one might wish for delight therein. "Having abandoned sensual pleasures" means having relinquished both kinds of sensual pleasure.
"Possessing nothing" means being free from all impediments. "In the relinquishing of grasping" refers to Nibbāna, which is characterized as the letting go of seizing.

"Those who rejoice without clinging" refers to those who take no hold whatsoever by means of the four types of clinging. "Completely extinguished" means they have attained final Nibbāna through the conditionless parinibbāna.
They should be understood as "fully extinguished" (*parinibbūta*). This is the sixth discourse taught to the bhikkhus.
7–8. Commentary on the Two *Paccorohaṇī* Suttas (119–120).
In the seventh, *paccorohaṇī* means the descending from evil. *Pattharitvā* means having spread out. *Antarā*...
"And between the time" (*velam antarā*) means between the time [of the sacrifice] and the fire-hall (*agyāgāra*).
It was taught to the Saṅgha of monks at the sand-hut (*vālikārāsi*) and the fire-hall. The eighth [sutta] was taught to the Saṅgha of monks. The remainder is clear in meaning throughout.
Thus ends the second chapter, the Chapter on the Descent from the Ladder (*Paccorohaṇivagga*).
(13) 3. Explanation of the Chapter on Purity (Parisuddhavagga) 123.

Regarding the first [sutta] of the third [chapter]: "Pure" (*parisuddha*) means stainless (*nimmala*). "Brightly radiant" (*pariyodāta*) means luminous (*pabhassara*). The second and subsequent [terms] have their meanings self-evident.
Thus ends the third chapter, the Chapter on Purity.
(14) 4. Commentary on the Chapter on the Good (Sādhuvagga). 134.

Regarding the first [verse] of the fourth [chapter], "good" (*sādhu*) means auspicious (*bhaddaka*) and well-knit (*siliṭṭhaka*). The second and subsequent [verses] have their meanings already explained. Thus, the Chapter on the Noble Path (*Ariyamaggavagga*) has its meaning already explained.
This is the fourth chapter, the Chapter on the Good.
The Third Fifty is finished.
4. The Fourth Fifty: 155.
The first [sections] of the fourth [fifty] have their meaning already explained.

8. Commentary on the *Kammanidāna Sutta* (174). In the eighth [sutta], "even that which has greed as its cause": for the taking of life, greed is a cause by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*), even when associated with hatred and delusion. The meaning should be understood in this manner throughout all instances. 9. Commentary on the *Parikkamana Sutta* (175). In the ninth [sutta], "even that which has greed as its cause": for false speech, greed is a cause by way of decisive support, even when associated with hatred and delusion. The meaning should be understood in this manner throughout all instances. In the tenth [sutta], "even that which has greed as its cause": for divisive speech, greed is a cause by way of decisive support, even when associated with hatred and delusion. The meaning should be understood in this manner throughout all instances. For those in hell, what is called "food" is simply the kamma that causes rebirth there; for by that alone do they subsist there. Regarding those of the animal womb...
Furthermore, food should be understood by way of grass, leaves, and so forth; for humans, by way of boiled rice, sour gruel, and so forth;
for devas, by way of ambrosial food (*sudhā*) and so forth; and for those in the realm of hungry ghosts (*pettivisayika*), by way of saliva, nasal mucus, and so forth.

Furthermore, the donor is not without fruit: regardless of whether that gift—which was given with a specific intention—actually benefits the recipient or not, the donor cannot be without result;

"Even in an improper case, Master Gotama speaks of a postulation"—this means that even when that kinsman has arisen in an inappropriate place, Master Gotama still merely postulates and merely explains the fruit of the gift; thus he asks.

"He does not meditate depending on the earth" means that due to the absence of attachment to the bliss of attainment, he does not [meditate] with the earth as his object.
