"The perception of earth regarding earth is made manifest" means that the perception of the fourfold and fivefold jhānas, having arisen with earth as its object, becomes manifest and clear.

"In this sutta, ‘the perception of form has been eliminated, the perception of the skeleton has not been eliminated,’ the state of being ‘eliminated’ (vibhūtatā) is stated because of the existence of transcendence (*samatikkama*).
But here, however, they have become ‘eliminated’ in the sense that they are seen as impermanent, suffering, and non-self by way of insight (*vipassanā*).
The same method applies to the perception of water and so forth. Thus, in this case, unlike below, it is by way of attainment (*samāpatti*)."
Without mentioning transcendence [by means of serenity], transcendence is spoken of here by way of the practice of insight (*vipassanā*).
"One who meditates thus" means one who meditates by means of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) produced after having arrived at it through the sequence of insight.

Although the Teacher knew who this monk Subhūti was, he asked, "Who is this monk Subhūti? for the purpose of initiating the discourse.

"In the accounts (apadāna) of faithful individuals" means in the characteristics of those persons endowed with faith.
5. Commentary on the *Mettasutta* 15.
Regarding the fifth verse, "he sleeps in comfort": unlike other people who sleep in discomfort, tossing and turning and scratching like crows, he does not sleep thus, but sleeps in comfort.
Even when falling asleep, he is as if one who has entered meditative absorption (*samāpatti*).

He wakes up in comfort. "He wakes up in comfort" means that, unlike others who wake up in pain by yawning, stretching, and tossing about, he does not wake with such agitation; rather, like a lotus flower opening, he wakes peacefully and composedly.
"He sees no evil dream" means that even when dreaming, he sees only auspicious dreams, such as [seeing] a cetiya...
He feels as if he were paying homage, as if he were making an offering, and as if he were listening to the Dhamma.
Unlike others, who see themselves surrounded by thieves, oppressed by wild beasts, or falling into a precipice,
he does not see such an evil dream.
"He is dear to human beings" means that he is dear and pleasing to people, like a pearl necklace worn upon the breast or a garland bound upon the head.
"He is dear to non-human beings" means that just as with humans, he is likewise dear to non-humans, such as the Elder Visākha.
The story is already explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga* in the section on the meditation subject of loving-kindness (*mettā-kammaṭṭhāna*).
"Deities protect him": just as parents protect their own child, deities protect him. "Neither fire, nor poison, nor weapons affect him":

for one who dwells in loving-kindness (*mettāvihārin*), neither fire, nor poison, nor weapons affect—that is, they do not penetrate or enter his body, nor do they cause it harm—just as with the female lay follower Uttarā, or the Elder Cūḷasīva, a reciter of the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*, or the novice Saṅkicca.
This has been stated. In this connection, they also relate the story of the cow. It is said that a certain cow stood there letting fall a stream of milk for her calf.
A hunter, thinking "I shall pierce her," whirled a long-handled spear with his hand and hurled it.
It struck her body and passed through, spinning like a palm leaf; yet, by the power of her proximity [to the calf], it did not kill her.
It is not by the power of absorption (appanā), but solely through the strength of his concentrated mind, like that of a calf. Such is the great majesty of loving-kindness (mettā).
"The mind quickly becomes concentrated": for one who dwells in loving-kindness, the mind becomes concentrated very swiftly;
there is no sluggishness in him. "The complexion of the face becomes serene": it is as if a ripe palm fruit has been released from its bond.
The complexion of the face becomes serene. "He dies unconfused" means that for one who dwells in loving-kindness (*mettā*), there is no such thing as a confused death;

rather, he passes away as if falling into sleep while remaining undeluded. "Failing to penetrate further" means being unable to attain *arahantship* beyond the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) of loving-kindness, and thus, having passed away from here, waking up like one who has risen from sleep—
...is reborn as if in the Brahma-world.

Knowing by means of the three true knowledges (*vijjā*) or the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*);

“Human beings are known, as well as whatever other happy destinies there may be. But rather, monks, it is through action born of greed,
action born of hatred, and action born of delusion that hell is known,
the animal realm is known, the sphere of hungry ghosts is known, and whatever other unhappy destinies there may be.”

He should be informed in this way. If he understands, let him understand. If he does not understand, he should be sent away with the words: "Go, enter the monastery early in the morning and drink rice-gruel.
"This one thing, householder, has been declared"—because when asked about one thing, it was spoken by way of questioning in the form, "This one thing has been declared;
this one thing too has been declared," all eleven things [are thus included].

It is called "a single dhamma" because it has been made so; or rather, it is appropriate to say that all [the treasures] are a single dhamma in the sense that they have arisen from the Deathless (*amata*).
"Seeking the entrance to the treasure" means searching for the treasure. "All at once" means by a single effort.
But how can there be the attainment of eleven treasures by a single effort? Here, someone [seeks] a livelihood in the forest...
He wanders about seeking [food]. Seeing him, a certain benefactor asks, "Sir, what are you doing?
He replies, "I am searching for a means of livelihood. The other says, "In that case, my friend, come; roll this rock down.
Having rolled it down, [he sees] eleven [stones] standing one above the other, or touching belly to belly.
He sees the cauldrons. Thus, by a single application, there is the realization of eleven [powers].

"They will seek the teacher’s fee"—for those of other sects give wealth to the one from whom they learn a craft, having brought it out from their homes either before, after, or during the time of learning that craft. To those...
Those who have nothing in their own homes seek it from among their kinsmen; those who have even that seek it from among their associates.
Failing to obtain it in this way, they go so far as to wander for alms and still give. It is with reference to this that it was said.
But what of them? First, even the outsiders seek wealth from one who gives merely a craft within a teaching that does not lead to liberation.

"But as for me, why should I not offer worship to the Teacher who teaches such a liberating dispensation and the elevenfold path leading to the arising of the Deathless? Indeed, I shall do so," he said.
"He clothed each one with a pair of garments" means that he gave a pair of garments to each individual bhikkhu. This, however, is a statement concerning their customary conduct.
It was of such a kind; therefore, it is said that "he covered it. "A vihāra worth five hundred" means he had a leaf-hut built at a cost of five hundred [kahāpanas].
7. Commentary on the Gopāla Sutta:
17. In the seventh [chapter], there are three discourses: the Single-Channel (ekanāḷikā), the Quadruple (caturassa), and the Sitting-Rule (nisinnavattikā).
Therein, after reciting the canonical text (pāḷi), the explanation of the meaning of each individual word is called the "Single-Channel.
Having shown the unwise cowherd, having shown the unwise bhikkhu, having shown the wise cowherd, and having shown the wise bhikkhu—thus forming a tetrad—[the discourse proceeds].
The exposition called "The Fourfold Square" consists of: reaching the conclusion by showing an unwise cowherd;
reaching the conclusion by showing an unwise bhikkhu; reaching the conclusion by showing a wise cowherd; and reaching the conclusion by showing a wise bhikkhu.
This is known as the "Method of Sitting in a Circle," and it is the practice followed here by all the teachers.
"By eleven factors, monks"—that is, by eleven divisions of non-virtue. "A herd of cattle" means a group of cows.
"To tend" means to move about after having taken possession of them. "To increase" means to cause them to grow. "In this world" means in this very world.
"He is not one who knows form" means he does not know form either by way of number or by way of color. "He does not know by way of number" means [he does not know] his own...
He does not know the number [of cattle] as "a hundred or a thousand.

When his cows have been seized or have fled, he counts the herd and, thinking, "So many are not seen today," he wanders through two or three villages or into the forest, yet he does not search for them.
Even when other people's cows have entered his own herd, he counts his herd and thinks, "These are so many..."
Thinking, "The cows are not ours," he beats them with a staff and does not drive them out. Thus, his own cows that have strayed remain lost, while he wanders about taking other people's cows.
When the owners of the cattle see this, they say, "This man milked our cows for all this time," and after rebuking him, they take their own cows and depart.
Consequently, his herd of cattle diminishes, and he is deprived even of the five products of the cow.

He is an outsider. In terms of color, he does not know; that is to say, he does not know: "so many cows are white, so many are red, so many are black, so many are pale, so many are brindled, so many are blue. When the cows have been driven away or have fled...
[as before] ...he is also an outsider from the enjoyment of the five products of the cow.
"One unskilled in marks" means he does not know the marks such as the wounds from bows, spears, or spikes inflicted upon the bodies of cows.
When those cows have been slaughtered or have fled, he thinks, "Today, cows with such-and-such marks and such-and-such marks are not to be seen," and so forth...
he is thus excluded even from the enjoyment of the five products of the cow.
"Not one who removes flies": when cattle are struck by stumps, thorns, and the like, sores arise.
Blue flies lay eggs there; these are called "āsāṭikā. One must remove them with a stick and apply medicine, but a foolish cowherd does not do so.
Therefore it is said: "he is not one who removes flies. Of him...
The forests of cattle increase and become deep; small creatures enter their bellies, and the cows, overcome by illness, are unable to eat grass or drink water to their heart's content.
Therein, the milk of the cows ceases, the speed of the bulls diminishes, and there is a threat to the lives of both; thus his herd of cattle also declines... [and so on].
He is excluded even from the five products of the cow.

"He does not dress a wound" means that a wound occurring in a cow, in the manner already described for cattle, should be dressed with medicine and bound with a piece of cloth or rags; the foolish cowherd does not do this. Then, for him—
Suppurations flow from the wounds of the cattle and they rub against one another; because of that, wounds arise on others as well.
Thus, the cattle, overcome by illness, are unable to eat grass to their fill... [and so on] ...he becomes an outsider.
"He does not produce smoke" means that during the rainy season, when gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like are abundant, he does not drive the herd of cattle into the pen.
In various places, smoke ought to be made. An unwise cowherd does not do this;

the herd of cattle, harassed all night by gadflies and other insects, fails to find sleep and instead lies down to sleep in various places such as at the roots of trees in the forest on the following day.
Thus, they are unable to eat grass to their heart’s content... [and so forth]... and they become excluded from the fold.
"He does not know the ford" means he does not know whether the ford is even or uneven, or whether it has a current or is stagnant.
He drives the cows down by way of a non-ford. As they step onto stones and such at the uneven fords, their feet break.
When they have entered a deep ford that has a current, crocodiles and other creatures seize the cows. "Today... [he thinks].
They fall into the habit of saying, "So many cows are lost; today there are so many. In this way, even his herd of cattle diminishes...
[and so on] ...until he is excluded from the five products of the cow.
"He does not know whether it has been drunk" means he knows neither what has been drunk nor what has not been drunk. For by the cowherd [thinking], "This was drunk by this cow..."
One must know what has been drunk and what has not by observing: "This one has not drunk; this one found a place at the watering-place, while that one did not.
Now, during the day, having guarded a herd of cattle in the forest, [the cowherd] goes down into a river or a pond with the thought, "I shall give them water to drink.
Therein, the great bulls and the subordinate bulls, as well as the strong cows—
The weak and aged cattle, having struck one another with their horns or flanks to make way for themselves, enter the water knee-deep and drink as much as they desire.
The rest, finding no space, stand on the bank and drink muddy water mixed with silt, or do not drink at all. Then that cowherd—
Having struck them on the back, he drives them back into the forest again.
There, the cows, not having drunk and wasting away from thirst, are unable to eat as much grass as they require. Consequently, the milk of the cows dries up; the speed of the oxen diminishes...
[and so forth] ...until he becomes an outcast.
"He does not know the path" means he does not know: "This road is level and safe; this one is uneven, dangerous, and fearful.
Passing by the level, safe road, he leads the herd of cattle onto the other path.
There, the cattle—overwhelmed by the scent of lions, tigers, and the like, and by robbers and threats—are like bewildered deer, [with their] necks...
Having driven them out, they stand there; they neither eat grass to their heart’s content nor drink water.
Consequently, the cows’ milk fails... [and so on] ...he becomes an outsider.
"He is not skilled regarding pastures" means that a cowherd must indeed be skilled regarding pastures, whether it be a five-day circuit or—
Or, the seven-day grazing period must be understood. Having grazed the herd of cattle in one direction, they should not be grazed there again on the following day;
for a place frequented by a large herd of cattle becomes as clean and bare as the surface of a drum, and even the water becomes turbid.
Therefore, it is permissible to graze them there again on the fifth or seventh day. For by that much, even the grass—
It sprouts again, and even the water becomes clear;
yet this [cow] does not know of this five-day or seven-day grazing period, but guards her place of protection day after day.
Consequently, her herd of cattle finds no green grass and, eating dry grass, drinks muddy water mixed with silt. In that situation, the milk of the cows—
It wastes away... [and so on] ...it becomes an outsider.

"And he milks it dry" means that a wise cowherd, until the flesh and blood of the calf have been restored, should leave one or two teats untouched and milk with remainder; this [cowherd], however, leaves nothing at all for the calf.
She milks [the cow]. A milk-drinking calf, parched with thirst for milk, unable to remain steady, trembles and falls before its mother and dies.
Seeing her young son, the mother thinks, "My little son does not get to drink his own mother's milk," and out of grief for her son, she is unable to eat grass or drink water to her heart's content.
He is unable [to milk them], and in certain instances the milk dries up. Thus his herd of cows diminishes... [and so on] ...until he is excluded even from the five products of the cow.
Those who provide a place for the cows to drink are the "cow-fathers" (*gopitaro*). Those who lead the cows away, taking them wherever they please, are the "cow-leaders" (*gopariṇāyakā*).
It is not by means of excessive honor that these are [honored]; for a wise cowherd honors such a bull [in this way].

[Others] honor [the bull], give it choice fodder, adorn it with scents and five-finger marks, place garlands upon it, carry golden and silver ornaments on its horns, and having lit a lamp at night, let it lie beneath a cloth canopy.
But this one does not perform even a single such act of honor. Since the bulls receive no extra honor, they do not [attend to] the herd.
They guard [the cattle], yet they do not ward off dangers. Thus his herd of cattle diminishes... and so forth... he is excluded even from the five products of the cow.

"Here" means in this teaching. "He is not one who knows form" means that he does not know, in two ways—either by way of enumeration or by way of origination—the form described as "the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements."
Or, he does not know by way of enumeration, namely: "the eye-base, ear-base, nose-base, tongue-base, body-base, visible-form-base, sound-base, odor-base, taste-base, tangible-object-base;
the femininity-faculty, masculinity-faculty, life-faculty; bodily intimation, verbal intimation; the space-element, water-element;
lightness of matter, malleability of matter, wieldiness of matter, integration of matter, continuity of matter, aging of matter, impermanence of matter; and edible food."
He does not know the twenty-five categories of form as they have come down in the text, thinking "this is nutriment.
Just as that cowherd does not know the nature of the cattle by way of their number, so too is this bhikkhu.
Not knowing form by way of its number, he should discern form, define the formless, discern both form and the formless, and observe the condition.
Having applied the characteristics [of the meditation subject], he is unable to bring the *kammaṭṭhāna* to its culmination.
Just as that cowherd’s herd does not increase, so too in this teaching there is no growth in terms of virtue, concentration, insight, the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna.
And just as that cowherd is excluded from the five products of the cow, even so is this person excluded from the state of one beyond training (*asekha*).
He is excluded from the five aggregates of Dhamma: the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training, and the aggregates of concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Regarding their origination, he does not know: "This much form has a single origination; this much has a double origination."
He does not know: "This much originates from three sources; this much originates from four sources; this much originates from none at all.
Just as that cowherd does not know the appearance of the cows by their color, so too is this bhikkhu.
Not knowing form by way of its origination, even after having discerned form... [as before] ...he remains an outsider.

“He is not skilled in characteristics” means that he does not know that the wholesome and unwholesome kamma described as “the fool is characterized by his kamma; the wise person is characterized by his kamma” is the characteristic of the wise and the fool. Not knowing this, he does not avoid fools and attend upon the wise.

By not avoiding fools and not attending upon the wise, [he fails to understand] what is allowable and what is unallowable, what is wholesome and what is unwholesome, and what is blameworthy and what is blameless.
He does not know what is heavy or light, what is curable or incurable, or what is appropriate and inappropriate.
Not knowing these things, he is unable to take up and develop the subject of meditation (*kammaṭṭhāna*).

Just as that cowherd’s herd does not increase, so too one does not grow in this Dispensation through the aforementioned virtues such as moral discipline (*sīla*). And like that cowherd, [he is deprived] of the five products of the cow.
He stands outside the five aggregates of Dhamma.
"He does not remove the gadfly" means that when "arisen sensual thought" is mentioned, he does not dispel such thoughts as sensual thoughts.
Having failed to remove this unwholesome thought—the gadfly—he wanders about, becoming a slave to his own thoughts.
Having taken up a meditation subject, he is unable to develop it. Just as that cowherd... [omission] ...he becomes an outsider.
"He does not dress the wound" means that by way of the method beginning with "having seen a form with the eye, he grasps at its signs," he grasps at signs in all objects;
thus, just as that cowherd did not dress the wound, so too he fails to exercise restraint.
He does not accomplish it. Wandering about with his doors open, he is unable to take up and develop the meditation subject...
[and so on] ...he becomes an outsider. "He does not produce smoke" means that this cowherd does not produce the smoke of the teaching of the Dhamma;
he does not deliver a discourse on the Dhamma, nor a recitation, nor a seated talk, nor an expression of thanks; therefore, people [do not honor him].
“They do not know him as one who is learned and virtuous. Not knowing his virtues and faults, they do not provide him with support through the four requisites.

Being distressed by a lack of these requisites, he is unable to recite the Buddha’s word, fulfill his duties and obligations, or take up and develop a meditation subject... [and so on] ...until he becomes an outsider.
"He does not know the ford" means that he does not approach learned bhikkhus who serve as a ford. Not approaching them, he does not inquire or question them thus:

"Venerable sir, how should this phrasing be applied? What is the meaning of this statement? What does the text say in this passage? What does the meaning illustrate in this passage? Thus he does not inquire and does not question.
The meaning is that he does not make [the matter] known. Thus, when they have not been questioned by him in this way, they do not reveal what has not been revealed;
they do not explain by dividing it up; they do not clarify what has not been clarified; and they do not make manifest what is not manifest.
And regarding "various kinds of states that are grounds for doubt," they do not dispel even a single doubt among the many types of doubts.
For indeed, it is doubt itself that is called "states that are grounds for doubt. In this context, the meaning is that they do not even resolve a single point of doubt.

Just as that cowherd did not know the ford, so too this bhikkhu, having failed to approach such a ford of great learning, is unable to take up and develop the meditation subject while still harboring doubts. He is like that cowherd who does not know the ford.
He does not know. Not knowing, he asks questions outside his field of competence: having approached an Abhidhamma specialist, he asks about what is allowable and what is unallowable;
having approached a master of the Vinaya, he asks about the delimitation of the material and the immaterial.

Being questioned on matters outside their field, they are unable to explain them. Doubtful himself, he is unable to take up a meditation subject and develop it... [and so on] ...he becomes an outsider.
"He does not know what has been drunk" means that just as that cowherd does not know whether [the cows] have drunk or not, so too he does not know or obtain the joy associated with the Dhamma.
Relying on the basis of meritorious action consisting in hearing, he does not experience its benefit;
having gone to the head of the assembly for hearing the Dhamma, he does not listen attentively; while sitting, he falls asleep or engages in idle chatter.
He is preoccupied with something else. Not listening to the Dhamma with proper attention, he is unable to take up and develop his meditation subject...
[and so on] ...he becomes an outsider.
"He does not know the path" means that, like a cowherd who does not know the right and wrong paths, he does not know the noble [Dhamma], thinking, "This is mundane; this is supramundane."
He does not understand the Eightfold Path as it really is. Not understanding it, he adheres to mundane paths and is unable to produce the supramundane;

thus he remains an outsider. "He is not skilled in his domain" means that, like a cowherd who wanders for five or seven days [away from his herd], he is unskilled in the four foundations of mindfulness.
“He does not understand as it really is: ‘These are mundane; these are supramundane.

Not knowing this, he exercises his own knowledge regarding subtle matters, becomes fixated on mundane foundations of mindfulness, and is unable to produce the supramundane... [he] remains an outsider. He is one who milks dry:
not knowing the proper measure in receiving, he milks [the cow] completely dry. Furthermore, in the section on the exposition (niddesa):
"Inviting by bringing forth" means they invite after having brought [the requisites] forward. In this context, there are two kinds of "bringing forward":

the bringing forward of speech and the bringing forward of requisites. "Bringing forward of speech" refers to people going to a bhikkhu and inviting him, saying, "Venerable sir, please speak what you need.
"Bringing forward of requisites" refers to [offering] robes and so forth, or ghee, fresh butter, molasses, and so forth.
Or, having taken [the requisites], they go to the presence of the bhikkhu and say, "Venerable sir, please accept as much as you need.
In this context, "the bhikkhu does not know moderation" means that the bhikkhu does not know the proper measure regarding those requisites.
According to this method: "The authority of the donor must be understood; the nature of the gift must be understood; and one's own capacity must be understood."
The meaning is that he takes everything they bring, rather than taking only what is measured. People, feeling remorseful, do not bring more and offer it again.
Exhausted by these requisites, he is unable to take up and develop his meditation subject...
[and so on] ...until he becomes an outsider.

"He honors them with superlative honor"—this cowherd does not honor the elder bhikkhus with this superlative honor, consisting of acts of loving-kindness through body and so forth, both openly and in private, as one would toward great bulls.
Consequently, the elders, thinking, "These do not show us due respect," do not win over the junior bhikkhus by means of the two methods of attraction (*saṅgaha*). Nor indeed...

They gather [disciples] through the gathering of the Dhamma, not through the gathering of material things; even when one is exhausted by [the lack of] robes, alms-bowls, requisites belonging to the bowl, or a dwelling place, they do not look after them.
They do not teach the Pāḷi, the commentary, the composition of Dhamma discourses, or the secret texts.
Thus, the novices are entirely deprived of these two kinds of gathering from the elders.
Being unable to find a footing in this teaching, they are not able to establish themselves.
Just as that cowherd’s herd does not increase, so too they do not grow in virtue and the other [perfections].

And just as that cowherd is excluded from the five products of the cow, so too they are excluded from the five aggregates of Dhamma. The bright side (the positive sequence) is to be understood by applying the reverse of what was stated for the dark side.
The Second Chapter on Recollections (*Anussativagga*).
The commentary on the Eleventh Book of the *Aṅguttara Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā*,
titled the *Manorathapūraṇī*, is completed.
The Conclusion:
And to this extent—
having been requested by the Elder Sumati, the Venerable Jotipāla;
While previously dwelling together with me in places such as Kāñcīpura,
and even during the time I was residing in the Mahāvihāra on the excellent island of Tambapaṇṇi,
the True Dhamma was being practiced like a tree that has reached full maturity.
Having reached the far shore of the ocean of the Three Piṭakas, the one of excellent intelligence,
who lives a life of complete purity, namely Jīvaka, made this request;
and thus he began this commentary on the most subtle and supreme Nikāyas for the sake of a discourse on the Dhamma.
Desiring the long endurance of the sublime Dispensation,
this work was completed by extracting the essence from the Great Commentary (Mahā-aṭṭhakathā),
consisting of ninety-four recitation sections (bhāṇavāra) of the Pāḷi.
And because my desire to comment upon all the scriptures has been fulfilled by this work,
it therefore receives the name *Manorathapūraṇī* (The Fulfilled Desire).
Furthermore, the *Visuddhimagga* consists of fifty-nine *bhāṇavāras*.
Since this [work] was composed for the purpose of elucidating the meaning of the scriptures,
therefore, together with that, according to the method of counting verses,
the commentary is to be understood as consisting of one hundred and two and a half recitation sections (bhāṇavāra).
This [work], measuring one hundred and fifty-three sections (*bhāṇavāra*),
elucidates the tradition of those who dwell in the Mahāvihāra; by me,
in composing this, having taken the essence of the *Mūlaṭṭhakathā*.
"By whatever merit has been accumulated, may the world always be happy.
[This was written] by one adorned with supreme purity of faith, wisdom, and energy; endowed with a multitude of virtues such as virtue, conduct, integrity, and gentleness;
capable of plunging into the depths of both his own and other systems of doctrine; possessed of analytical discernment; and [versed] in the various divisions of the Tipiṭaka scriptures.
In the Teacher’s dispensation, together with its commentaries, there were Elders who were lamps of the lineage of the Elders, residents of the Mahāvihāra,

whose intellects were firmly established in superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) adorned with various qualities such as the six direct knowledges (chaḷabhiññā) and the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), who were pre-eminent among speakers, great poets, and masters of speech endowed with sweet and noble words flowing from the bliss produced by perfection of expression through the power of unimpeded knowledge;
and who, through their mastery of exposition, were like great grammarians in the Teacher’s word.

This commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya, named the Manorathapūraṇī, was composed by the Elder named Buddhaghosa— his name having been conferred by his teachers— who is an ornament to the lineage and possesses vast, purified wisdom:
"May it remain in the world as long as those seeking to cross over the world [endure]..."
Thus it is said, leading the sons of noble family toward the purification of the mind:
"As long as even the mere name 'Buddha'— belonging to the Pure-Minded One,
the Tathāgata, the World-Chief, the Great Seer— is current in the world."
The commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya,
entitled Manorathapūraṇī, is thus completed in every respect.
